 /   Unit Tests   \   Many — JVM, fast, isolated
/------------------\

Costs and trade-offs:

Layer Speed Cost Confidence Failure isolation
Unit~msVery lowPartial (mocked deps)Precise
Integration~secondsMediumHigh (real components)Moderate
UI (Espresso)~minutesHighHigh (real UI)Coarse
E2E~10+ minVery highHighest (full stack)Very coarse

Android CI strategy: The allocation follows directly from the cost table. Unit tests run on every commit — they're fast at roughly 2 to 5 minutes. Integration and smoke UI tests run on every PR at medium cost and gate merges. Full E2E runs nightly or pre-release, where the higher cost is acceptable.

Repository Integration Tests

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "A repository integration test wires the real collaborators together but stubs the edges of the system — a real Room in-memory DB, MockWebServer for the network, and zero mocked business logic — so I exercise the full data path: parse the response, map it, persist it, and read it back. The value over unit tests is that it catches the seams unit tests mock away, like a wrong column mapping or a serialization mismatch. The gotcha I watch is teardown — I must shutdown() MockWebServer and close() the DB in @After, or the dispatcher thread and the in-memory DB leak across tests in the reused JVM."

Integration tests wire real components together but substitute external dependencies like the network and hardware. For a repository, the concrete recipe is: a real Room in-memory database, MockWebServer for the network layer, and no mocked business logic. The result is a test that exercises the full data path through real code.

@RunWith(JUnit4::class)
class UserRepositoryIntegrationTest {

    private lateinit var db: AppDatabase
    private lateinit var mockWebServer: MockWebServer
    private lateinit var sut: UserRepositoryImpl

    @Before
    fun setUp() {
        db = Room.inMemoryDatabaseBuilder(
            ApplicationProvider.getApplicationContext(),
            AppDatabase::class.java
        ).allowMainThreadQueries().build()

        mockWebServer = MockWebServer()
        mockWebServer.start()

        val retrofit = Retrofit.Builder()
            .baseUrl(mockWebServer.url("/"))
            .addConverterFactory(GsonConverterFactory.create())
            .build()

        sut = UserRepositoryImpl(
            remoteSource = retrofit.create(UserApi::class.java),
            localSource = db.userDao()
        )
    }

    @After
    fun tearDown() {
        db.close()
        mockWebServer.shutdown()
    }

    @Test
    fun `fetches from network and persists to database`() = runTest {
        mockWebServer.enqueue(
            MockResponse()
                .setResponseCode(200)
                .setBody("""{"id":1,"name":"Alice","email":"alice@test.com"}""")
        )

        val user = sut.getUser(1)

        assertEquals("Alice", user.name)
        assertEquals("Alice", db.userDao().getUser(1)?.name)  // verify persisted
    }
}

Under the hood

MockWebServer isn't a mock object — it's a real HTTP server. On start() it binds an actual ServerSocket on localhost:0 (the OS assigns a free port), and url("/") returns that loopback address. When the test points Retrofit at it, OkHttp opens a genuine TCP socket and writes a real HTTP/1.1 (or HTTP/2) request; the server pulls the next queued MockResponse off an internal BlockingQueue (FIFO, set via enqueue) and writes real response bytes back. So the path under test includes OkHttp's connection pool, the converter factory, and Gson actually parsing the JSON — the only thing faked is what's on the wire.

sut.getUser(1)
  -> Retrofit proxy -> OkHttp -> TCP socket -> 127.0.0.1:<port>
       MockWebServer dequeues MockResponse (FIFO) -> writes real bytes
  -> GsonConverterFactory deserializes -> UserEntity
  -> Room DAO INSERT into in-memory SQLite -> SELECT verifies

This is also why ordering and teardown matter: responses are consumed in enqueue order regardless of which endpoint is called, so a mismatched count silently feeds the wrong body to the wrong call. And because start() leaves an accept thread parked on the socket, skipping shutdown() leaks both the thread and the port across the reused test JVM.

Database Tests (Room)

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "Room DAO tests run against a real in-memory SQLite database, which is fast and self-cleaning since it vanishes on close. The catch interviewers look for is why they need instrumentation: Room generates code that calls Android's bundled SQLite via JNI, and that native library isn't on the plain JVM — so the test lives in androidTest, or I bring in Robolectric to shim the Android runtime and run it on the JVM at the cost of a few seconds of startup. I also test the Flow queries with Turbine to confirm they re-emit when the underlying table changes."

Room tests use an in-memory database, which is fast — but they require instrumentation because Room uses Android's SQLite bindings, which aren't available on the plain JVM. The alternative is Robolectric, which emulates enough of the Android runtime to run them on the JVM.

Pattern:

@RunWith(AndroidJUnit4::class)
class UserDaoTest {

    private lateinit var db: AppDatabase
    private lateinit var dao: UserDao

    @Before
    fun setUp() {
        db = Room.inMemoryDatabaseBuilder(
            ApplicationProvider.getApplicationContext(),
            AppDatabase::class.java
        ).build()
        dao = db.userDao()
    }

    @After
    fun tearDown() {
        db.close()
    }

    @Test
    fun insertAndRetrieveUser() = runTest {
        val user = UserEntity(id = 1, name = "Alice", email = "alice@test.com")
        dao.insert(user)
        val retrieved = dao.getUser(1)
        assertEquals(user, retrieved)
    }

    @Test
    fun updateUserName() = runTest {
        dao.insert(UserEntity(id = 1, name = "Alice", email = "alice@test.com"))
        dao.updateName(1, "Bob")
        assertEquals("Bob", dao.getUser(1)?.name)
    }

    @Test
    fun deleteUser() = runTest {
        dao.insert(UserEntity(id = 1, name = "Alice", email = "alice@test.com"))
        dao.delete(1)
        assertNull(dao.getUser(1))
    }

    @Test
    fun flowEmitsOnInsert() = runTest {
        dao.observeUsers().test {
            assertEquals(emptyList<UserEntity>(), awaitItem())  // initial
            dao.insert(UserEntity(id = 1, name = "Alice", email = "alice@test.com"))
            val users = awaitItem()
            assertEquals(1, users.size)
            cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents()
        }
    }
}

Important: Room's in-memory database runs in-process but still needs Android's SQLite, so these tests must live in /androidTest/ unless you use Robolectric.

Robolectric for JVM Room tests:

@RunWith(RobolectricTestRunner::class)
@Config(sdk = [33])
class UserDaoRobolectricTest {
    // same setup as above — runs on JVM, no emulator needed
}

Robolectric adds roughly 5 to 10 seconds of startup overhead, but removes the device requirement entirely.

Under the hood

Room is an annotation-processor (KSP/kapt) framework: at compile time it generates a UserDao_Impl and an AppDatabase_Impl containing the actual SQL strings and the cursor-to-entity binding code. None of that is reflection at runtime — db.userDao() just returns the generated impl. The reason these can't run on a bare JVM is that the generated code ultimately drives SQLiteDatabase/SQLiteConnection, whose query execution is implemented in native code (libsqlite) reached through JNI. The desktop JVM has no such library loaded, so you either run on a device/emulator or let Robolectric load its shadow + bundled native SQLite.

@Dao interface -> KSP -> UserDao_Impl (raw SQL + cursor binding)
in-memory builder -> SQLiteDatabase(":memory:") -> JNI -> native libsqlite
                                                   (absent on plain JVM)

The observeUsers() Flow re-emits because Room registers an InvalidationTracker: each table maintains a flag in a room_table_modification_log temp table updated by triggers Room installs, and after a write transaction commits the tracker checks those flags and notifies registered observers, which re-run the query. An in-memory database (:memory:) lives entirely in the connection's heap and is discarded the instant the last connection closes — that's why db.close() in @After gives perfect isolation with no file cleanup.

Room Migration Tests

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "Migration tests matter because a migration runs exactly once on a real device, and if it corrupts data the user can never recover it. So I seed a database at the old schema version, run the actual migration, and assert that existing rows survived and new columns got their defaults. The gotcha interviewers love is NOT NULL without a DEFAULT — that crashes on any populated table — and the other one is forgetting MigrationTestHelper validates the resulting schema against Room's exported JSON, which is why you have to commit those schema files."

Migrations are critical because they run exactly once on a user's real device. A bad migration corrupts data that the user can never get back. Migration tests verify that the schema transition is correct, that existing data survives, and that new columns have the right defaults.

Setup:

androidTestImplementation "androidx.room:room-testing:$room_version"
@RunWith(AndroidJUnit4::class)
class MigrationTest {

    @get:Rule
    val migrationTestHelper = MigrationTestHelper(
        InstrumentationRegistry.getInstrumentation(),
        AppDatabase::class.java
    )

    @Test
    fun migrate1to2() {
        // Create DB at version 1
        var db = migrationTestHelper.createDatabase(TEST_DB_NAME, 1)

        // Insert data in version-1 schema
        db.execSQL("INSERT INTO users (id, name) VALUES (1, 'Alice')")
        db.close()

        // Run migration from 1 to 2
        db = migrationTestHelper.runMigrationsAndValidate(
            TEST_DB_NAME,
            2,
            true,  // validateDroppedTables
            MIGRATION_1_2
        )

        // Verify data survived migration
        val cursor = db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = 1")
        assertTrue(cursor.moveToFirst())
        assertEquals("Alice", cursor.getString(cursor.getColumnIndex("name")))
        // Verify new column added by migration
        assertNotEquals(-1, cursor.getColumnIndex("email"))
        cursor.close()
        db.close()
    }

    companion object {
        private const val TEST_DB_NAME = "migration_test_db"
    }
}

Migration definition:

val MIGRATION_1_2 = object : Migration(1, 2) {
    override fun migrate(db: SupportSQLiteDatabase) {
        db.execSQL("ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN email TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT ''")
    }
}

What migration tests verify:

  1. The schema at version N matches what Room expects.
  2. Existing data is preserved — not dropped or corrupted.
  3. New columns have correct defaults.
  4. New tables exist after migration.
  5. Old tables are dropped where specified.

Common migration bugs:

  • Adding a NOT NULL column without a DEFAULT value — the migration crashes on any non-empty table.
  • A column type mismatch between the migration SQL and the Room entity annotation.
  • A missing migration path — for example, providing 1→2 and 2→3 individually but no direct 1→3 path for users skipping versions.

Under the hood

createDatabase uses Room's exported schema JSON (the files emitted by the room.schemaLocation annotation-processor argument, committed under schemas/) to physically build a SQLite file whose CREATE TABLE statements exactly match version N — it does not run your entity definitions. runMigrationsAndValidate then applies your Migration.migrate() SQL against that real SQLite database, and afterward reads SQLite's own catalog (PRAGMA table_info, PRAGMA foreign_key_list, PRAGMA index_list) and diffs it against the expected version-N+1 schema JSON. A mismatch throws IllegalStateException — this is why a column type that differs between your migration SQL and your @Entity (e.g. you ADD COLUMN email TEXT but annotate the field non-null with a different affinity) fails validation even when the SQL itself succeeds.

exported schema JSON (v1) ──► createDatabase ──► real .db file at v1
                                                      │
                          your Migration(1,2).migrate(SupportSQLiteDatabase)
                                                      ▼
                              PRAGMA table_info / index_list  ──diff──►  expected schema JSON (v2)
                                                      │
                                          mismatch → IllegalStateException

SupportSQLiteDatabase here is the framework SQLite binding (FrameworkSQLiteDatabase wrapping android.database.sqlite.SQLiteDatabase), so execSQL goes straight through JNI to the device's bundled SQLite engine — the test exercises the same C library that runs in production.

API Contract Tests with MockWebServer

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "MockWebServer spins up a real HTTP server on localhost in the test process, so my Retrofit client does actual socket I/O against it — real headers, real status codes, real JSON parsing. That catches things a mock can't: a misspelled JSON field, a broken interceptor, wrong serialization. I point Retrofit at mockWebServer.url('/'), enqueue canned responses, and then call takeRequest() to assert on what my client actually sent. The trade-off is it's milliseconds-per-call slower than a pure mock and it doesn't validate the real backend — that's still E2E's job."

OkHttp's MockWebServer runs a real HTTP server in-process. Your Retrofit client makes actual HTTP requests to it — real serialization, real headers, real status codes — which means these tests verify the contract between your app and the API in a way that pure mocks cannot.

Dependency:

testImplementation "com.squareup.okhttp3:mockwebserver:4.x.x"

Full example:

@RunWith(JUnit4::class)
class UserApiContractTest {

    private val mockWebServer = MockWebServer()

    private lateinit var api: UserApi

    @Before
    fun setUp() {
        mockWebServer.start()
        val retrofit = Retrofit.Builder()
            .baseUrl(mockWebServer.url("/"))
            .addConverterFactory(GsonConverterFactory.create())
            .build()
        api = retrofit.create(UserApi::class.java)
    }

    @After
    fun tearDown() {
        mockWebServer.shutdown()
    }

    @Test
    fun `GET user returns parsed User`() = runTest {
        mockWebServer.enqueue(
            MockResponse()
                .setResponseCode(200)
                .addHeader("Content-Type", "application/json")
                .setBody("""{"id":1,"name":"Alice","email":"alice@test.com"}""")
        )

        val user = api.getUser(1)

        assertEquals(1, user.id)
        assertEquals("Alice", user.name)

        val request = mockWebServer.takeRequest()
        assertEquals("GET", request.method)
        assertEquals("/users/1", request.path)
    }

    @Test
    fun `401 response throws AuthException`() = runTest {
        mockWebServer.enqueue(MockResponse().setResponseCode(401))

        assertFailsWith<AuthException> {
            api.getUser(1)
        }
    }

    @Test
    fun `network timeout propagates as IOException`() = runTest {
        mockWebServer.enqueue(
            MockResponse()
                .setBodyDelay(5_000, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
                .setBody("{}")
        )

        assertFailsWith<IOException> {
            api.getUser(1)  // client timeout < 5s
        }
    }

    @Test
    fun `request includes authorization header`() = runTest {
        mockWebServer.enqueue(MockResponse().setResponseCode(200).setBody("{}"))

        api.getUser(1)

        val request = mockWebServer.takeRequest()
        assertTrue(request.getHeader("Authorization")?.startsWith("Bearer ") ?: false)
    }
}

What MockWebServer enables that mocks cannot:

  • It exercises OkHttp interceptors — auth, logging, retry — which pure mocks skip entirely.
  • It tests the JSON deserialization path: if a field name has a typo, a mock wouldn't catch it, but MockWebServer would.
  • It tests HTTP error code handling end-to-end.
  • It lets you inspect the actual request — headers, query params, body — to verify the client is constructing it correctly.

Trade-offs:

  • Slower than pure mocks, roughly 50ms per request versus microseconds.
  • More fragile to API shape changes — you have to keep test JSON in sync with the actual API.
  • Doesn't test the real backend — that's what E2E tests are for.

Under the hood

MockWebServer.start() binds a real ServerSocket on 127.0.0.1 at an OS-assigned ephemeral port (port 0 → kernel picks a free one), spins up a dispatcher thread to accept connections, and url("/") returns an HttpUrl pointing at that loopback port. Enqueued MockResponse objects sit in a BlockingQueue; the default QueueDispatcher pops one per incoming request and writes raw HTTP/1.1 (or HTTP/2) bytes back over the socket. Your Retrofit call therefore goes through the full OkHttp stack — interceptor chain, connection pool, Okio buffered socket source/sink, and the converter's JsonReader parsing the response body — none of which is stubbed. Each received request is parsed into a RecordedRequest and pushed onto another queue that takeRequest() drains (blocking up to a timeout), which is how you can assert on the method, path, headers, and body bytes the client actually transmitted.

api.getUser(1)
  └─ Retrofit invocation handler builds Request
       └─ OkHttp interceptor chain (auth/logging/retry)
            └─ TCP connect to 127.0.0.1:<ephemeral>  ◄─── MockWebServer ServerSocket
                 └─ QueueDispatcher pops next MockResponse → writes HTTP bytes
            └─ converter parses body → User
  takeRequest() ◄── RecordedRequest (method, path, headers, body) recorded on accept

Hilt Test Injection

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "Hilt owns the whole dependency graph, so for tests I don't hand-build fakes — I swap bindings inside the graph. @HiltAndroidTest plus HiltAndroidRule regenerates the components against a HiltTestApplication, and I replace a production module with @TestInstallIn(replaces = ...), or for a one-off I use @BindValue to push a field straight into the graph. The classic gotcha is rule ordering: the Hilt rule has to be order = 0 so injection finishes before ActivityScenarioRule launches the Activity, otherwise the component isn't ready when the Activity asks for its dependencies."

Hilt manages the entire dependency graph in production. The testing challenge is that you need to swap out specific components with fakes — without touching any production wiring. Hilt provides dedicated annotations for exactly that.

Hilt testing annotations:

// Marks a test class to use Hilt injection
@HiltAndroidTest
@RunWith(AndroidJUnit4::class)
class UserRepositoryHiltTest {

    @get:Rule
    val hiltRule = HiltAndroidRule(this)

    @Inject
    lateinit var userRepository: UserRepository  // real binding from graph

    @Before
    fun setUp() {
        hiltRule.inject()
    }
}

Replacing modules with test fakes:

// Production module
@Module
@InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
object NetworkModule {
    @Provides
    fun provideUserApi(): UserApi = Retrofit.Builder()...build().create(UserApi::class.java)
}

// Test replacement
@Module
@TestInstallIn(
    components = [SingletonComponent::class],
    replaces = [NetworkModule::class]
)
object FakeNetworkModule {
    @Provides
    fun provideUserApi(): UserApi = FakeUserApi()
}

@UninstallModules — removes a module for a specific test class without a replacement:

@HiltAndroidTest
@UninstallModules(AnalyticsModule::class)
class SomeTest {
    // AnalyticsModule is gone; inject your own fake manually or via @BindValue
}

@BindValue — injects a field directly into Hilt's binding graph from test:

@HiltAndroidTest
class SomeTest {
    @BindValue
    @JvmField
    val fakeUserApi: UserApi = FakeUserApi()
}

Testing Activities/Fragments with Hilt:

@HiltAndroidTest
class MainActivityTest {

    @get:Rule(order = 0)
    val hiltRule = HiltAndroidRule(this)

    @get:Rule(order = 1)
    val activityRule = ActivityScenarioRule(MainActivity::class.java)

    // ...
}

Note: @HiltAndroidTest requires that a @HiltAndroidApp Application exists. For tests, use HiltTestApplication — Hilt provides it — as the test application class. Configure it in the AndroidManifest.xml for the androidTest source set.

HiltAndroidRule order matters when combining multiple rules. Set order = 0 for the Hilt rule so Hilt injects before any Activity launches.

Under the hood

These annotations are processed at compile time by Hilt's annotation processor (running on top of Dagger). @HiltAndroidTest makes the processor generate a per-test Dagger component (e.g. a test variant of SingletonComponent) instead of relying on the app's single generated graph, which is why each test class can have a different binding set. @TestInstallIn and @UninstallModules work by altering which @Module classes are aggregated into that generated component: replaces tells the processor to drop the named production module's @Provides methods and substitute the test module's, all resolved statically — no runtime reflection or bytecode rewriting. @BindValue is the one runtime-ish piece: the processor generates a synthetic @Module whose @Provides method returns the field value read from your test instance, so the binding is created when hiltRule.inject() runs and reads that field. Rule ordering is enforced by JUnit's RuleChain: @get:Rule(order = 0) makes JUnit wrap the Hilt rule as the outermost statement, so its before() (which builds the component and performs field injection) executes before ActivityScenarioRule.before() launches the Activity via ActivityScenario, guaranteeing the graph exists when the Activity's onCreate triggers member injection.

JUnit RuleChain (outer → inner):
  HiltAndroidRule(order=0).before()   → build test component, inject @Inject/@BindValue fields
    ActivityScenarioRule(order=1).before() → ActivityScenario.launch(...) → Activity.onCreate
                                              → Hilt member-injects Activity from ready graph

CI Strategy

A well-structured CI test strategy has three goals. First, fast feedback on every PR — under 10 minutes for blocking checks. Second, full regression coverage before any release. And third, a quarantine system so flaky tests don't block the pipeline while they're being investigated.

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "My CI strategy maps directly onto the test pyramid: unit and integration tests gate every PR because they're fast and deterministic, UI smoke tests cover only the critical flows on the PR, and the slow full UI and device-farm suites run pre-release where a longer runtime is acceptable. To keep PR feedback under ten minutes I shard instrumentation tests across parallel emulators and merge the results. The discipline part is flaky-test quarantine — I tag and exclude a flake with a linked bug, but with a hard fix-or-delete policy so the quarantine list doesn't quietly become a graveyard of untrusted tests."

Recommended layer allocation:

Layer Trigger Time budget Gates PR?
Unit testsEvery commit2–5 minYes
Integration (Room + MockWebServer)Every PR5–10 minYes
UI smoke tests (critical flows)Every PR10–20 minYes
Full UI regression suitePre-release / nightly1–2 hoursNo (blocks release)
E2E on real device farmPre-release2–4 hoursNo (blocks release)

Test sharding in CI:

./gradlew connectedAndroidTest \
  -Pandroid.testInstrumentationRunnerArguments.numShards=4 \
  -Pandroid.testInstrumentationRunnerArguments.shardIndex=0

Run on 4 parallel emulators and combine results.

Flaky test quarantine:

  • Tag with @FlakyTest(bugId = "ZD-123") to exclude a test from the blocking suite while it's under investigation.
  • Never leave quarantined tests sitting indefinitely — set a policy of fix or delete within 2 sprints.

Test result aggregation: Use allure or junit-merge to combine results across parallel shards into a single report.

Under the hood

numShards/shardIndex are consumed by AndroidJUnitRunner, not Gradle: the runner enumerates every discovered test method, computes a stable hash of each, and runs only those where hash % numShards == shardIndex. That partition is deterministic and disjoint, so N machines each running a different shardIndex collectively run every test exactly once with no coordination — which is why merging is just concatenating each shard's TEST-*.xml JUnit reports. @FlakyTest is a JUnit filter annotation: the runner's -e annotation/-e notAnnotation arguments (or a CI filter) drop annotated methods from the run set before execution, so a quarantined test never even instantiates. Each shard typically targets its own emulator/device instance to avoid contention on the single ADB/instrumentation channel per device.

AndroidJUnitRunner discovers M test methods
   for each test:  shard = stableHash(testName) % numShards
   run if shard == shardIndex            ── disjoint partition, no overlap
emulator 0 → shard 0 ─┐
emulator 1 → shard 1 ─┤ each emits TEST-*.xml
emulator 2 → shard 2 ─┤
emulator 3 → shard 3 ─┘ → junit-merge / allure → single aggregated report

How to Test a Login Flow

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "I'd answer this as three tests at three layers, not one. Unit tests on the ViewModel and interactor cover validation and the success/error mapping — blank email, token returned. A repository integration test with MockWebServer proves the 200 actually persists the token and a 401 maps to invalid-credentials. Then one or two UI tests with a FakeAuthRepository bound via Hilt verify that a success navigates to home and a failure shows the error. The key principle I'd state out loud: never hit the real backend — the server isn't my system under test, my app's behavior is."

This is the canonical multi-layer testing interview question. The right answer isn't one test — it's three tests at three different layers, each catching a different class of bug.

The flow covers: email input, password input, submit, API call, token storage, and navigation to home.

Layer 1: Unit tests (fastest)

// ViewModel unit test
@Test
fun `login shows error when email is blank`() = runTest {
    sut.login(email = "", password = "password")
    advanceUntilIdle()
    val state = sut.uiState.value
    assertTrue(state is LoginUiState.ValidationError)
    assertEquals("Email is required", (state as LoginUiState.ValidationError).message)
}

// Use case unit test
@Test
fun `login interactor returns token on success`() = runTest {
    coEvery { fakeAuthApi.login(any()) } returns LoginResponse(token = "abc123")
    val result = loginInteractor("user@test.com", "password")
    assertEquals("abc123", result.token)
}

Layer 2: Repository integration test (MockWebServer)

@Test
fun `login stores token in preferences after successful API call`() = runTest {
    mockWebServer.enqueue(
        MockResponse().setResponseCode(200)
            .setBody("""{"token":"abc123","userId":1}""")
    )

    val result = authRepository.login("user@test.com", "password")

    assertTrue(result is AuthResult.Success)
    assertEquals("abc123", tokenStore.getToken())
}

@Test
fun `login returns error on 401`() = runTest {
    mockWebServer.enqueue(MockResponse().setResponseCode(401))
    val result = authRepository.login("user@test.com", "wrongpassword")
    assertTrue(result is AuthResult.InvalidCredentials)
}

Layer 3: UI instrumented test (Espresso/Compose)

@HiltAndroidTest
@RunWith(AndroidJUnit4::class)
class LoginScreenTest {

    @get:Rule(order = 0) val hiltRule = HiltAndroidRule(this)

    @BindValue @JvmField
    val authRepository: AuthRepository = FakeAuthRepository()

    @get:Rule(order = 1)
    val activityRule = ActivityScenarioRule(LoginActivity::class.java)

    @Test
    fun successfulLoginNavigatesToHome() {
        (authRepository as FakeAuthRepository).setLoginResult(AuthResult.Success)

        onView(withId(R.id.email_field)).perform(typeText("user@test.com"), closeSoftKeyboard())
        onView(withId(R.id.password_field)).perform(typeText("password"), closeSoftKeyboard())
        onView(withId(R.id.login_button)).perform(click())

        onView(withId(R.id.home_feed)).check(matches(isDisplayed()))
    }

    @Test
    fun failedLoginShowsErrorMessage() {
        (authRepository as FakeAuthRepository).setLoginResult(AuthResult.InvalidCredentials)

        onView(withId(R.id.email_field)).perform(typeText("user@test.com"), closeSoftKeyboard())
        onView(withId(R.id.password_field)).perform(typeText("wrong"), closeSoftKeyboard())
        onView(withId(R.id.login_button)).perform(click())

        onView(withId(R.id.error_message))
            .check(matches(isDisplayed()))
            .check(matches(withText("Invalid email or password")))
    }
}

What NOT to do: Never test login with real network calls. The backend is not your system under test — you're testing your app's behavior, not the server's.

Under the hood

The three layers run on entirely different machinery, which is why they catch different bug classes. Layer 1 runs on a local JVM (no Android framework) under runTest, whose TestCoroutineScheduler virtualizes the clock — advanceUntilIdle() drains all queued coroutine continuations on the test dispatcher instantly rather than waiting real time, so there is no actual concurrency and assertions are deterministic. Layer 2 still runs on the JVM but adds real socket I/O to a loopback MockWebServer, exercising serialization and HTTP status mapping. Layer 3 runs on a device/emulator inside an instrumentation APK; Espresso's value-add is its UiController, which loops on the main thread's MessageQueue and only proceeds when the app is idle — no pending main-thread messages and all registered IdlingResources reporting idle — which is what makes onView(...).check(...) reliable instead of racing the UI. The @BindValue FakeAuthRepository is wired in by Hilt's generated test component so the production network path is never touched, and Espresso ViewMatchers/ViewActions resolve views by walking the view hierarchy from the activity's decor view.

Layer 1  JVM only        runTest virtual clock → continuations drained, 0 real ms
Layer 2  JVM + loopback  Retrofit ↔ MockWebServer socket → real JSON + status mapping
Layer 3  emulator        Espresso UiController waits for MessageQueue idle + IdlingResources
                         FakeAuthRepository bound via Hilt test component (no real network)

How to Test Network Error Handling

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "Network error handling isn't one scenario — it's a matrix: timeouts, no connectivity, 4xx, 5xx, malformed JSON, and cancellation, each tested at the right layer. At the ViewModel layer I make the interactor throw an IOException and assert the UI goes to a retryable error state. At the integration layer MockWebServer is the star: SocketPolicy lets me simulate a connection refused, a mid-response disconnect, or a never-responding server for timeouts, and a setBodyDelay to force a SocketTimeoutException. The nuance is matching the exception type the layer below actually surfaces — a timeout is a SocketTimeoutException, a bad body is a parse exception — not just catching a generic Exception."

Network error handling is a broad category — it covers timeouts, no connectivity, HTTP 4xx and 5xx responses, malformed JSON, and cancelled requests. Each of these requires a different test at a different layer.

Unit test — ViewModel handles errors:

@Test
fun `network error shows retry UI`() = runTest {
    coEvery { getUserInteractor(any()) } throws IOException("Connection refused")

    sut.loadUser(1)
    advanceUntilIdle()

    val state = sut.uiState.value
    assertTrue(state is UiState.Error)
    assertTrue((state as UiState.Error).isRetryable)
}

Integration test — MockWebServer 500:

@Test
fun `server error propagates as ServerException`() = runTest {
    mockWebServer.enqueue(
        MockResponse().setResponseCode(500).setBody("""{"error":"Internal server error"}""")
    )
    assertFailsWith<ServerException> {
        api.getUser(1)
    }
}

Integration test — malformed JSON:

@Test
fun `malformed JSON throws ParseException`() = runTest {
    mockWebServer.enqueue(
        MockResponse().setResponseCode(200).setBody("not valid json")
    )
    assertFailsWith<JsonParseException> {
        api.getUser(1)
    }
}

Integration test — network timeout:

@Test
fun `request timeout propagates as SocketTimeoutException`() = runTest {
    mockWebServer.enqueue(
        MockResponse()
            .setBodyDelay(10_000, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
            .setBody("{}")
    )

    // OkHttpClient configured with 1s timeout
    assertFailsWith<SocketTimeoutException> {
        api.getUser(1)
    }
}

Integration test — no connectivity (simulate with throttling):

@Test
fun `socket disconnect mid-response throws IOException`() = runTest {
    mockWebServer.enqueue(
        MockResponse()
            .setBody("partial")
            .setSocketPolicy(SocketPolicy.DISCONNECT_DURING_RESPONSE_BODY)
    )
    assertFailsWith<IOException> {
        api.getUser(1)
    }
}

MockWebServer SocketPolicy options:

  • DISCONNECT_AT_START — connection refused (simulates no network)
  • DISCONNECT_AFTER_REQUEST — disconnects before sending response
  • DISCONNECT_DURING_RESPONSE_BODY — partial response
  • NO_RESPONSE — server accepts connection but never responds (timeout)
  • RESET_STREAM_AT_START — TCP RST

Retry logic test:

@Test
fun `repository retries 3 times on 503`() = runTest {
    repeat(2) {
        mockWebServer.enqueue(MockResponse().setResponseCode(503))
    }
    mockWebServer.enqueue(MockResponse().setResponseCode(200).setBody("""{"id":1,"name":"Alice"}"""))

    val user = retryableRepository.getUser(1)

    assertEquals(3, mockWebServer.requestCount)
    assertEquals("Alice", user.name)
}

Under the hood

Each SocketPolicy maps to a concrete manipulation of the TCP socket by MockWebServer's dispatcher thread, which is why the resulting exception types differ. DISCONNECT_AT_START closes (or refuses) the socket before any bytes flow, surfacing in OkHttp as a connection failure (ConnectException/IOException). NO_RESPONSE accepts the connection but writes nothing, so OkHttp's read on the Okio source eventually trips the configured readTimeout and throws SocketTimeoutException — the same mechanism setBodyDelay exploits by stalling the body write past the client's timeout. DISCONNECT_DURING_RESPONSE_BODY writes a partial body then drops the connection, so the OkHttp source hits EOF before the declared/expected length and throws an IOException. Malformed JSON gets through the socket layer intact and only fails deeper in the stack, when the converter's streaming parser (Gson's JsonReader / Moshi's JsonReader) encounters an unexpected token. Crucially, OkHttp does not automatically retry HTTP 5xx responses — retryOnConnectionFailure only covers transport-level failures — so the "retries 3 times on 503" test is exercising your application-level retry interceptor or repository loop, which is exactly why requestCount is the right assertion.

SocketPolicy            socket action                     exception surfaced
DISCONNECT_AT_START     refuse/close before bytes      →  ConnectException / IOException
NO_RESPONSE             accept, never write            →  SocketTimeoutException (readTimeout)
setBodyDelay > timeout  stall body write               →  SocketTimeoutException
DISCONNECT_DURING_BODY  partial body then close        →  IOException (unexpected EOF)
malformed body (200)    full bytes delivered           →  JsonReader parse exception (in converter)
5xx (200-level socket)  clean response, status 503     →  no OkHttp auto-retry → app-level retry loop

Quick-Reference Interview Cheat Sheet

Unit Testing

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "Unit tests cover the pieces that hold logic but no Android framework — ViewModels, use cases, repositories, mappers, and pure functions — so they run on the JVM in milliseconds with no emulator. The discipline that makes coroutine tests deterministic is injecting dispatchers and using runTest with a TestDispatcher, because that swaps the real scheduler for a virtual clock I can fast-forward with advanceUntilIdle(). The gotcha interviewers love is StandardTestDispatcher versus Unconfined: Standard queues coroutines so I have to advance time explicitly, while Unconfined runs them eagerly inline — pick Standard when you want to assert intermediate states, Unconfined when you just want the final result."
Question Answer
What should be unit tested?ViewModels, use cases, repositories, mappers, validators, pure functions
Fake vs mock?Fake = working impl; mock = programmed with expectations. Use fakes for domain logic, mocks for side effects.
How do you test coroutine code?runTest + TestDispatcher; inject dispatchers; use advanceUntilIdle()
How do you test Flow emissions?toList() for finite flows; Turbine .test {} for ViewModel state/events
Why unmockkAll()?Prevents mock leaks between test classes in same JVM worker
StandardTestDispatcher vs UnconfinedTestDispatcher?Standard: explicit advance needed. Unconfined: runs eagerly inline.

Under the hood

runTest builds a TestScope backed by a TestCoroutineScheduler — a virtual-time clock, not the wall clock. Both test dispatchers share that single scheduler; they differ only in when they dispatch. StandardTestDispatcher enqueues every resumption into the scheduler's task queue and runs nothing until you call advanceUntilIdle(), advanceTimeBy(), or runCurrent(), which drain the queue in when-timestamp order. UnconfinedTestDispatcher resumes coroutines eagerly on the current thread up to their first real suspension point, so child coroutines execute as soon as they're launched. Crucially, delay() does not sleep — the dispatcher intercepts it and registers a when timestamp on the scheduler, so advanceTimeBy(10_000) advances "10 seconds" instantly. runTest also installs an auto-advancing mechanism and asserts at the end that no coroutines were left uncompleted, throwing UncompletedCoroutinesError if a launched job never finished.

runTest
  └─ TestScope
       └─ TestCoroutineScheduler  (virtual clock, priority queue keyed by `when`)
            ├─ StandardTestDispatcher  → enqueue, drain only on advance*/runCurrent
            └─ UnconfinedTestDispatcher → resume eagerly on current thread

MockK's unmockkAll() matters because mockkStatic/mockkObject install a JVM-wide bytecode/objenesis transformation on the class — the test JVM worker is reused across classes (Gradle's forkEvery is not 1), so an un-reset static mock stays patched into the shared classloader and silently corrupts later, unrelated tests.

UI Testing

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "UI tests drive the real screen on a device or emulator, and which framework I use depends on what rendered it — Espresso walks the View hierarchy, while Compose tests query the semantics tree that composables publish. The thing seniors get asked about is flakiness: it almost always comes from unsynchronized async work, animations, real network, or shared state between tests. My fixes are to disable animations, hook async work into Espresso's idling mechanism — Idling Resources or awaitIdle() in Compose — mock the network, and isolate test data so tests don't leak into each other. And I'm deliberate about what I don't test in UI: business logic and platform behavior belong in unit tests, not slow instrumentation runs."
Question Answer
Espresso vs Compose testing?Espresso: View hierarchy. Compose: semantics tree. Use each for the UI framework that rendered the screen.
Why are UI tests flaky?Async ops unsynchronized, animations, shared state, real network, emulator instability
How to reduce flakiness?Disable animations, use Idling Resources / awaitIdle(), mock network, isolate test data
What not to test in UI?Business logic, platform behavior, pixel metrics, third-party SDKs, animations themselves
What is an Idling Resource?Callback that tells Espresso "app is busy/idle" so it waits before proceeding

Under the hood

Espresso's core guarantee is synchronization: every onView(...).perform/check posts work onto the main thread's MessageQueue and then blocks until the app is idle. It does this through a UiController that watches three things — the MessageQueue (via the Looper's IdleHandler and an internal queue interrogation), the AsyncTask thread pool, and any registered IdlingResources. Only when all report idle does Espresso dispatch the next interaction, which is why custom async work (custom thread pools, OkHttp dispatchers) is invisible to Espresso unless you wrap it in an IdlingResource whose isIdleNow() returns false while busy and calls back via ResourceCallback when done. Animations break this because a running Animator/ValueAnimator keeps posting frame callbacks through the Choreographer, so the queue never appears idle (or the view's final state isn't settled) — hence disabling them at the system level.

Compose has no View hierarchy, so it can't be walked by Espresso. Instead each composable can attach a SemanticsConfiguration (via Modifier.semantics, testTag, content descriptions), and these merge into a SemanticsTree. ComposeTestRule matchers like onNodeWithText query that tree, and synchronization runs through the Compose Recomposer / Snapshot system: waitForIdle()/awaitIdle() pumps the test clock and blocks until there are no pending recompositions, layout, or draw passes. Under Espresso interop, Compose registers itself as an IdlingResource so the two frameworks stay coordinated.

onView(matcher).perform(click())
   → UiController.loopMainThreadUntilIdle()
        ↳ MessageQueue idle?  AsyncTask pool idle?  all IdlingResources idle?
        ↳ when ALL true → inject the MotionEvent / ViewAction

Integration / E2E

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "I think about this as the test pyramid — lots of fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, very few full UI and E2E tests, because the higher you go the slower and flakier they get. For integration I lean on MockWebServer rather than mocking the API class, because it exercises the whole stack — interceptors, JSON deserialization, HTTP error handling, even request construction — against a real socket. So a login flow gets tested at three levels: unit for the ViewModel validation and use case, integration for the repository talking to MockWebServer, and a thin UI test with a fake repository. The detail interviewers probe is Room migrations: I use MigrationTestHelper to create the DB at the old version, write data, run the migration, then assert both the schema and that the data survived."
Question Answer
Test pyramid?Many unit → some integration → few UI → very few E2E
How to test Room migrations?MigrationTestHelper: create DB at version N, insert data, run migration, assert schema + data
How to test network errors?MockWebServer with SocketPolicy (disconnect, timeout, 500s, malformed JSON)
How to test login flow?Unit: ViewModel validation + use case. Integration: repository + MockWebServer. UI: fake repository + ActivityScenario.
What does MockWebServer add over mocks?Tests interceptors, JSON deserialization, HTTP error handling, request construction end-to-end
Hilt in tests?@HiltAndroidTest, HiltAndroidRule, @TestInstallIn to replace modules, @BindValue for per-test bindings

Under the hood

MockWebServer is a real HTTP server: it binds a ServerSocket on localhost, accepts connections on a background thread, and serves responses you enqueue() from a FIFO BlockingQueue. Because the client connects over an actual socket, the entire OkHttp/Retrofit stack runs for real — DNS to localhost, the connection pool, every Interceptor, the converter factory (Moshi/Gson/kotlinx) deserializing the byte stream — which a mocked ApiService skips entirely. SocketPolicy lets you inject failures at the transport layer: DISCONNECT_AT_START closes the socket before sending bytes, NO_RESPONSE hangs to trigger read timeouts, and you can return malformed bodies to exercise converter-level parse failures — fault modes a return-stubbed mock can never reproduce.

Room's MigrationTestHelper is a JUnit TestRule that reads the schema JSON Room exports at compile time (the room.schemaLocation annotation-processor arg). createDatabase(name, version) materializes a real SQLite file using the exported schema for that version so you can insert legacy rows; runMigrationsAndValidate(name, newVersion, validateDroppedTables, migration) then opens that file with SupportSQLiteOpenHelper, applies your Migration.migrate() SQL, and diffs the resulting live schema (via PRAGMA table_info / PRAGMA foreign_key_list) against the exported schema for newVersion — throwing if columns, indices, or types don't match, while your own assertions confirm the data survived.

MigrationTestHelper
  1. createDatabase(v1)  → real .db file built from exported schema_v1.json
  2. insert legacy rows  → SupportSQLiteDatabase.execSQL(...)
  3. runMigrationsAndValidate(v2, MIGRATION_1_2)
        ↳ apply your migrate() SQL
        ↳ compare live PRAGMA schema vs exported schema_v2.json  → throws on mismatch
  4. query + assert rows preserved

Hilt's test machinery rewrites the dependency graph at compile time: @HiltAndroidTest makes the annotation processor generate a per-test ApplicationComponent against a HiltTestApplication; HiltAndroidRule.inject() performs members-injection into the test instance. @TestInstallIn generates a replacement module that uninstalls the production module from the component, and @BindValue binds a field's runtime value straight into the graph — so you swap fakes without touching production wiring, all resolved by Dagger's generated factory code, not reflection.

12.1 Gradle Basics

Project vs Module

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "A Gradle project is the whole build rooted at settings.gradle.kts, and a module — Gradle calls it a subproject — is an independently buildable unit you declare with include. The reason we split into modules isn't aesthetics: each module is its own compilation unit, so a change in :feature:search doesn't force :core:network to recompile. The gotcha interviewers probe is that modularization is only a win if your dependency graph stays acyclic and you keep api leakage in check — otherwise you get recompile cascades and you've paid the complexity cost for nothing."

Definition

A Gradle project is the top-level build — the root build.gradle(.kts) and settings.gradle(.kts) files represent it. A Gradle module (Gradle calls them "subprojects") is an independently buildable unit declared in settings.gradle.kts via include(":moduleName").

How it works

settings.gradle.kts
  rootProject.name = "MyApp"
  include(":app")
  include(":feature:search")
  include(":core:network")

Each module has its own build.gradle.kts. The root project aggregates them. Gradle resolves the dependency graph by walking include declarations and evaluating each module's build script.

Under the hood

settings.gradle.kts is evaluated first by the Settings object during the initialization phase, before any build.gradle.kts is touched. Each include(":a:b") creates a ProjectDescriptor and maps the path to a directory (default a/b). Gradle then builds an in-memory Project object tree and runs the configuration phase, evaluating every project's build script to register tasks and wire dependencies into a single TaskExecutionGraph (the DAG). Modules are nodes in a project-dependency graph; Gradle topologically sorts it, which is exactly why a cycle is fatal — there is no valid linear order to execute.

init phase:    Settings → ProjectDescriptor tree
config phase:  each Project.evaluate() → tasks + dependency edges
exec phase:    topological sort of TaskExecutionGraph → run

Android implications

  • :app is almost always the only com.android.application module.
  • Libraries are com.android.library modules.
  • Pure Kotlin/Java logic (no Android SDK) can be org.jetbrains.kotlin.jvm — these build fastest because they skip Android resource/manifest processing.
  • Modules can depend on each other: :app → :feature:search → :core:network.

Trade-offs

Monolithic (single module) Multi-module
Simple setupComplex dependency graph
Full recompile on any changeIncremental compilation per module
Slower CI builds as codebase growsParallelisable builds
Easier initial navigationHigher initial investment

Failure modes

  • Circular dependencies: Gradle will throw Circular dependency between the following tasks. Break cycles by extracting shared code into a :core module.
  • Accidentally including a module that doesn't have a build.gradle → Project directory ... does not exist.

Android Gradle Plugin (AGP)

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "AGP is the Gradle plugin that bolts Android onto generic Gradle — it's what knows about aapt2, manifest merging, DEX-ing, variants, signing, and AAB packaging. When you apply com.android.application, it registers hundreds of tasks behind friendly lifecycle names like assembleDebug. The thing interviewers always check is the version coupling: AGP, the Gradle wrapper, the Kotlin Gradle plugin, and the JDK all have to line up — AGP 8 needs Gradle 8 and JDK 17 — and a mismatch surfaces as a cryptic NoSuchMethodError, not a clear message."

Definition

AGP is the Gradle plugin that layers Android-specific build logic on top of standard Gradle — it handles resource compilation with aapt2, manifest merging, DEX compilation, APK/AAB packaging, signing, lint, and instrumented test support.

How it works

// root build.gradle.kts
plugins {
    id("com.android.application") version "8.4.0" apply false
    id("com.android.library")     version "8.4.0" apply false
    id("org.jetbrains.kotlin.android") version "1.9.24" apply false
}

AGP registers hundreds of Gradle tasks behind assembleDebug, bundleRelease, etc. It consumes android { } DSL blocks and wires source sets, build variants, and outputs.

AGP → Gradle → JDK compatibility matrix

Always check the AGP release notes before upgrading. A version mismatch — for example, AGP 8.x paired with Gradle 7.x — causes immediate build failure. AGP 8.x requires Gradle 8.x and JDK 17 or higher.

Key AGP responsibilities

  1. aapt2 — compiles XML resources, produces R.java/R.txt
  2. Manifest merger — merges library manifests into the app manifest
  3. d8/r8 — Kotlin/Java bytecode → DEX (release: R8 with shrink/obfuscate)
  4. Resource shrinking (shrinkResources)
  5. APK/AAB assembly and signing

Under the hood

AGP is itself a Gradle plugin written against Gradle's Plugin<Project> API plus internal Variant/Component APIs. When applied, it reads the android { } extension (a Gradle ExtensionContainer object), enumerates the build-type × flavor matrix, and programmatically registers a task per variant — aapt2 compile/link tasks, merge* tasks, the dexBuilder/d8/r8 tasks, package and sign tasks — wiring their inputs and outputs so Gradle's up-to-date and caching machinery can track them. The NoSuchMethodError failure mode happens because AGP and the Kotlin Gradle Plugin both link against Gradle's internal (non-stable) APIs; if AGP calls a Gradle method that a mismatched Gradle/KGP version removed or changed signature on, the JVM resolves the call at runtime and throws.

apply AGP → read android{} extension
          → expand variants (buildType × flavor)
          → for each variant: register aapt2 / merge / d8|r8 / package / sign tasks
          → expose lifecycle tasks (assemble*, bundle*) depending on them

Failure modes

  • Version mismatch between AGP and Kotlin Gradle Plugin → obscure NoSuchMethodError at build time.
  • AGP's minimum SDK enforcement: if a library requires minSdk 21 and your app has minSdk 19, the manifest merger will fail.
  • aapt2 errors are often resource ID conflicts from merged libraries.

Gradle Tasks

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "A Gradle task is a unit of work with declared inputs, outputs, and an action, and tasks form a DAG that Gradle executes in dependency order. The power comes from incremental builds: Gradle fingerprints each task's inputs and outputs, and if nothing changed it skips the task as UP-TO-DATE or pulls it FROM-CACHE. The classic gotcha is non-deterministic inputs — if a task reads System.currentTimeMillis() or forgets its @Input/@OutputFile annotations, Gradle can't fingerprint it correctly, so it either never goes up-to-date or silently serves stale outputs."

Definition

A Gradle task is a unit of work with declared inputs, outputs, and an action. Tasks form a DAG — a directed acyclic graph — and Gradle executes them in dependency order.

Key concepts

  • UP-TO-DATE: Gradle checks input/output fingerprints. If nothing changed, the task is skipped. This is the cornerstone of incremental builds.
  • FROM-CACHE: Output was fetched from the build cache rather than re-executed.
  • Task configuration vs execution: Configuration phase wires the task graph. Execution phase runs actions. Doing heavy work at configuration time is a common performance anti-pattern.

Common AGP tasks

Task What it does
preBuildEntry point, dependency checks
compile{Variant}KotlinKotlin → JVM bytecode
compile{Variant}JavaWithJavacJava → JVM bytecode
merge{Variant}ResourcesMerges resources from all modules
merge{Variant}AssetsMerges assets
package{Variant}Packages DEX + resources into APK/AAB
assemble{Variant}Lifecycle task that triggers full APK build
bundle{Variant}Produces AAB
lint{Variant}Runs Android Lint
test{Variant}UnitTestRuns JVM unit tests

Custom tasks

// build.gradle.kts
abstract class GenerateVersionTask : DefaultTask() {
    @get:OutputFile
    abstract val outputFile: RegularFileProperty

    @TaskAction
    fun generate() {
        outputFile.get().asFile.writeText("VERSION=${project.version}")
    }
}

tasks.register<GenerateVersionTask>("generateVersion") {
    outputFile.set(layout.buildDirectory.file("version.txt"))
}

Under the hood

Up-to-date checking is built on input/output snapshots, not timestamps. For each task, Gradle hashes the declared inputs — file contents (a hash per file, combined into a fingerprint), input properties, and the task's own implementation/classpath — and stores them with the previous execution in .gradle. Before running, it recomputes those hashes; if they match the prior run AND the output fingerprints are unchanged, it reports UP-TO-DATE and skips the action entirely. The build cache extends this: the input fingerprint becomes a cache key, and the task's outputs are stored as an archive keyed by that hash (locally or in a remote cache), so a matching key on any machine yields FROM-CACHE. This is precisely why @Input/@OutputFile annotations matter — they tell Gradle what to put in the fingerprint. An unannotated input is invisible to hashing (stale-output risk); a volatile value like currentTimeMillis() makes the fingerprint differ every run (never cacheable). register is also lazy — the task is configured only if it ends up in the graph, unlike eager create.

inputs (files+props+impl) ──hash──▶ fingerprint ──┐
                                                   ├─ == previous? & outputs intact? → UP-TO-DATE
prev run fingerprint  ◀── stored in .gradle ───────┘
fingerprint as key ──▶ build cache lookup ──▶ hit → FROM-CACHE (unpack outputs)

Failure modes

  • Tasks that read System.currentTimeMillis() or random values as outputs break UP-TO-DATE checks — outputs always differ.
  • Forgetting @Input/@Output annotations on custom tasks → Gradle cannot fingerprint correctly → stale outputs.
  • Task ordering vs dependency: mustRunAfter doesn't create a dependency — if Task B mustRunAfter Task A but nothing depends on B, A won't run. Use dependsOn for hard dependencies.

Build Variants, Build Types, Product Flavors

Build Types

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "A build type controls how the same code is compiled and packaged — debuggability, minification, signing config, and id/version suffixes — with debug and release as the defaults. The mental model I use: build type is the how, flavor is the what. A subtlety is that initWith lets a custom type like staging inherit from debug and then override pieces, which is cleaner than copy-pasting the whole block, and applicationIdSuffix lets you install debug and release side by side."

Definition: A build type controls how the code is compiled and packaged. The two default types are debug and release.

android {
    buildTypes {
        debug {
            isDebuggable = true
            applicationIdSuffix = ".debug"
            versionNameSuffix = "-DEBUG"
        }
        release {
            isMinifyEnabled = true
            isShrinkResources = true
            proguardFiles(getDefaultProguardFile("proguard-android-optimize.txt"), "proguard-rules.pro")
            signingConfig = signingConfigs.getByName("release")
        }
        create("staging") {
            initWith(getByName("debug"))
            applicationIdSuffix = ".staging"
        }
    }
}

What build type controls: debuggability, minification, signing config, application ID suffix, version name suffix.

Under the hood

applicationIdSuffix does not just change the installed package name — AGP appends it to the applicationId that gets written into the merged AndroidManifest.xml and the final DEX/resource table, which is what makes two build types installable on the same device as distinct apps. isDebuggable = true flips the android:debuggable manifest flag, which ART honors by disabling certain JIT/AOT optimizations and allowing a debugger to attach (JDWP). isMinifyEnabled = true inserts the R8 task into the variant's task chain between compilation and DEX, and signingConfig selects which key AGP uses in the apksigner/zipalign step that produces the final signed artifact.

Product Flavors

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "A product flavor controls what goes into the build — different endpoints, branding, or feature sets — like a free vs paid tier, or prod vs staging. Flavors live in dimensions, and AGP produces the Cartesian product: every combination of one flavor per dimension, crossed with each build type, becomes a variant. The gotcha is variant explosion — three dimensions of two flavors each is eight combos times two build types equals sixteen variants — and that library modules need missingDimensionStrategy if they don't declare every dimension the app does."

Definition: A product flavor controls what is in the build — different API endpoints, feature sets, or branding for different market segments.

android {
    flavorDimensions += listOf("environment", "payment")

    productFlavors {
        create("prod") {
            dimension = "environment"
            buildConfigField("String", "BASE_URL", "\"https://api.zocdoc.com\"")
        }
        create("staging") {
            dimension = "environment"
            buildConfigField("String", "BASE_URL", "\"https://staging.api.zocdoc.com\"")
            applicationIdSuffix = ".staging"
        }
        create("free") {
            dimension = "payment"
        }
        create("paid") {
            dimension = "payment"
        }
    }
}

Flavor dimensions: When multiple dimensions exist, every combination of one flavor per dimension × each build type creates a variant: prodFreeDebug, prodFreeRelease, stagingPaidDebug, etc.

Under the hood

buildConfigField causes AGP to generate a BuildConfig.java per variant during the generate{Variant}BuildConfig task; each field becomes a public static final constant compiled into bytecode, so BuildConfig.BASE_URL is resolved at compile time, not read from a file at runtime. Flavor resolution is implemented through Gradle's variant-aware dependency management: each variant publishes a set of attributes (the flavor of each dimension plus the build type), and when :app depends on a library, Gradle's attribute-matching engine selects the library variant whose attributes match. missingDimensionStrategy supplies a default attribute value for a dimension the library never declared, which is why its absence produces No matching variant of project :core found — the matcher has an unsatisfiable attribute.

Build Variants

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "A build variant is exactly one flavor combination plus one build type — stagingPaidDebug, say — and AGP generates a dedicated source set, BuildConfig, output artifact, and full task chain for each. What's worth knowing is how sources merge: AGP layers variant-specific over build-type over flavor over main, with higher priority winning. That layering is what lets you, for example, swap in a fake network module just for debug without touching production code."

A build variant is one flavor combination plus one build type. Gradle creates a variant-specific source set, output APK/AAB, and compile/assemble tasks for each combination.

Variant matrix (2 env flavors × 2 payment flavors × 2 build types = 8 variants):
  prodFreeDebug
  prodFreeRelease
  prodPaidDebug
  prodPaidRelease
  stagingFreeDebug
  ...

How flavors work under the hood

  1. AGP creates a SourceSet for each flavor, each build type, and each combination.
  2. Source sets are merged in priority order: buildType > flavor > main.
  3. Resources, manifests, and Java/Kotlin sources from higher-priority sets override lower ones.
  4. BuildConfig fields are generated per variant.

Under the hood

For each variant AGP builds a merged view from the contributing source sets and feeds it to the compilers. Java/Kotlin sources from different source sets are additive — they're concatenated into one compilation unit, so two source sets defining the same fully-qualified class is a duplicate-class compile error, not an override. Resources, by contrast, are merged by the merge{Variant}Resources task: it walks source sets in priority order and the highest-priority definition of a given name+type wins, silently shadowing lower ones (a same-priority duplicate is a hard error). Manifests are combined by the manifest merger using node markers and tools: rules. Because every variant gets its own compile/dex/package task chain keyed by the merged inputs, adding a flavor dimension multiplies the number of task chains Gradle must configure and potentially execute — that's the literal source of variant-count build-time growth.

Trade-offs

  • Each additional flavor dimension multiplies the variant count — 3 dimensions × 2 flavors each = 8 combos × 2 build types = 16 variants. Build times grow.
  • Use missingDimensionStrategy in library modules that don't have all flavor dimensions to tell AGP which flavor to fall back to.

Failure modes

  • Forgot to add missingDimensionStrategy in a library module → No matching variant of project :core found build error.
  • Resource conflicts when two source sets define the same resource name with conflicting values — AGP merge picks highest priority silently, which can cause subtle runtime differences.

Source Sets

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "A source set is just a named bundle of source directories — Kotlin/Java, res, assets, and a manifest — tied to a variant or one of its components. Android gives you main plus one per build type, per flavor, and per combination, and they merge by priority: variant-specific beats build-type beats flavor beats main. The practical use is injecting different code per variant — a fake NetworkModule in debug/, the real google-services.json in release/ — and the gotcha is that for code a duplicate class across source sets is an error, while for resources the higher-priority one just silently wins."

Definition: A source set is a named collection of source directories — Java/Kotlin, resources, assets, and manifest — associated with a specific variant or one of its components.

Default source set layout

app/src/
  main/           ← base source set
    java/
    kotlin/
    res/
    assets/
    AndroidManifest.xml
  debug/          ← debug build type source set
  release/        ← release build type source set
  prod/           ← prod flavor source set
  staging/        ← staging flavor source set
  prodDebug/      ← prod+debug combined source set

Custom source set paths

android {
    sourceSets {
        getByName("main") {
            java.srcDirs("src/main/kotlin", "src/generated/kotlin")
            res.srcDirs("src/main/res", "src/main/res-overrides")
        }
    }
}

Priority (highest wins)

variant-specific > build-type > flavor > main

For resources, duplicate resource names at the same priority level are a build error. At different priority levels, the higher one wins silently.

Under the hood

A source set is represented by AGP as an AndroidSourceSet object holding AndroidSourceDirectorySets (one each for java, kotlin, res, assets, manifest, jniLibs, etc.) — these are just configurable lists of directories, which is why srcDirs(...) can point them anywhere. The directory naming convention (debug/, prodDebug/) is pure convention: AGP derives the expected folder names from the variant's build type and flavor names and registers those paths automatically; renaming a flavor renames the expected directory. At build time the resolved per-variant set is the ordered concatenation of every contributing source set, and the priority ordering you see is literally the order in which those directories are presented to the resource merger and prepended to the compiler's source roots. Nothing physically moves on disk — the merge is a virtual, in-memory composition done by the relevant merge*/compile* task.

Use cases

  • Put mock NetworkModule.kt in debug/ so debug builds wire a fake API.
  • Put real google-services.json in release/ and a dummy one in debug/.
  • Override strings/drawables per flavor for white-labeling.

Dependency Configurations

implementation

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "implementation puts a dependency on this module's own compile classpath but hides it from consumers — they see my public ABI, not my internal Retrofit dependency. The big payoff is incremental compilation: if Retrofit changes internally but my module's public API doesn't, Gradle won't recompile any downstream module. That's why the default advice is implementation everywhere and only reach for api when a type genuinely leaks into your public signatures."

Definition: The dependency is on the compile classpath of this module only — it is not exposed to consumers of this module.

dependencies {
    implementation("com.squareup.retrofit2:retrofit:2.9.0")
}

How it works: Consumers of this module see the compiled ABI (public API), but Retrofit is hidden from their compile classpath. Consumers can still use Retrofit at runtime if they declare it themselves.

Key benefit: If Retrofit changes internally but the module's own public API doesn't change, Gradle will NOT recompile downstream modules. This is the primary mechanism for incremental compilation gains in a multi-module project.

Under the hood

The distinction is realized through Gradle's outgoing-variant configurations. Every module publishes two relevant configurations: apiElements (consumed at compile time by downstream modules) and runtimeElements (consumed at runtime). An implementation dependency is added to the implementation bucket, which feeds only runtimeElements — it never appears in apiElements, so it's literally absent from the consumer's compile classpath. On top of that, Gradle tracks the ABI fingerprint (public method/field signatures) of upstream modules; the Kotlin/Java incremental compiler skips recompiling a consumer when an upstream change doesn't alter that ABI. Since an implementation dependency's internals can't be part of your ABI (consumers can't reference them), changes there can't trigger downstream recompilation.

module :core:network
  ├─ apiElements      → exposed at compile time to consumers
  └─ runtimeElements  → exposed at runtime
implementation dep ─▶ runtimeElements only  (hidden from consumer compile classpath)
api dep            ─▶ apiElements + runtimeElements (leaks to consumers)

api

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "api is like implementation but it transitively exposes the dependency to consumers — anyone depending on my module gets it on their compile classpath automatically. You only want this when the dependency's types actually appear in your public API signatures, like returning an OkHttpClient. The cost interviewers want you to name is the recompile cascade: change an api dependency and every downstream module recompiles, so over-using api silently erodes the whole point of modularization."

Definition: The dependency is on the compile classpath of this module and is transitively exposed to all consumers.

// In :core:network
dependencies {
    api("com.squareup.okhttp3:okhttp:4.12.0") // OkHttp types leak into consumer APIs
}

How it works: Any module depending on :core:network sees OkHttp on its compile classpath automatically. If OkHttp updates, Gradle must recompile all downstream modules.

When to use api

Use api only when the dependency's types appear in the module's own public API signatures (method parameters, return types, public fields). If you expose OkHttpClient in a public function, consumers need it on their classpath to compile.

Under the hood

api dependencies are placed in the api bucket, which Gradle wires into both apiElements and runtimeElements of the publishing module. When a consumer resolves its compile classpath, Gradle transitively pulls everything from upstream apiElements, so OkHttp's types are present and resolvable. The recompile cascade follows from ABI tracking: because an api dependency's types can legally appear in your public signatures, a change to that dependency can change your module's effective ABI, so Gradle must conservatively assume downstream consumers may be affected and recompile them. This transitivity is also what pollutes consumer classpaths — they can now accidentally import okhttp3.* even if they never declared OkHttp.

api vs implementation — the key interview question

Aspect implementation api
Consumer compile classpathNoYes
Transitive leakNoYes
Recompilation on changeOnly direct moduleAll downstream modules
Default choiceYesOnly when needed
RiskNoneRecompile cascade, polluted classpaths

The rule of thumb is to start with implementation everywhere. Only upgrade to api when the compiler tells you a consumer can't find a type it needs.

compileOnly

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "compileOnly puts a dependency on the compile classpath but does not package it into the output — perfect for annotations like javax.inject that are only needed at compile time, or APIs the platform itself provides at runtime, which is exactly how android.jar is wired. The trap: if you mark something compileOnly whose classes are actually needed at runtime, you'll compile fine and then crash with NoClassDefFoundError once you hit that code path on device."

Definition: On the compile classpath but not packaged into the output. Used for compile-time annotations or APIs that the platform provides at runtime.

dependencies {
    compileOnly("javax.annotation:javax.annotation-api:1.3.2")
    compileOnly("com.google.dagger:dagger:2.51") // when using kapt for code gen only
}

Android use cases: javax.inject annotations, provided annotations for annotation processors, APIs available on Android platform (android.jar is automatically compileOnly).

Under the hood

compileOnly artifacts are added to the compileClasspath configuration but deliberately excluded from runtimeClasspath, so the DEX/packaging step never sees them and they don't ship in the APK. This works for annotations because many have @Retention(SOURCE) or CLASS retention — they're consumed by the compiler/annotation processor and either discarded or left only as metadata, never needed by the running VM. android.jar is the canonical case: AGP adds it as a bootclasspath-style compile-only dependency so your code can reference android.app.Activity, but the actual implementation lives in the framework on the device. The failure mode is direct: a compileOnly library's class is absent from runtimeClasspath, so the class loader (ART's PathClassLoader walking the DEX files) can't find it, and the first reference throws NoClassDefFoundError/ClassNotFoundException.

Failure mode: If you compileOnly a library whose classes are needed at runtime, you get ClassNotFoundException or NoClassDefFoundError at runtime.

runtimeOnly

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "runtimeOnly is the mirror image of compileOnly — the dependency is packaged into the output but kept off the compile classpath, so you can't reference its types directly in code. It's for pluggable implementations chosen at runtime, like an SLF4J logging backend or a JDBC driver. It's pretty rare in Android app modules and shows up more in plain JVM modules where you wire the implementation via service loading or reflection."

Definition: Not on the compile classpath, but packaged into the output. Used for implementations selected at runtime — SLF4J backends, JDBC drivers, and similar.

dependencies {
    runtimeOnly("org.slf4j:slf4j-android:1.7.36")
}

Rare in Android app modules, more common in JVM modules.

Under the hood

runtimeOnly adds the artifact to runtimeClasspath (and thus into the packaged output) but excludes it from compileClasspath, so the compiler can't see the types — that's intentional, because the consumer is expected to discover the implementation indirectly. The common mechanism is java.util.ServiceLoader: a façade like SLF4J calls ServiceLoader.load(...), which reads META-INF/services/ provider files from whatever is on the runtime classpath and instantiates the backend by reflection. Because nothing in your source references the backend directly, keeping it off the compile classpath prevents accidental hard coupling while still shipping the bytecode so the loader can find it at runtime.

kapt

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "kapt runs Java annotation processors against Kotlin code, but Java APs can't read Kotlin directly, so kapt first generates Java stubs — signature-only representations of your Kotlin classes — runs the processors against those, then feeds the generated sources back for a final Kotlin compile. That stub-generation round is the expensive part and it doesn't play well with incremental compilation, which is the whole reason the ecosystem moved to KSP."

Definition: Runs an annotation processor through the Kotlin Annotation Processing Tool. The processor runs after Kotlin compilation and generates Java/Kotlin source files.

plugins {
    id("kotlin-kapt")
}
dependencies {
    implementation("com.google.dagger:dagger:2.51")
    kapt("com.google.dagger:dagger-compiler:2.51")
}

How it works: KAPT creates stubs (Java-compatible representation of Kotlin classes), runs Java annotation processors against those stubs, then feeds the generated sources back into the Kotlin compiler. Two compilation rounds: stubs + Java AP → generated sources → final Kotlin compile.

Under the hood

KAPT exists because the standard javax.annotation.processing API (and javax.lang.model mirror types) only understands Java source/elements, not Kotlin. KAPT runs the Kotlin compiler in a special mode that emits Java stub files — classes with correct signatures but empty/throwing method bodies — then launches a real javac annotation-processing round over those stubs so existing processors like Dagger's see familiar TypeElement/ExecutableElement models. Generated sources are collected and then compiled in the final Kotlin/Java passes. The cost is twofold: stub generation requires fully resolving and re-emitting your Kotlin as Java for the whole compilation unit, and because the AP round operates on regenerated stubs, KAPT's incremental support is coarse — small Kotlin edits often invalidate the stubs and force broad reprocessing.

Kotlin sources ─▶ KAPT stub gen ─▶ Java stubs ─▶ javac annotation processing ─▶ generated sources
                                                                                       │
                          final compile ◀──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Performance cost: Stub generation is expensive. KAPT cannot benefit from Kotlin incremental compilation as effectively as KSP.

ksp

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "KSP is a first-class Kotlin compiler plugin API for annotation processing — it operates directly on Kotlin's symbol/resolution model with no Java stub-generation step, which is why it's roughly twice as fast as kapt and supports proper incremental processing. Room, Moshi, and Hilt all ship KSP processors now. The migration nuance is that KSP gives processor authors a Kotlin-native API, so each library had to write a dedicated KSP processor — you can't just point kapt config at it."

Definition: Kotlin Symbol Processing is a first-class Kotlin compiler plugin API for building annotation processors that work directly on the Kotlin IR, with no stub generation step.

plugins {
    id("com.google.devtools.ksp") version "1.9.24-1.0.20"
}
dependencies {
    implementation("com.google.dagger:hilt-android:2.51")
    ksp("com.google.dagger:hilt-android-compiler:2.51")
    implementation("androidx.room:room-runtime:2.6.1")
    ksp("androidx.room:room-compiler:2.6.1")
}

Under the hood

KSP runs as a Kotlin compiler plugin and exposes its own abstraction layer — KSClassDeclaration, KSFunctionDeclaration, Resolver — backed by the compiler's already-resolved symbol table, so processors read Kotlin declarations (nullability, suspend, properties, default args) without any Java stub round. Processors implement SymbolProcessor and run in rounds: each round returns the symbols it couldn't yet process (deferred) and can generate new files via a CodeGenerator, which records the originating source files. That dependency tracking is what enables true incremental processing — when a source file changes, KSP only reprocesses the symbols and regenerates the outputs whose recorded dependencies were touched, instead of re-running over rebuilt stubs. The net effect is fewer compiler invocations and finer-grained invalidation, hence the roughly 2× speedup over KAPT.

KSP advantages over KAPT: Up to 2× faster, supports incremental processing, no stub generation step, works natively with Kotlin types. Room, Moshi, Hilt all support KSP.

Dependency Configuration Summary

dependencies {
    // Standard app dependency, hidden from consumers
    implementation("androidx.core:core-ktx:1.13.1")

    // Expose Kotlin stdlib types in public API
    api("org.jetbrains.kotlin:kotlin-stdlib:1.9.24")

    // Annotation only, not shipped
    compileOnly("javax.inject:javax.inject:1")

    // Runtime SLF4J binding
    runtimeOnly("org.slf4j:slf4j-android:1.7.36")

    // KSP processor
    ksp("androidx.room:room-compiler:2.6.1")

    // Test-only
    testImplementation("junit:junit:4.13.2")
    testImplementation("io.mockk:mockk:1.13.11")
    androidTestImplementation("androidx.test.espresso:espresso-core:3.5.1")
}

Version Catalogs

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "A version catalog is a single TOML file — gradle/libs.versions.toml — where I declare every dependency version and coordinate once, and Gradle generates type-safe libs.* accessors with IDE autocomplete instead of me memorizing string keys. It replaces ext {} blocks and buildSrc constants. The gotcha interviewers like is scope: those generated accessors only exist in the build.gradle.kts DSL — inside buildSrc or a convention plugin you don't get libs. for free, you have to resolve the catalog through the VersionCatalogsExtension and findLibrary(...)."
