Android vitals themselves are aggregated server-side from DropBoxManager/ActivityManager crash and ANR reports that the framework collects on-device and uploads via Play services; the "crash-free users" rate you watch is a backend rollup of those reports keyed by versionCode. There is no per-device flag the framework reads to decide "am I in the rollout" — staging is purely a delivery-time gate on which APK splits the device is offered.

Account ID --hash--> stable bucket in [0,100)
   bucket < rolloutPercent  ->  offered new versionCode
   bucket >= rolloutPercent ->  stays on old versionCode
expanding percent only lowers the threshold => cohort grows, never churns

Feature Flags and Remote Config

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "Feature flags let me decouple deploy from release — I merge code to main and ship it dark, then turn it on for 1% independently of the Play release cadence, and flip it off server-side as a kill switch within minutes if it misbehaves. With Firebase Remote Config the critical detail is that fetch is asynchronous and cached, so on a cold start before the first fetch completes the app reads the bundled XML defaults — which means my defaults must always be the safe, off state for anything risky. The nuance interviewers probe is the fetch throttle: in production the minimum fetch interval defaults to several hours, so you can't expect a flag flip to propagate instantly to a device that just fetched."

Definition: Feature flags — also called feature toggles — let you enable or disable features at runtime without shipping a new app release. Remote Config extends this by allowing flag values to be configured from the server side.

Why feature flags for risky features

  1. Decouple deploy from release: Merge code to main and ship it to all users, but behind a flag that's false. Turn it on for 1% of users first, independently of the Play Store release cadence.
  2. Kill switch: If a feature causes crashes in production, flip the flag server-side to false — it takes effect within minutes, with no waiting for app review or staged rollout completion.
  3. A/B testing: Run an experiment with control and treatment groups from the same binary.
  4. Gradual rollout independent of Play Store: Roll out by percentage using your own backend instead of relying solely on Play's mechanism.

Firebase Remote Config pattern

// RemoteConfigManager.kt
@Singleton
class RemoteConfigManager @Inject constructor(
    private val remoteConfig: FirebaseRemoteConfig
) {
    init {
        remoteConfig.setConfigSettingsAsync(remoteConfigSettings {
            minimumFetchIntervalInSeconds = if (BuildConfig.DEBUG) 0 else 3600
        })
        remoteConfig.setDefaultsAsync(R.xml.remote_config_defaults)
    }

    fun isNewCheckoutEnabled(): Boolean =
        remoteConfig.getBoolean("new_checkout_flow_enabled")

    suspend fun fetchAndActivate(): Boolean =
        remoteConfig.fetchAndActivate().await()
}
<!-- res/xml/remote_config_defaults.xml -->
<defaultsMap>
    <entry>
        <key>new_checkout_flow_enabled</key>
        <value>false</value>
    </entry>
</defaultsMap>

Internal feature flags (without Firebase)

For development and internal testing, a simpler approach:

// FeatureFlags.kt
object FeatureFlags {
    var newCheckoutEnabled: Boolean = BuildConfig.DEBUG  // on by default in debug
}

Zocdoc's PhiAbWrapper pattern (from CLAUDE.md)

// Inject PhiAbWrapper to check experiment variants
class CheckoutViewModel @Inject constructor(
    private val phiAbWrapper: PhiAbWrapper,
) {
    val showNewCheckout: Boolean
        get() = phiAbWrapper.isNewCheckoutFlowEnabled()
}

Risk mitigation strategy for risky features

  1. Put the feature behind a feature flag that defaults to false in production.
  2. Enable it for QA and internal users on the internal test track first.
  3. Enable for opted-in beta users on the open beta track.
  4. Production staged rollout: 1% → 5% → 20% → 50% → 100%.
  5. Monitor crash rates, ANRs, and business metrics at each stage before expanding.
  6. If metrics degrade at any stage, flip the flag to false server-side immediately, then investigate.

Remote config fetch latency

Remote config values are fetched asynchronously and cached locally. If the app launches before a fetch completes, it falls back to the default values from remote_config_defaults.xml. That is the safe state — defaults should always be the conservative, off setting for any risky feature.

Under the hood

Remote Config keeps three separate value stores on-device: a defaults map (seeded from your XML), a fetched store (the most recent values pulled from the server but not yet live), and the active store (what getBoolean/getString actually read). fetch() does an HTTP request and writes into the fetched store; activate() atomically copies fetched → active. fetchAndActivate() chains the two. Crucially, a getter never blocks on the network — it reads the active store synchronously, and the resolution order is active value → default → static type default (false/0/""). Each fetched value also carries a source enum (REMOTE, DEFAULT, STATIC) you can inspect. The minimumFetchIntervalInSeconds is a client-side throttle: if you call fetch() again inside the window, the SDK short-circuits and returns the cached result without a network round-trip, which is why production uses hours and debug uses 0. Values persist across process death in app-private storage, so a returning user already has the last-activated flags before the first fetch of the new session even starts.

getBoolean("flag")
  -> active store has key?   yes -> return it (source REMOTE/DEFAULT)
  -> no -> static type default (false)   (source STATIC)

fetch(): network -> fetched store   (throttled by minFetchInterval)
activate(): fetched store --atomic copy--> active store

Versioning

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "Every Android app has two version identifiers: versionCode, an integer Play uses purely for update ordering, and versionName, the human-readable string shown to users — they're completely independent. The one rule that bites people is that versionCode must strictly increase for every upload to Play, which is exactly why a 'rollback' has to be a new, higher versionCode publishing the old code. In practice I never hand-bump it; I derive it in CI from the build number or git commit count so it's monotonic and reproducible, and both values are emitted into BuildConfig so I can stamp them into crash reports and analytics."

Definition: Android apps have two version identifiers. versionCode is an integer the Play Store uses for update ordering. versionName is the human-readable string shown to users.

android {
    defaultConfig {
        versionCode = 1042            // integer, monotonically increasing
        versionName = "4.2.1"         // user-visible string
    }
}

versionCode rules

  • Must be a positive integer.
  • Play Store requires each release to have a higher versionCode than the previous. Play uses versionCode to determine update ordering.
  • No relation to versionName — you can have versionCode = 1042 and versionName = "4.2.1".
  • Maximum value: 2,100,000,000 (Android limit).

versionName conventions

Common schemes:

  • Semantic versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH (e.g., 4.2.1)
  • Date-based: 2024.06.18
  • Automatic from CI: combine Git commit count or timestamp.

Automating versionCode in CI

// build.gradle.kts
val ciVersionCode = System.getenv("BUILD_NUMBER")?.toIntOrNull()
android {
    defaultConfig {
        versionCode = ciVersionCode ?: 1
        versionName = "4.2.${ciVersionCode ?: 0}"
    }
}

Many teams use the Git commit count:

fun gitCommitCount(): Int {
    return Runtime.getRuntime()
        .exec(arrayOf("git", "rev-list", "--count", "HEAD"))
        .inputStream.bufferedReader().readText().trim().toInt()
}

Per-ABI version codes (if distributing split APKs manually, not via AAB)

When publishing ABI splits, each ABI must have a unique versionCode because Play stores them as separate APKs:

// arm64 → base * 1000 + 1, x86 → base * 1000 + 2, etc.
android {
    splits {
        abi {
            isEnable = true
            isUniversalApk = false
        }
    }
}
// In app/build.gradle.kts variant filter or applicationVariants loop

BuildConfig versioning

BuildConfig.VERSION_CODE and BuildConfig.VERSION_NAME are generated constants available at runtime, useful for including in analytics events, crash reports, and support tooling.

Under the hood

versionCode and versionName are not Gradle inventions — they are manifest attributes (android:versionCode, android:versionName) that AGP merges into the final AndroidManifest.xml, then aapt2 encodes them into the binary resource table of the APK. At install time PackageManagerService reads versionCode out of the parsed manifest into the PackageInfo/ApplicationInfo it tracks; an update is only accepted if the incoming package's versionCode is greater than or equal to the installed one (Play enforces strictly greater on the store side). The integer is actually stored as a 32-bit value, which is the origin of the ~2.1 billion ceiling — and modern AGP splits it into versionCode (lower bits) plus versionCodeMajor (upper bits) for apps that exhaust the range. BuildConfig.VERSION_CODE/VERSION_NAME are a separate artifact: AGP generates a BuildConfig.java per variant with these as public static final fields, so they're baked into the compiled bytecode as constants — meaning the runtime value comes from the build, not from re-reading the manifest at startup.

build.gradle versionCode/versionName
   |
   +--> merged AndroidManifest.xml (android:versionCode/Name)
   |         |--> aapt2 -> binary resource table in APK
   |         |--> PackageManagerService: update allowed iff newCode > installedCode
   |
   +--> generated BuildConfig.{VERSION_CODE,VERSION_NAME} (static final consts)

Interview Angles 12.3

Q: What does R8 do?

"R8 is a combined shrinker, optimizer, obfuscator, and DEX compiler that runs in a single pass on every release build. There are four things it does.

First, tree-shaking: it builds a call graph starting from every entry point declared in your manifest — Activities, Services, BroadcastReceivers — and walks every reachable method and class. Anything that isn't reachable gets removed entirely. That kills dead code from both your own modules and from third-party libraries that you only use a fraction of.

Second, optimization: it inlines short methods, merges classes, propagates constants, eliminates dead branches — so an if (BuildConfig.DEBUG) block is literally removed from the release binary when DEBUG is false — and converts enums to int constants where possible. These all improve runtime performance and shrink the binary further.

Third, obfuscation: it renames classes, methods, and fields to short identifiers like a and b. That produces mapping.txt, which is what you use to de-obfuscate crash stack traces later. It also reduces binary size because shorter names compress better, and it raises the cost of reverse engineering.

Fourth, DEX compilation: it converts JVM bytecode to Dalvik/ART DEX format, replacing the separate d8 step that debug builds use.

R8 replaced ProGuard in AGP 3.4. The key advantage is that single pass — combining all four operations is faster than running ProGuard then D8 in sequence, and R8 has much deeper integration with the Kotlin toolchain."

Q: How do you debug obfuscated crashes?

"There are four steps. First, retrieve the obfuscated stack trace from your crash tool — Sentry, Crashlytics, whatever you use. Second, find the mapping.txt for the exact build that crashed; you match it by versionCode and build timestamp, which is why you archive mapping files for every release. Third, run retrace:

java -jar retrace.jar mapping.txt obfuscated_crash.txt

And fourth, read the de-obfuscated output — you get back the original class names, method names, and line numbers.

The best practice is to automate all of this. Both the Sentry Gradle plugin and the Crashlytics Gradle plugin can upload mapping.txt at build time so the tool de-obfuscates crashes automatically without you needing to run retrace manually.

The one catastrophic case is when you've lost the mapping.txt for a build. At that point, the crash is permanently unreadable — you can only correlate symptoms with the code changes in that version range. That's why every serious team stores mapping files in long-term storage keyed by versionCode, whether that's S3 or an artifact repository."

Q: Why use staged rollout?

"Staged rollout exists to limit the blast radius of bugs that make it through QA. There are four reasons I always use it.

First, risk containment: a crash affecting 1% of users is recoverable, a crash affecting 100% is a P0 incident. Staging gives you the window to detect and halt before you've hit the full audience.

Second, real-world signals: synthetic tests in CI cover known scenarios, but real users surface edge cases that testing simply cannot replicate — specific device models, OS versions, carrier configurations, locale-specific content.

Third, time to investigate: a 10% rollout that bumps crash rate by 0.5% gives the team time to diagnose and fix. By the time you'd expand to 100%, you either have a fix ready or you've already halted.

Fourth, business metric validation: for feature changes specifically, you can monitor conversion rate or session length or whichever KPI matters at 10% before you commit to full rollout."

Q: How do you safely release risky features?

"I think about this as a layered strategy — there are seven layers, and each one adds an independent safety net.

First, the feature flag at rest: merge the code to main behind a flag that's false in production defaults. The code ships in every release but stays dormant until you enable it.

Second, internal testing: enable the flag for the dev and QA team via the debug panel or a BuildConfig override, and validate against real production infrastructure.

Third, alpha and beta tracks on Play: enable via remote config for opted-in beta users to collect real-world feedback with a small, self-selected audience.

Fourth, production staged rollout: start at 1–5% on Play Console and monitor crash-free sessions, ANR rate, and business metrics for 24–48 hours before expanding.

Fifth, the remote kill switch: if metrics degrade at any stage, you flip the flag server-side to false — that takes effect within minutes, which is far faster than any hotfix release cycle.

Sixth, a hotfix pipeline: have CI/CD ready to publish a previous signed AAB or a targeted hotfix within 30 minutes in case the feature flag alone isn't enough.

And seventh, observability: instrument the feature with structured logging keyed to the flag state so you can split your dashboards between flag-on and flag-off users and see exactly what's changing."

Summary Table: Quick Reference

Topic Key Points
implementation vs apiapi leaks to consumers, triggers recompile cascade. Default to implementation.
KAPT vs KSPKSP is 2× faster, incremental, no stub gen. Prefer KSP for new code.
Configuration cacheCaches task graph. Saves 10–30s on warm builds. Requires AGP 8.1+.
Build cacheCaches task outputs. Survives clean. Remote cache enables cross-machine reuse.
Convention pluginsDRY shared build config. Use :build-logic (not buildSrc) for config cache compat.
APK vs AABAPK = installable. AAB = Play upload; Play generates device-optimized APKs.
R8Shrink + optimize + obfuscate + DEX in one pass. Runs on release builds.

13.1 Android Security Basics

App Sandbox and UID Isolation

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "Every Android app gets its own Linux UID at install time, and the sandbox is really just standard Linux file permissions plus process isolation enforced by the kernel — my app's process literally can't open another app's files because they're owned by a different UID with 0700-style permissions. The thing I'd flag is that this is kernel-enforced, not a JVM-level check, so it can't be bypassed from userspace — but root gives a process UID 0, which bypasses all of it, and that's exactly why we never store secrets assuming the sandbox alone protects them on a compromised device."

Definition

Every Android app runs in its own Linux process with a unique User ID assigned at install time. The key insight is that the Linux kernel enforces the boundary — one app's process literally cannot read or write another app's memory or files unless you go through an explicit sharing mechanism.

How it works

  1. The Package Manager assigns a unique UID (e.g., u0_a123) per app at install time. This UID is permanent for the life of the installation.
  2. Each app process runs under that UID. The kernel denies cross-UID file access by default.
  3. App data is stored in /data/data/<package.name>/ with permissions rwx------ (owner = app's UID). Other UIDs cannot traverse this path.
  4. Apps can share a UID by declaring android:sharedUserId in the manifest (deprecated since API 29; use explicit content sharing instead). Both APKs must be signed with the same key.
  5. The Dalvik/ART VM provides a second layer: each app has its own VM instance, so a crash in one app does not corrupt another app's heap.

Under the hood

The sandbox is built directly on Linux DAC (discretionary access control) plus SELinux MAC (mandatory access control), not on anything VM-specific. At install, installd (running as root) creates the data directory and chowns it to the app's assigned UID/GID; the kernel's inode permission bits then deny any other UID at the open(2)/stat(2) syscall level. The "u0_a123" string decodes to a real numeric UID: userId * 100000 + (appId - 10000) for app UIDs in the 10000–19999 range, so multi-user (u0, u10) and per-app IDs are packed into one integer. On top of DAC, every process and file is labeled with an SELinux domain (e.g., untrusted_app), and the kernel rejects cross-domain access even if DAC bits were somehow permissive. Each app also runs its own ART runtime in a process forked from the Zygote, which shares preloaded framework classes copy-on-write but has a completely separate heap and address space.

UID packing:   appUid = userId * 100000 + (appId - AID_APP_START)
               u0_a123  -> userId 0, appId 10123  -> uid 10123
               u10_a123 -> userId 10, appId 10123 -> uid 1010123

Enforcement layers:  open("/data/data/other.app/...")
   1. DAC inode check (owner UID mismatch, mode 0700) -> EACCES
   2. SELinux: untrusted_app domain not allowed app_data_file of peer -> EACCES

Android implications

  • Storage: Internal storage is private by default. External storage (SD card, getExternalFilesDir) is world-readable pre-API 19 and scoped-storage-restricted from API 29+.
  • IPC: To share data across apps you must use defined IPC surfaces: ContentProvider, BroadcastReceiver, Service, Activity — all subject to permission checks.
  • Root breaks the sandbox: A rooted device grants a process UID 0 (root), which the kernel allows to bypass all UID-based checks.

Trade-offs

Benefit Cost
Strong default isolation — no extra code neededApps cannot directly read each other's data even for legitimate use cases
Kernel-enforced — can't be bypassed in userspaceSharing requires explicit APIs (ContentProvider, FileProvider) with their own complexity
Process crash is containedShared UID pattern (sharedUserId) breaks isolation and is deprecated

Failure modes

  • Declaring android:sharedUserId with an untrusted or compromised partner app gives that partner full read/write access to your private files.
  • World-readable files set programmatically via openFileOutput(name, MODE_WORLD_READABLE) break sandbox — this mode was deprecated in API 17.
  • Leaving files in external storage without scoped storage protection allows any app with READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE to read them.

Debug/test

# Verify your app's UID
adb shell ps | grep com.yourapp

# Confirm private files are not world-readable
adb shell ls -la /data/data/com.yourapp/

Permissions

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "Permissions are a declarative gate — I declare every sensitive capability in the manifest, and either the OS auto-grants it for normal permissions or the user has to approve dangerous ones at runtime. The protection level is the part interviewers probe: signature permissions are great for locking down IPC between my own apps because they're only granted when the caller is signed with the same key, so there's no user prompt and no spoofing. The gotcha is that a manifest declaration alone is necessary but not sufficient for dangerous permissions on API 23+ — without the runtime grant the call just throws SecurityException."

Definition

Android permissions are a gating mechanism — every sensitive capability an app needs must be declared upfront in AndroidManifest.xml, and the OS or the user decides whether to grant it.

How it works

Permissions are categorized by protection level:

Level Description Example
normalAuto-granted at install; no user promptINTERNET, VIBRATE
dangerousRequires runtime user approval (API 23+)CAMERA, READ_CONTACTS
signatureGranted only to apps signed with the same key as the defining appCustom permissions between your own apps
signatureOrSystemsignature OR pre-installed system appInternal OEM APIs
appopManaged through AppOps; toggled in SettingsMANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE

Declaring permissions in the manifest

<!-- Declaring a permission your app uses -->
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.CAMERA" />
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.READ_CONTACTS" />

<!-- Defining a custom permission (protect your own components) -->
<permission
    android:name="com.yourapp.permission.ACCESS_DATA"
    android:protectionLevel="signature" />

<!-- Requiring it on a component -->
<activity
    android:name=".SensitiveActivity"
    android:permission="com.yourapp.permission.ACCESS_DATA" />

Under the hood

Permission grants are tracked by PackageManagerService and persisted on disk — historically in /data/system/packages.xml and, on modern releases, in runtime-permission state files (runtime-permissions.xml) per user. A normal permission is recorded as granted at install; a dangerous one is stored as a flag the user flips at runtime. When code reaches a guarded API, the framework ultimately calls down to ActivityManagerService.checkPermission, which compares the caller's UID (obtained from the trusted Binder.getCallingUid(), set by the kernel binder driver — not spoofable) against the set of granted permissions for that UID. signature permissions are special: at install, PackageManagerService compares the APK signing certificate of the requesting app against the certificate of the app that defined the permission, and grants it only on an exact match — there's no user involvement, which is why it's safe for inter-app IPC. dangerous permissions are also mapped to AppOps entries, letting the user toggle them in Settings independently of the original grant.

Guarded call  ->  Binder transaction
   kernel binder driver stamps real callerUid (cannot be forged)
   AMS.checkPermission(perm, callerUid)
       lookup PackageManagerService grant state for callerUid
       signature-level: match signing cert of caller vs definer
   granted? proceed : throw SecurityException

Android implications

  • From API 23+, declaring a dangerous permission in the manifest is necessary but not sufficient — the user must grant it at runtime.
  • Permissions are granted per group (e.g., READ_CONTACTS and WRITE_CONTACTS belong to the CONTACTS group). Granting one may implicitly grant others in the group, but this behavior changed in API 26+ — always request each permission explicitly.
  • From Android 11 (API 30), if the user denies a permission twice, future calls to requestPermissions are silently ignored and you must redirect to Settings.

Failure modes

  • Requesting permissions you do not use: Google Play policy violation, and Play Store may flag your app.
  • Not handling the denial path: app crashes or shows a broken state.
  • Assuming a previously-granted permission is still granted — users can revoke permissions at any time in Settings.

Runtime Permissions

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "Runtime permissions, since API 23, move the dangerous-permission ask out of install time and into the moment the feature actually runs, so I check checkSelfPermission, optionally show a rationale, then request via the Activity Result API. The nuance interviewers want is the three-state flow: granted, denied-with-rationale, and permanently denied — on Android 11+ a second denial is treated as 'don't ask again,' so shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale returns false and the system silently drops further requests, meaning my only path left is deep-linking the user into Settings. I also always re-check on resume because the user can revoke while I'm backgrounded."

Definition

Runtime permissions, introduced in API 23, require apps to explicitly ask the user for dangerous permissions while the app is running — at install time the user sees nothing; the ask happens in context, at the moment the feature actually needs it.

How it works

  1. Check if permission is already granted: ContextCompat.checkSelfPermission().
  2. If not granted, optionally show rationale with shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale().
  3. Request it via the ActivityResultContracts.RequestPermission API (preferred over the older requestPermissions).
  4. Handle the result.
// Modern approach using Activity Result API (preferred)
private val requestPermissionLauncher = registerForActivityResult(
    ActivityResultContracts.RequestPermission()
) { isGranted ->
    if (isGranted) {
        openCamera()
    } else {
        // Check if we should show rationale or go straight to settings
        if (!shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale(Manifest.permission.CAMERA)) {
            // User selected "Don't ask again" — redirect to settings
            showGoToSettingsDialog()
        } else {
            showPermissionDeniedExplanation()
        }
    }
}

fun checkAndRequestCameraPermission() {
    when {
        ContextCompat.checkSelfPermission(
            this, Manifest.permission.CAMERA
        ) == PackageManager.PERMISSION_GRANTED -> {
            openCamera()
        }
        shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale(Manifest.permission.CAMERA) -> {
            // Show UI explaining why you need the permission
            showCameraRationaleDialog {
                requestPermissionLauncher.launch(Manifest.permission.CAMERA)
            }
        }
        else -> {
            requestPermissionLauncher.launch(Manifest.permission.CAMERA)
        }
    }
}

Multiple permissions at once

private val requestMultiplePermissions = registerForActivityResult(
    ActivityResultContracts.RequestMultiplePermissions()
) { permissions ->
    val allGranted = permissions.values.all { it }
    if (allGranted) {
        proceedWithFeature()
    } else {
        handlePartialDenial(permissions)
    }
}

Key API 30+ changes

  • One-time permissions: ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION, READ_MEDIA_* can be granted just for this session.
  • Auto-reset: permissions are auto-revoked for apps unused for months.
  • Background location requires a separate two-step flow: foreground first, then background.

Under the hood

The Activity Result API isn't magic — under it, registerForActivityResult allocates a unique string key into the ActivityResultRegistry, and launch() ultimately starts the system permission-controller Activity (the PermissionController APK, an updatable Mainline module) via a startActivityForResult-style flow. Because registration must survive process death and configuration changes, the registry persists pending keys in the saved-instance-state bundle and re-dispatches the callback after recreation — which is why you must register at construction time (unconditionally), not inside a click handler. The actual grant is written by PermissionController into PackageManagerService runtime-permission state. shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale reads a per-permission flag tracked by the system: it returns false both before the user has ever seen the dialog and after a permanent denial, so it cannot by itself distinguish "never asked" from "don't ask again" — the canonical pattern checks it inside the deny callback, where a false reliably means permanently denied. One-time grants are modeled as a transient flag the system clears when the app's process is no longer foreground.

registerForActivityResult(...)   // at field-init time, key -> ActivityResultRegistry
   launch(perm)
      ActivityResultRegistry -> startIntentSenderForResult to PermissionController
      user taps -> result Intent -> registry matches key -> your callback(isGranted)
config change / process death:
      registry keys saved in instanceState, re-bound on recreate, callback re-fires

Failure modes

  • Calling requestPermissions on a non-resumed Activity — can cause silent drops.
  • Not re-checking after returning from background — permission may have been revoked while the app was paused.
  • Requesting permissions in onCreate before the user has context for why they're needed.

Least Privilege

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "Least privilege means I only request the permission a feature needs at the moment it needs it, and I reach for scoped alternatives first — a photo picker or GetContent instead of READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE, ACTION_IMAGE_CAPTURE instead of the CAMERA permission. Every permission I hold is attack surface I don't benefit from, and the subtle risk is the supply chain: a compromised third-party library inherits my app's UID and every permission I've been granted, so an unused ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION becomes a free capability for an attacker. So I audit the merged manifest each release and delete anything without a live code path."

Definition

Least privilege means requesting only the permissions your feature genuinely needs right now — never speculatively acquiring them "in case we need them later." The trade-off is that extra permissions are pure attack surface with no benefit.

How it works in practice

  1. Audit your manifest before each release: remove any uses-permission that no longer corresponds to an active code path.
  2. Use scoped alternatives before reaching for broad permissions:
    • Instead of READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE: use ActivityResultContracts.GetContent() (user picks file, you get a URI — no permission needed).
    • Instead of READ_CONTACTS: use ACTION_PICK on the contacts URI.
    • Instead of CAMERA: use ACTION_IMAGE_CAPTURE — the camera app handles it.
  3. Request permissions only when the user triggers the action that needs them, not upfront.

Under the hood

The delegation pattern works because of how the binder and grantUriPermission machinery passes data across the sandbox without granting your app a standing permission. When you fire ACTION_GET_CONTENT or ACTION_IMAGE_CAPTURE, the picker/camera app — running under its own UID with its own permissions — does the privileged read, then returns a content:// URI. The result Intent is flagged FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION, and ActivityManagerService records a temporary, per-URI grant scoped to your UID that survives only until your task is finished (or the process dies). So you read one file through a ContentResolver without ever holding READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE. The supply-chain point is mechanical: a library you bundle is compiled into your APK and runs in your process under your single shared UID, so the kernel and PackageManagerService see all of its API calls as your app exercising your granted permissions — there is no per-library permission boundary at runtime.

ACTION_GET_CONTENT:
   your app (no storage perm)  --startActivityForResult-->  picker (has access)
   picker reads file, returns Intent{ data=content://..., FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION }
   AMS adds transient URI grant for yourUid (revoked when task ends)
   you ContentResolver.openInputStream(uri)  // legal, no manifest permission

Android implications

  • Google Play requires a Privacy Policy and justification for sensitive permissions (location, contacts, SMS, camera).
  • ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION, MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE, USE_EXACT_ALARM: require additional Play Store review.
  • Unused permissions are a security surface: a supply-chain attack on a library you ship can exploit them.

Trade-offs

Using intents to delegate to system apps (camera, contacts, file picker) means you lose control over the UX, but gain zero permission overhead and a narrower attack surface.

Exported Components

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "A component is exported when apps with a different UID can reach it, and I control that with android:exported. The detail people miss is the default: pre-API 31, a component with an intent-filter defaulted to exported true, which silently opened things up; since Android 12 you must declare exported explicitly or the build fails. My defense is layered — don't export unless I have to, guard with a signature permission when only my own apps should call it, and always treat the incoming Intent as untrusted input and validate it, because exported plus no permission plus blind trust of extras is the classic privilege-escalation or SQL-injection-into-a-provider bug."

Definition

An Android component — Activity, Service, BroadcastReceiver, or ContentProvider — is exported when it can be reached by components in other apps. You control this with android:exported in the manifest, and getting it wrong is one of the most common Android security mistakes.

How it works

  • android:exported="true": any app can interact with this component.
  • android:exported="false": only components within the same app (same UID or shared UID) can use it.
  • Default behavior (pre-API 31): if an <intent-filter> is present, exported defaults to true. Without an intent-filter, it defaults to false.
  • API 31+ (Android 12) breaking change: every Activity, Service, and BroadcastReceiver that has an <intent-filter> MUST explicitly declare android:exported. The build will fail if you omit it.

Securing exported components

Three layers of defence:

Layer 1: Don't export unless you have to.

<activity
    android:name=".InternalActivity"
    android:exported="false" />

Layer 2: Require a permission for access.

<!-- Define the permission -->
<permission
    android:name="com.yourapp.permission.LAUNCH_INTERNAL"
    android:protectionLevel="signature" />

<!-- Require it on the component -->
<activity
    android:name=".SensitiveActivity"
    android:exported="true"
    android:permission="com.yourapp.permission.LAUNCH_INTERNAL" />

Layer 3: Validate inputs inside the component.

// In the Activity/Service — never trust incoming Intent data
override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
    super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
    val action = intent.action ?: run {
        finish()
        return
    }
    // Whitelist allowed actions
    if (action !in setOf(ACTION_SHOW_DETAIL, ACTION_OPEN_FROM_NOTIFICATION)) {
        finish()
        return
    }
    val id = intent.getLongExtra(EXTRA_ID, -1L)
    if (id < 0) {
        finish()
        return
    }
}

ContentProvider specifics

<provider
    android:name=".InternalDataProvider"
    android:authorities="com.yourapp.internal"
    android:exported="false" />

<!-- If you need to share with specific apps, use grantUriPermissions -->
<provider
    android:name=".ShareProvider"
    android:authorities="com.yourapp.share"
    android:exported="false"
    android:grantUriPermissions="true" />

Under the hood

"Exported" is resolved by PackageManagerService when it parses the merged manifest at install/scan time, and the result is stored on each component's ComponentInfo.exported field. Every cross-app launch is a binder transaction into ActivityManagerService (or, for providers, into the ContentResolver/PackageManagerService provider lookup): the framework reads exported, and if false, compares Binder.getCallingUid() against the component owner's UID and rejects with SecurityException on mismatch. If exported="true" but an android:permission is set, AMS additionally calls checkPermission against the caller's granted set. The reason the API 31 change exists is that the implicit default was computed from the presence of an <intent-filter> — easy to get wrong — so the manifest merger now hard-errors at build time unless the attribute is explicit. For ContentProvider, the same machinery supports finer grants: grantUriPermissions lets the provider hand out transient per-URI access (via FLAG_GRANT_*_URI_PERMISSION) to callers who otherwise have no provider permission at all.

other app --binder--> AMS.startActivity(intent, callerUid)
   resolve target ComponentInfo from PackageManagerService
   if !exported && callerUid != ownerUid           -> SecurityException
   if exported && component.permission != null:
        checkPermission(perm, callerUid)            -> deny -> SecurityException
   else dispatch

Failure modes

  • Exported Activity that accepts a URL extra and opens it in a WebView → open redirect / JavaScript injection.
  • Exported Service that performs privileged operations without permission checks → privilege escalation.
  • BroadcastReceiver exported without permission that triggers sensitive actions → any app can trigger it.
  • ContentProvider exported with no read/write permissions → full database readable by any app.

Debug/test

# List all exported components of your app
adb shell dumpsys package com.yourapp | grep -A 2 "ActivityResolver"

# Drozer (security testing framework) to enumerate exported components
dz> run app.activity.info -a com.yourapp
dz> run app.service.info -a com.yourapp
dz> run app.provider.info -a com.yourapp

Intent Spoofing

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "Intent spoofing exploits the fact that Intents carry no built-in caller authentication — any app can craft an Intent to my exported component with arbitrary action, extras, and URI data, and the receiver can't trust that the sender is who it claims to be. The defense is to prefer explicit Intents and exported=false for everything internal, gate genuinely-shared components with a signature permission, and validate every extra as hostile input. The one trustworthy signal interviewers like is Binder.getCallingUid() — that's stamped by the kernel binder driver and can't be forged from userspace — but note that getCallingPackage is only populated for startActivityForResult flows, not plain startActivity, so you can't always rely on knowing the caller."

Definition

Intent spoofing is when a malicious app sends a crafted Intent to an exported component of your app, either impersonating a legitimate caller or injecting malicious data to trigger behaviour you didn't intend. The root cause is that Android Intents carry no built-in caller authentication.

How it works

Android Intents carry no built-in authentication. When a component is exported, any app on the device can send it an Intent — including setting arbitrary action strings, extras, and URI data. The receiving component cannot verify that the sender is who it claims to be (there is no trusted sender field that can't be spoofed from user space).

Attack scenarios

  1. Fake login callback: Your app registers an exported Activity to receive OAuth redirect Intents. An attacker app sends a spoofed Intent with a stolen authorization code.
  2. Data injection: Your exported Service accepts a URL extra and fetches it. An attacker passes an internal URL (http://localhost/admin).
  3. UI spoofing: An attacker launches your exported Activity with crafted extras to display misleading UI.

How to defend

// 1. Check the calling package (for Activities called via startActivityForResult)
override fun onActivityResult(requestCode: Int, resultCode: Int, data: Intent?) {
    // Note: callingPackage is set by Android; not spoofable from user space
    // but only available for startActivityForResult flows, not plain startActivity
}

// 2. Use LocalBroadcastManager for in-process broadcasts (deprecated; use Flow/LiveData instead)
// 3. Use explicit Intents for internal communication — don't rely on implicit Intents
val intent = Intent(this, MyInternalService::class.java)
startService(intent)

// 4. Require a signature-level permission on your exported component
// <activity android:permission="com.yourapp.permission.INTERNAL" ... />

// 5. Validate all data from Intents as untrusted input
val amount = intent.getDoubleExtra("amount", 0.0)
require(amount > 0 && amount <= MAX_TRANSFER_LIMIT) { "Invalid amount" }

Under the hood

An Intent is just a Parcelable bag of data — action string, categories, data URI, and an extras Bundle — that gets marshalled across the binder boundary; nothing in that payload is a signed or kernel-attested identity, which is precisely why the action and extras are spoofable. The only authentic sender signal comes from the binder transaction itself: the kernel binder driver stamps every transaction with the caller's real PID and UID, retrievable via Binder.getCallingUid()/getCallingPid(), and that value cannot be forged from userspace. getCallingPackage()/getCallingActivity() are derived identity that the framework only fills in for the startActivityForResult round-trip (where the system tracks the originating record); a plain startActivity deliberately drops it, so it returns null and can't be relied on. This is also why implicit Intents are riskier: the system resolves them by matching intent-filters across all installed apps, so a malicious app can register a matching filter and intercept or impersonate — whereas an explicit Intent (Intent(ctx, Foo::class.java)) names the exact component and bypasses filter resolution entirely.

// Authentic vs. forgeable signals on the receiving side
val realCaller = Binder.getCallingUid()   // kernel-stamped, NOT spoofable
val claimedPkg = callingPackage           // null on plain startActivity; only set for *ForResult
val action     = intent.action            // attacker-controlled, spoofable
val extras     = intent.extras            // attacker-controlled, validate as hostile

Key rules

  • Never trust Intent.getStringExtra() or any extras from exported components without validation.
  • Prefer android:exported="false" + explicit Intents for all internal communication.
  • For broadcast Intents you need to receive from the system (e.g., ACTION_BOOT_COMPLETED), use android:permission to limit who else can send you broadcasts.

PendingIntent Mutability

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "A PendingIntent is a token that lets another app or the system fire off one of my components using my app's identity and permissions. Mutability decides whether the holder can fill in or rewrite the wrapped Intent. The classic vulnerability is handing out a mutable PendingIntent wrapping an empty Intent — the recipient sets the component and now my app launches the attacker's target with my privileges. So the default should always be FLAG_IMMUTABLE, and since API 31 the framework forces me to declare one explicitly or it throws."

Definition

A PendingIntent is a token you hand to another app or the system so it can launch one of your components using your app's identity. Mutability controls whether the recipient is allowed to modify the Intent that's wrapped inside — and getting this wrong is a privilege-escalation vulnerability.

How it works

Flag Meaning
FLAG_IMMUTABLEThe PendingIntent's Intent cannot be modified by the recipient
FLAG_MUTABLEThe recipient can fill in unspecified fields of the Intent

The vulnerability

A mutable PendingIntent with empty or partially-specified wrapped Intent can be hijacked. The receiver fills in the action, component, or extras and your app executes the attacker's Intent under your app's identity (with your permissions).

// DANGEROUS — mutable with no action/component specified
val badPendingIntent = PendingIntent.getActivity(
    context, 0, Intent(), PendingIntent.FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT
    // Missing FLAG_IMMUTABLE — attacker can specify any Action/Component
)

// CORRECT — immutable for all cases where you don't need the recipient to fill fields
val safePendingIntent = PendingIntent.getActivity(
    context,
    requestCode,
    Intent(context, MyActivity::class.java).apply {
        action = ACTION_SHOW_NOTIFICATION
        putExtra(EXTRA_ID, notificationId)
    },
    PendingIntent.FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT or PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE
)

When FLAG_MUTABLE is legitimate

The primary case is AlarmManager.setAlarmClock() and MediaSession where the system framework needs to write the ClipData or fill in a FILL_IN_COMPONENT. Even then, always specify as much of the Intent as possible.

// Mutable only when genuinely needed (e.g., inline reply notifications)
val replyPendingIntent = PendingIntent.getService(
    context,
    requestCode,
    Intent(context, ReplyService::class.java),
    PendingIntent.FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT or PendingIntent.FLAG_MUTABLE
)

Android 12+ enforcement

From API 31, creating a PendingIntent without explicitly setting either FLAG_IMMUTABLE or FLAG_MUTABLE throws IllegalArgumentException — you have to make a deliberate choice. The right default is FLAG_IMMUTABLE; reach for FLAG_MUTABLE only when you have a specific framework reason and can document it.

Under the hood

A PendingIntent is not a wrapper object you own — it's a reference to a record (PendingIntentRecord) held inside the ActivityManagerService (AMS) in the system_server process. When you call getActivity()/getService()/getBroadcast(), AMS interns a record keyed by the tuple of (requesting UID, target package, request code, intent "filterEquals" identity, flags). That's why two calls with the same key return the same token and why FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT mutates the existing record rather than creating a new one. The flags (FLAG_IMMUTABLE, FLAG_MUTABLE) are stored on that server-side record, so mutability is enforced by the system process, not your app. When the holder later calls send() with a "fill-in" Intent, AMS calls Intent.fillIn() on the original; fillIn() only copies fields the base Intent left unset and only those the fill-in mask permits — but an immutable record rejects the fill-in entirely. Because the record runs the eventual startActivity/sendBroadcast under the creator's UID and identity, an attacker who can supply the fill-in is effectively executing as you. The API 31 hard requirement to pass one of the flags is a checkArgument in PendingIntent.buildServicePendingIntent/getIntentSender that throws IllegalArgumentException when neither bit is present.

Your app                  system_server (AMS)              Recipient app
  getActivity(IMMUTABLE) → PendingIntentRecord{uid, intent, flags}
                                  │  token (IBinder ref)  →  holds token
                                  │
                          send(fillInIntent) ←──────────────┘
                          intent.fillIn(fillInIntent, mask)
                          (no-op if IMMUTABLE) → startActivity as YOUR uid

Failure modes

  • Mutable PendingIntent given to a notification manager → if a malicious app intercepts the notification before the system, it can modify the wrapped Intent to launch its own component with your app's permissions.
  • Passing a mutable PendingIntent to a third-party SDK — the SDK (or its dependencies) could be compromised.

Deep Link Validation

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "I treat every deep link as untrusted external input — the URI and its params can come from anywhere. Custom schemes are the weakest because any app can register the same scheme and intercept; HTTP intent filters can be shared by multiple apps; verified App Links with autoVerify and an assetlinks.json file are the only ones where I'm guaranteed to be the exclusive handler. Even with App Links I still validate scheme, host, and path against an allowlist and range-check params in code. The gotcha interviewers love is OAuth: you must validate the state parameter against what you stored, or you've got a CSRF hole."

Definition

Deep links are URIs — HTTP/HTTPS or a custom scheme — that launch your app directly to a specific screen. Without proper validation they become a vector for open redirects, parameter injection, and data theft, so treating every deep link as untrusted external input is non-negotiable.

Types of deep links

Type Definition Security Level
Custom schememyapp://pathLow — any app can intercept or send
HTTP/HTTPS Intent filterhttp://yourapp.com/pathMedium — multiple apps may handle the same URL
App Links (verified)HTTPS with android:autoVerify="true"High — only your app handles your domain

How App Links work

  1. Declare intent-filter with android:autoVerify="true" in manifest.
  2. Host a Digital Asset Links file at https://yourapp.com/.well-known/assetlinks.json.
  3. Android verifies the association at install time. If verified, your app is the exclusive handler for those URLs — no disambiguation dialog, no other app can intercept.
<!-- AndroidManifest.xml -->
<activity
    android:name=".DeepLinkActivity"
    android:exported="true">
    <intent-filter android:autoVerify="true">
        <action android:name="android.intent.action.VIEW" />
        <category android:name="android.intent.category.DEFAULT" />
        <category android:name="android.intent.category.BROWSABLE" />
        <data
            android:scheme="https"
            android:host="www.yourapp.com"
            android:pathPrefix="/appointments" />
    </intent-filter>
</activity>

Validating deep link parameters in code

// In DeepLinkActivity.onCreate or handleIntent()
private fun handleDeepLink(intent: Intent) {
    val uri = intent.data ?: return

    // 1. Validate scheme and host — never trust them blindly even with autoVerify
    if (uri.scheme != "https" || uri.host != "www.yourapp.com") {
        finish()
        return
    }

    // 2. Whitelist known paths
    val allowedPrefixes = listOf("/appointments/", "/profile/", "/search")
    val path = uri.path ?: run { finish(); return }
    if (allowedPrefixes.none { path.startsWith(it) }) {
        finish()
        return
    }

    // 3. Sanitize and range-check parameters
    val appointmentId = uri.getQueryParameter("id")?.toLongOrNull() ?: run {
        finish()
        return
    }
    if (appointmentId <= 0) { finish(); return }

    // 4. Never pass raw URI strings to WebView
    navigateToAppointment(appointmentId)
}

Custom scheme risks

Custom schemes like myapp:// have no verification step, which means any other app can declare the same scheme and intercept your links. For any sensitive flow — authentication, payment — avoid custom schemes entirely. Always prefer App Links, which are cryptographically verified at install time.

OAuth redirect validation

// OAuth callback: validate state parameter to prevent CSRF
private fun handleOAuthCallback(uri: Uri) {
    val code = uri.getQueryParameter("code") ?: return
    val state = uri.getQueryParameter("state") ?: return

    // Compare against the state you generated and stored before launching the flow
    val expectedState = prefs.getString(KEY_OAUTH_STATE, null) ?: return
    if (state != expectedState) {
        // CSRF attack — discard
        return
    }
    exchangeCodeForToken(code)
}

Under the hood

App Link verification is driven by the DomainVerificationManager (pre-S it was the IntentFilterVerifier). At install — and asynchronously after, since Android 12 made verification more robust and re-runnable via pm set-app-links / pm verify-app-links — the system collects every host from intent-filters marked autoVerify="true", then makes an HTTPS GET to https://<host>/.well-known/assetlinks.json. It matches the JSON's sha256_cert_fingerprints against the signing certificate of your installed APK. Only an exact cert-fingerprint match flips the domain to the "verified" state in DomainVerificationManager's per-package, per-domain state machine; until then your app is just one of several candidate handlers and the URL goes to the browser or a disambiguation dialog. When an Intent arrives, PackageManagerService/IntentResolver filters candidate activities by matching the Intent's data (scheme/host/path) against each IntentFilter, and verified App Link handlers are given priority so no chooser appears. Crucially, none of this validates query parameters or path values — the framework only matches the structural filter (scheme, host, pathPrefix), so uri.getQueryParameter("id") is fully attacker-controlled and must be parsed and bounds-checked in your code. The OAuth state check is pure application logic: there is no framework CSRF protection on the redirect Intent.

Install / pm verify-app-links
  ├─ collect autoVerify hosts from <intent-filter>
  ├─ GET https://host/.well-known/assetlinks.json
  ├─ compare assetlinks sha256 fingerprint == APK signing cert
  └─ match? → DomainVerificationManager marks host VERIFIED (exclusive handler)
             no match → host stays unverified → browser/chooser

VIEW Intent → IntentResolver matches scheme/host/path ONLY
            → query params + path values are NEVER validated by the OS

Failure modes

  • Loading uri.toString() directly in a WebView → open redirect to phishing site.
  • Not validating the state parameter in OAuth flows → CSRF token theft.
  • Using custom scheme for payment redirects → any app can intercept the payment callback.

FileProvider

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "FileProvider is a ContentProvider that hands other apps a content:// URI plus a temporary, per-grant permission instead of a raw filesystem path. The reason it exists is that since Android 7 passing a file:// URI across apps throws FileUriExposedException — it would leak your sandbox layout and require the other app to have filesystem access. With FileProvider the receiver just opens an input stream through the ContentResolver and never sees where the file lives. The gotcha is you must add FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION on the Intent, keep the provider non-exported, and scope your paths tightly — a wide external-path exposes the whole SD card."

Definition

FileProvider is a ContentProvider subclass that lets you share files from your app's private directories with other apps through temporary URI grants, without ever exposing the actual filesystem path.

Why avoid direct file paths

  • file:// URIs reference absolute filesystem paths. If you pass a file:// URI to another app, that app must have filesystem access to that path — which violates the sandbox.
  • From API 24 (Android 7), passing file:// URIs via Intents to other apps throws FileUriExposedException. The OS enforces this.
  • Even if no exception occurs (e.g., you're targeting < API 24), exposing the path lets any app that can read the intent know where your private files are stored.

How FileProvider works

  1. Declare it in the manifest.
  2. Define accessible paths in an XML resource.
  3. Generate a content:// URI using FileProvider.getUriForFile().
  4. Grant temporary read/write permission on that URI to the receiving app.
  5. The receiving app uses ContentResolver.openInputStream() to access the file — it never sees the path.

Setup

<!-- AndroidManifest.xml -->
<provider
    android:name="androidx.core.content.FileProvider"
    android:authorities="${applicationId}.fileprovider"
    android:exported="false"
    android:grantUriPermissions="true">
    <meta-data
        android:name="android.support.FILE_PROVIDER_PATHS"
        android:resource="@xml/file_provider_paths" />
</provider>
<!-- res/xml/file_provider_paths.xml -->
<paths>
    <!-- App's private files dir: /data/data/com.yourapp/files/ -->
    <files-path name="private_files" path="." />

    <!-- App's cache dir: /data/data/com.yourapp/cache/ -->
    <cache-path name="cache" path="." />

    <!-- External files dir: /sdcard/Android/data/com.yourapp/files/ -->
    <external-files-path name="external_files" path="." />

    <!-- Avoid <external-path> (maps to root of external storage) unless truly needed -->
</paths>

Sharing a file

fun shareFile(file: File) {
    val uri = FileProvider.getUriForFile(
        context,
        "${context.packageName}.fileprovider",
        file
    )

    val shareIntent = Intent(Intent.ACTION_SEND).apply {
        type = "application/pdf"
        putExtra(Intent.EXTRA_STREAM, uri)
        // Grant read permission to whichever app the user picks
        addFlags(Intent.FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION)
    }

    context.startActivity(Intent.createChooser(shareIntent, "Share file"))
}

Camera capture example

private var photoUri: Uri? = null

private val takePictureLauncher = registerForActivityResult(
    ActivityResultContracts.TakePicture()
) { success ->
    if (success) {
        photoUri?.let { processPhoto(it) }
    }
}

fun launchCamera() {
    val photoFile = File(context.cacheDir, "photo_${System.currentTimeMillis()}.jpg")
    val uri = FileProvider.getUriForFile(
        context,
        "${context.packageName}.fileprovider",
        photoFile
    )
    photoUri = uri
    takePictureLauncher.launch(uri)
}

Under the hood

FileProvider.getUriForFile() doesn't copy or open the file — it walks the <paths> XML (parsed once and cached into a PathStrategy map of name→root File), finds the configured root that is a prefix of your file's canonical path, then builds a content://<authority>/<path-name>/<relative-path> URI by stripping the root and re-encoding the remainder. If the file isn't under any declared root it throws IllegalArgumentException — that's the tight-scoping enforcement. The temporary permission is the interesting part: FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION causes AMS to create a UriPermission grant entry scoped to the specific recipient package (the one the chooser resolves to) and tied to a lifetime — by default it's revoked when the granting component's task finishes, which is why retaining the URI past the activity fails. When the recipient calls ContentResolver.openInputStream(uri), Binder routes to your FileProvider.openFile(), which re-resolves the URI back to the File and returns a ParcelFileDescriptor — i.e., it hands over an open fd over Binder, not a path. The kernel's fd duplication is what lets the other app read bytes without ever holding filesystem permission to your sandbox. FileUriExposedException itself is thrown by StrictMode.onFileUriExposed(), invoked inside Uri.checkFileUriExposed() during Intent parceling on API 24+.

getUriForFile(file)
  └─ match file path against <paths> roots → content://authority/name/relpath
addFlags(FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION) + startActivity(chooser)
  └─ AMS records UriPermission{ grantee=resolvedPkg, uri, READ, ttl=task }
recipient.openInputStream(uri)
  └─ Binder → FileProvider.openFile() → ParcelFileDescriptor (open fd, not path)

Failure modes

  • Using <external-path path="."> in file_provider_paths.xml — exposes the entire external storage root. Scope paths as tightly as possible.
  • Not setting android:exported="false" on the FileProvider — other apps could enumerate or access files directly.
  • Forgetting FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION — the receiving app gets a URI it can't open.
  • Retaining content:// URIs beyond the activity lifecycle — grants expire.

WebView Security

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "A WebView is a full browser engine inside my process, so misconfiguring it is one of the easiest ways to ship remote code execution. The two things I never combine are JavaScript enabled on untrusted content and a JavaScript interface — addJavascriptInterface exposes my Kotlin methods to whatever page loads, so untrusted JS could call them and exfiltrate tokens. I disable file access, force MIXED_CONTENT_NEVER_ALLOW, allowlist navigations in shouldOverrideUrlLoading, and — the big one interviewers check — never call handler.proceed() in onReceivedSslError, because that silently accepts a bad cert and opens you to MITM."

Definition

WebView embeds a full browser engine inside your app. The reason misconfigured WebViews show up on so many security audit reports is that they can expose your app's Java and Kotlin interfaces directly to web content — and if that content is untrusted, that's essentially remote code execution.

Key security settings

webView.settings.apply {
    // JavaScript: disable unless your own trusted content requires it
    javaScriptEnabled = false // default; only enable for your own URLs

    // Never allow file access — prevents file:// scheme injection
    allowFileAccess = false          // API 29+ default; set explicitly for older targets
    allowContentAccess = false

    // Disable universal access from file URLs
    // (prevents file:// pages from fetching http:// resources)
    allowFileAccessFromFileURLs = false    // deprecated but set for older targets
    allowUniversalAccessFromFileURLs = false

    // Prevent mixed content (http:// loaded in https:// WebView)
    mixedContentMode = WebSettings.MIXED_CONTENT_NEVER_ALLOW

    // Disable geolocation (enable only if feature requires it)
    setGeolocationEnabled(false)

    // Disable saving form data
    saveFormData = false
    savePassword = false
}

JavaScript Interface (addJavascriptInterface)

This is the highest-risk WebView API. It exposes Kotlin/Java methods to JavaScript running in the WebView.

// DANGEROUS if webView loads untrusted content
webView.addJavascriptInterface(MyBridge(), "AndroidBridge")

class MyBridge {
    @JavascriptInterface // REQUIRED annotation — without it, methods are not exposed
    fun getUserToken(): String {
        // If untrusted JS can call this, it can steal the token
        return secureStore.getToken()
    }
}

Rules for safe JavaScript interfaces:

  1. Never add a JS interface if the WebView loads any untrusted URL.
  2. Annotate only with @JavascriptInterface — this is required from API 17+ for methods to be callable (pre-17 all public methods were exposed — a major attack surface).
  3. Never expose sensitive data (tokens, PII) through the bridge.
  4. Validate all parameters passed from JS as untrusted input.

URL interception — prevent open redirects

webView.webViewClient = object : WebViewClient() {
    override fun shouldOverrideUrlLoading(view: WebView, request: WebResourceRequest): Boolean {
        val url = request.url
        // Whitelist: only allow navigations within your domain
        if (url.scheme == "https" && url.host == "www.yourapp.com") {
            return false // let WebView handle it
        }
        // External URLs — open in system browser, not your WebView
        if (url.scheme == "https" || url.scheme == "http") {
            startActivity(Intent(Intent.ACTION_VIEW, url))
        }
        return true // block in WebView
    }

    override fun onReceivedSslError(view: WebView, handler: SslErrorHandler, error: SslError) {
        // NEVER call handler.proceed() — that ignores TLS errors
        handler.cancel()
        showTlsErrorToUser()
    }
}

Safe Browsing

// Enable Safe Browsing (checks URLs against Google's list of known bad URLs)
WebView.startSafeBrowsing(context) { success ->
    // success = false means Safe Browsing is unavailable on this device
}

webView.settings.safeBrowsingEnabled = true // API 26+

Additional hardening

  • Disable setWebContentsDebuggingEnabled(true) in production builds (it's only valid in debug). It exposes the WebView to Chrome DevTools over ADB.
  • Never load file:// URLs that the user or an external source controls.
  • Use WebResourceResponse to serve sensitive content from code rather than from files, when possible.
// Only enable debugging in debug builds
if (BuildConfig.DEBUG) {
    WebView.setWebContentsDebuggingEnabled(true)
}

Under the hood

The modern WebView is backed by the Chromium engine, packaged as the updatable "Android System WebView" / Chrome APK and loaded into your process via the WebViewFactory provider; your Java/Kotlin WebView object is a thin shim over Chromium's content layer running in a renderer. addJavascriptInterface registers your object with the V8 JavaScript engine: at injection time Chromium reflects over the object, and from API 17+ only methods carrying @JavascriptInterface are enumerated and exposed as a global JS property. When JS calls AndroidBridge.getUserToken(), the call is marshaled from the renderer across the Chromium IPC boundary back to the browser thread and dispatched to your method via JNI reflection — which is exactly why an untrusted page that can run JS gets a direct line into your app's process and its data. The pre-17 RCE history comes from reflection: older WebViews exposed all public methods, so attacker JS could reach getClass().forName(...) and invoke Runtime.exec. For TLS, when Chromium's network stack hits a certificate that fails chain/host validation it suspends the load and calls back into WebViewClient.onReceivedSslError with an SslErrorHandler that is essentially a resume/abort token; handler.proceed() tells the Chromium net stack to ignore the validation failure and continue the handshake, and handler.cancel() aborts it. shouldOverrideUrlLoading is consulted by the navigation throttle before a main-frame navigation commits — returning true cancels the in-engine navigation so you can route the URL yourself.

JS:  AndroidBridge.getUserToken()
      │  V8 (renderer process/thread)
      ▼  Chromium IPC  →  browser thread
   JNI reflective dispatch → MyBridge.getUserToken()   // your process, your data
   (pre-API-17: ALL public methods reflected → Runtime.exec reachable = RCE)

TLS fail → net stack pauses → onReceivedSslError(handler)
   handler.proceed() = ignore validation (MITM)  |  handler.cancel() = abort

Failure modes

  • onReceivedSslError calling handler.proceed() → app silently accepts invalid/expired certificates → MITM possible.
  • javaScriptEnabled = true with untrusted content + addJavascriptInterface → remote code execution equivalent.
  • allowFileAccess = true + allowUniversalAccessFromFileURLs = true → XSS in a local file can exfiltrate all app files.

13.2 Data Security

Android Keystore

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "The Keystore's whole point is that the private key material never leaves secure hardware — I get a handle to the key but the actual bytes live in the TEE or a StrongBox secure element, and every crypto op is done in there. So even on a rooted device an attacker can't extract the key, at most they can ask the daemon to use it while the app is running. The big gotcha is key invalidation: if I set setUserAuthenticationRequired(true), enrolling a new fingerprint permanently invalidates the key by default, so my code has to detect KeyPermanentlyInvalidatedException and regenerate. And keys can't be backed up — that's by design, not a limitation."

Definition

The Android Keystore System is a hardware-backed — or on older devices, OS-isolated — key storage facility. The defining property is that keys stored in the Keystore can never be extracted from the device in plaintext; all cryptographic operations happen inside the secure hardware, whether that's a StrongBox secure element, a TEE, or the isolated Keystore daemon.

What it is

  • Not a file on disk. It is a system service backed by hardware security where available.
  • Keys are bound to the app (via UID) — another app cannot use your Keystore keys.
  • Supports key usage policies: require biometric authentication, time-based expiry, user presence check.

How it works

// 1. Generate an AES key in the Keystore
fun generateAesKey(alias: String) {
    val keyGenerator = KeyGenerator.getInstance(
        KeyProperties.KEY_ALGORITHM_AES,
        "AndroidKeyStore" // This is the Keystore provider name
    )
    keyGenerator.init(
        KeyGenParameterSpec.Builder(
            alias,
            KeyProperties.PURPOSE_ENCRYPT or KeyProperties.PURPOSE_DECRYPT
        )
            .setBlockModes(KeyProperties.BLOCK_MODE_GCM)
            .setEncryptionPaddings(KeyProperties.ENCRYPTION_PADDING_NONE)
            .setKeySize(256)
            .setUserAuthenticationRequired(false) // set true to require biometrics
            .build()
    )
    keyGenerator.generateKey()
}

// 2. Encrypt data using the Keystore key
fun encrypt(alias: String, plaintext: ByteArray): Pair<ByteArray, ByteArray> {
    val keyStore = KeyStore.getInstance("AndroidKeyStore").apply { load(null) }
    val secretKey = keyStore.getKey(alias, null) as SecretKey

    val cipher = Cipher.getInstance("AES/GCM/NoPadding")
    cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, secretKey)
    val iv = cipher.iv
    val ciphertext = cipher.doFinal(plaintext)
    return Pair(iv, ciphertext)
}

// 3. Decrypt
fun decrypt(alias: String, iv: ByteArray, ciphertext: ByteArray): ByteArray {
    val keyStore = KeyStore.getInstance("AndroidKeyStore").apply { load(null) }
    val secretKey = keyStore.getKey(alias, null) as SecretKey

    val cipher = Cipher.getInstance("AES/GCM/NoPadding")
    val spec = GCMParameterSpec(128, iv)
    cipher.init(Cipher.DECRYPT_MODE, secretKey, spec)
    return cipher.doFinal(ciphertext)
}

Key generation for asymmetric (RSA/EC)

fun generateRsaKeyPair(alias: String) {
    val keyPairGenerator = KeyPairGenerator.getInstance(
        KeyProperties.KEY_ALGORITHM_RSA, "AndroidKeyStore"
    )
    keyPairGenerator.initialize(
        KeyGenParameterSpec.Builder(
            alias,
            KeyProperties.PURPOSE_SIGN or KeyProperties.PURPOSE_VERIFY
        )
            .setDigests(KeyProperties.DIGEST_SHA256)
            .setSignaturePaddings(KeyProperties.SIGNATURE_PADDING_RSA_PKCS1)
            .setKeySize(2048)
            .setUserAuthenticationRequired(true) // require biometric/PIN before signing
            .setUserAuthenticationValidityDurationSeconds(-1) // per-use auth (not time-based)
            .build()
    )
    keyPairGenerator.generateKeyPair()
}

StrongBox vs TEE

  • TEE (Trusted Execution Environment): An isolated processor within the main SoC. Keys cannot be extracted even with root, but a sophisticated hardware attack on the SoC could theoretically succeed.
  • StrongBox: A dedicated secure element (separate chip, e.g., Titan M on Pixel). Higher assurance — keys are isolated even from the main SoC.
// Request StrongBox (API 28+), fallback to TEE
val spec = KeyGenParameterSpec.Builder(alias, ...)
    .setIsStrongBoxBacked(true) // throws StrongBoxUnavailableException if not available
    .build()

When Keystore keys are invalidated

  • setInvalidatedByBiometricEnrollment(true) (default): adding a new fingerprint after key creation invalidates it. The app must re-generate the key.
  • Factory reset: Keystore is wiped.
  • Root: Keystore may be wiped as a security measure on stock ROMs.

Under the hood

KeyStore.getInstance("AndroidKeyStore") does not return your key bytes — it returns an opaque handle. The SecretKey/PrivateKey you get back is an AndroidKeyStoreKey that holds only an alias and a Binder reference to the keystore2 system daemon; there is no getEncoded() you can call. The actual key material lives behind the Keymaster/KeyMint HAL, implemented inside the TEE (e.g., ARM TrustZone) or, with setIsStrongBoxBacked(true), in a separate tamper-resistant secure element. When you call Cipher.init()/doFinal() on a Keystore key, the AndroidKeyStoreProvider JCA implementation doesn't run AES in your process — it begins a Keymaster operation over Binder, streams the plaintext blocks into the secure world, and the TEE/StrongBox performs the AES-GCM and returns ciphertext. That round-trip is why Keystore crypto is slower than in-process Bouncy Castle. Key usage policies (PURPOSE_*, setUserAuthenticationRequired) are encoded as Keymaster authorization tags enforced inside secure hardware, not by your app — so they can't be bypassed by patching your APK. For auth-bound keys, a successful biometric/PIN unlock produces a signed Hardware Auth Token (HAT) from Gatekeeper/Fingerprint HAL that the Keymaster checks before allowing the op. setInvalidatedByBiometricEnrollment(true) ties the key to the current biometric enrollment set's secure ID; enrolling a new fingerprint changes that ID, so the next use throws KeyPermanentlyInvalidatedException.

App process                         Secure world (TEE / StrongBox)
  Cipher.init(Keystore key)
   └─ alias + Binder handle ──────▶ keystore2 daemon
                                     └─ Keymaster/KeyMint op begin
  doFinal(plaintext) ────────────▶  AES-GCM runs HERE on raw key
                  ciphertext ◀─────  (key bytes never cross back)
  policy tags (PURPOSE, authReq) enforced inside, checked vs Hardware Auth Token

Android implications

  • Keys cannot be exported (by design). You cannot back up a Keystore key to a server.
  • On low-end devices pre-API 18, there is no hardware-backed Keystore — the software fallback is less secure.
  • Keystore keys survive app updates but are deleted on app uninstall.

Trade-offs

Benefit Cost
Key material never leaves secure hardwareCannot back up keys; if device is wiped, keys are gone
Per-app UID isolationSetup is complex (Cipher/KeyStore boilerplate)
Biometric auth binding availableStrongBox not available on all devices

EncryptedSharedPreferences

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "EncryptedSharedPreferences is a Jetpack Security wrapper that's a drop-in replacement for SharedPreferences but encrypts both keys and values — values with AES-256-GCM, keys deterministically with AES-256-SIV so lookups still work — and the master key that wraps the data key lives in the Keystore. It protects data at rest: ADB backups, offline storage access on a lost-but-locked device. What it does not protect against is a rooted live device or a malicious SDK in my own process, because they call the same decrypt API I do. And practically, there's no automatic migration from plain prefs and the library's been stuck on alpha, so I treat version bumps carefully."

Definition

EncryptedSharedPreferences is a Jetpack Security wrapper around SharedPreferences that transparently encrypts both keys and values — AES-256-GCM for values, AES-256-SIV for keys — with the master key living in the Android Keystore. From the outside it's a drop-in replacement; underneath, nothing touches disk in plaintext.

How it works

  1. A master key is created in (or retrieved from) the Keystore.
  2. The master key wraps a data encryption key stored in the encrypted prefs file.
  3. Every key and value is encrypted before being written to the XML file.

Setup

Add dependency:

// build.gradle.kts
implementation("androidx.security:security-crypto:1.1.0-alpha06")
import androidx.security.crypto.EncryptedSharedPreferences
import androidx.security.crypto.MasterKey

fun createEncryptedPrefs(context: Context): SharedPreferences {
    val masterKey = MasterKey.Builder(context)
        .setKeyScheme(MasterKey.KeyScheme.AES256_GCM)
        .build()

    return EncryptedSharedPreferences.create(
        context,
        "secure_prefs",                              // filename (stored in app's data dir)
        masterKey,
        EncryptedSharedPreferences.PrefKeyEncryptionScheme.AES256_SIV,
        EncryptedSharedPreferences.PrefValueEncryptionScheme.AES256_GCM
    )
}

// Usage — exactly like regular SharedPreferences
val prefs = createEncryptedPrefs(context)
prefs.edit()
    .putString("auth_token", token)
    .putLong("token_expiry", expiryMs)
    .apply()

val token = prefs.getString("auth_token", null)

What it protects against

  • ADB backup extraction of SharedPreferences XML files.
  • Physical access to the device storage (if the device is encrypted and locked).
  • Other apps reading your prefs (they can't, due to UID isolation, but encryption provides defence in depth).

What it does NOT protect against

  • Root: a root process can extract the Keystore keys on devices without StrongBox, allowing decryption.
  • A running process with the same UID (e.g., a malicious SDK in your own process) — it calls the same API you do.
  • Memory scraping of a live process — plaintext values exist in memory after decryption.

Under the hood

EncryptedSharedPreferences builds on Google's Tink crypto library and a two-tier key hierarchy. The MasterKey is an AES-256-GCM key generated in the Android Keystore (so it's hardware-backed and non-exportable); it never encrypts your data directly. Instead, Tink stores two data keysets — one DAEAD (deterministic AEAD, AES-256-SIV) keyset for keys and one AEAD (AES-256-GCM) keyset for values — inside a separate AndroidKeysetManager prefs file, and those keysets are themselves wrapped (encrypted) by the Keystore master key. On putString, the pref name is encrypted deterministically with AES-SIV — determinism is required so the same logical key always maps to the same ciphertext and can be looked up — while the value is encrypted with AES-GCM using a fresh random nonce, with the encrypted key mixed in as associated data to bind value to key and prevent swapping ciphertexts between entries. The result is Base64-encoded and written to a normal XML SharedPreferences file, so on disk you see only opaque strings. Because AES-SIV is deterministic, an attacker observing the file can still tell which entries are equal or repeated, even though they can't read them — that's the documented determinism trade-off. Decryption simply reverses this: Keystore unwraps the keysets, Tink decrypts. This is also why there's no automatic migration — the legacy plaintext file uses entirely different (unencrypted) storage and must be read and re-written through the encrypted instance once.

Android Keystore
  └─ MasterKey (AES-256-GCM, hardware-backed)
        │ wraps
        ▼
  Tink keysets file
   ├─ DAEAD keyset (AES-256-SIV)  → encrypts PREF KEYS (deterministic → lookups work)
   └─ AEAD  keyset (AES-256-GCM)  → encrypts PREF VALUES (random nonce, key as AAD)
        │
        ▼
  secure_prefs.xml  → Base64(ciphertext) for both key and value

Trade-offs

Benefit Cost
Drop-in replacement for SharedPreferencesSlower (encryption on every read/write)
Master key in Keystore — hardware-backedAlpha/beta API — can have migration issues between versions
Protects against offline storage accessDoes not protect a rooted live device

Migration from plain SharedPreferences

There is no automatic migration. You must read old plain prefs, write to encrypted prefs, and delete the old file. Do this once at app startup.

EncryptedFile

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "EncryptedFile is the Jetpack Security wrapper for storing arbitrary files encrypted with AES-256-GCM, with the master key sitting in the Android Keystore. Under the covers it uses Tink's streaming AEAD, so it chunks the file into segments and encrypts each one independently — that's what lets you stream large files without holding the whole thing in memory. The gotcha interviewers like is that it's not seekable: because every segment is GCM-authenticated, you can't random-access into the middle, and you can't recover anything if a segment is corrupted."

Definition

EncryptedFile from Jetpack Security gives you AES-256-GCM file encryption backed by the Android Keystore. Use it whenever you need to store sensitive files — PDFs, images, large JSON blobs — that must stay unreadable even if someone extracts the device storage or pulls an ADB backup.

How it works

Internally uses Tink's StreamingAead — the file is split into 4KB segments, each encrypted with AES-256-GCM. The key is derived from the master Keystore key.

fun writeEncryptedFile(context: Context, filename: String, data: ByteArray) {
    val masterKey = MasterKey.Builder(context)
        .setKeyScheme(MasterKey.KeyScheme.AES256_GCM)
        .build()

    val file = File(context.filesDir, filename)

    val encryptedFile = EncryptedFile.Builder(
        context,
