        file,
        masterKey,
        EncryptedFile.FileEncryptionScheme.AES256_GCM_HKDF_4KB
    ).build()

    encryptedFile.openFileOutput().use { outputStream ->
        outputStream.write(data)
    }
}

fun readEncryptedFile(context: Context, filename: String): ByteArray {
    val masterKey = MasterKey.Builder(context)
        .setKeyScheme(MasterKey.KeyScheme.AES256_GCM)
        .build()

    val file = File(context.filesDir, filename)

    val encryptedFile = EncryptedFile.Builder(
        context,
        file,
        masterKey,
        EncryptedFile.FileEncryptionScheme.AES256_GCM_HKDF_4KB
    ).build()

    return encryptedFile.openFileInput().use { inputStream ->
        inputStream.readBytes()
    }
}

When to use EncryptedFile vs EncryptedSharedPreferences

  • EncryptedSharedPreferences: key-value pairs, configuration, tokens, flags.
  • EncryptedFile: arbitrary binary data — PDFs, user documents, large JSON blobs, offline cache of sensitive content.

Failure modes

  • Passing a non-empty existing file to EncryptedFile.Builder where the file was NOT written by EncryptedFile → IOException on read.
  • Creating two EncryptedFile instances with different master keys for the same file → decryption failure.

Under the hood

The scheme name AES256_GCM_HKDF_4KB describes the actual mechanics: Tink generates a random Data Encryption Key (DEK) per file and wraps it — together with the Keystore master key — using HKDF to derive a unique per-segment key. The file layout is a header (containing the salt/nonce-prefix and segment size) followed by 4KB ciphertext segments. Each segment gets its own derived key + nonce where the nonce encodes the segment index plus a "last segment" flag, so an attacker can't truncate, reorder, or splice segments without GCM tag verification failing. The master key itself does symmetric AES-GCM in the Keystore; on hardware-backed devices that wrap/unwrap never exposes raw key bytes to the app process.

[ header: magic | DEK params | nonce-prefix ]
[ seg 0: nonce(prefix+0)      | ciphertext | GCM tag ]
[ seg 1: nonce(prefix+1)      | ciphertext | GCM tag ]
...
[ seg N: nonce(prefix+N+last) | ciphertext | GCM tag ]   <- last-segment bit set

Token Storage

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "Where I store auth tokens is a security decision, because a stolen token usually means a stolen session. My default is EncryptedSharedPreferences with the master key in the Keystore — AES-256-GCM at rest, key never leaves secure hardware. For the most sensitive material I drop to the Keystore directly and persist only ciphertext plus IV. The nuance is that 'encrypted at rest' doesn't protect a running, unlocked app — if the process is compromised the plaintext is in memory, so the real defenses are short token lifetimes, rotation, and server-side revocation."

Definition

Where and how you store authentication tokens — session tokens, OAuth access and refresh tokens, JWTs — is one of the highest-impact security decisions you make in a mobile app, because a stolen token is often equivalent to a stolen identity.

Storage options ranked by security

Option Security Notes
Android Keystore (key only)HighestKey never leaves hardware; use to encrypt the token
EncryptedSharedPreferencesHighAES-256-GCM, master key in Keystore
Internal storage (plain)MediumUID-isolated, but readable with root or ADB backup
SharedPreferences (plain)MediumSame as internal storage; XML readable with ADB backup on pre-M devices
External storageLowWorld-readable; avoid entirely for tokens
Hardcoded in code/resourcesNoneDecompilable; never do this

Best practice recommendation

// Pattern: store auth token in EncryptedSharedPreferences
class TokenRepository(context: Context) {

    private val prefs: SharedPreferences by lazy {
        val masterKey = MasterKey.Builder(context)
            .setKeyScheme(MasterKey.KeyScheme.AES256_GCM)
            .build()

        EncryptedSharedPreferences.create(
            context,
            "token_store",
            masterKey,
            EncryptedSharedPreferences.PrefKeyEncryptionScheme.AES256_SIV,
            EncryptedSharedPreferences.PrefValueEncryptionScheme.AES256_GCM
        )
    }

    fun saveToken(token: String) {
        prefs.edit().putString(KEY_AUTH_TOKEN, token).apply()
    }

    fun getToken(): String? = prefs.getString(KEY_AUTH_TOKEN, null)

    fun clearToken() {
        prefs.edit().remove(KEY_AUTH_TOKEN).apply()
    }

    companion object {
        private const val KEY_AUTH_TOKEN = "auth_token"
    }
}

For ultra-sensitive tokens: Keystore-encrypted

// Store the token encrypted with a Keystore key
// The raw token never persists to disk — only ciphertext + IV do
class KeystoreTokenRepository(context: Context) {
    private val prefs = context.getSharedPreferences("ks_token_store", Context.MODE_PRIVATE)
    private val keyAlias = "token_key"

    init {
        if (!KeyStore.getInstance("AndroidKeyStore").apply { load(null) }.containsAlias(keyAlias)) {
            generateAesKey(keyAlias)
        }
    }

    fun saveToken(token: String) {
        val (iv, ciphertext) = encrypt(keyAlias, token.toByteArray(Charsets.UTF_8))
        prefs.edit()
            .putString("iv", Base64.encodeToString(iv, Base64.DEFAULT))
            .putString("ct", Base64.encodeToString(ciphertext, Base64.DEFAULT))
            .apply()
    }

    fun getToken(): String? {
        val ivB64 = prefs.getString("iv", null) ?: return null
        val ctB64 = prefs.getString("ct", null) ?: return null
        val iv = Base64.decode(ivB64, Base64.DEFAULT)
        val ct = Base64.decode(ctB64, Base64.DEFAULT)
        return try {
            decrypt(keyAlias, iv, ct).toString(Charsets.UTF_8)
        } catch (e: Exception) {
            null // Key invalidated (e.g., new biometric enrolled)
        }
    }
}

Interview answer: "Where do you store auth tokens?"

"I store auth tokens in EncryptedSharedPreferences backed by a Keystore master key. That gives AES-256-GCM encryption at rest, with the key never leaving the secure hardware on supported devices. For extremely sensitive flows — like a private signing key — I go a level lower and use the Keystore directly, storing only the ciphertext and IV on disk. I never use plain SharedPreferences, external storage, or hardcoded values."

Under the hood

EncryptedSharedPreferences is not a special preferences implementation — it's a decorator over a normal XML-backed SharedPreferences. Keys are encrypted deterministically with AES-256-SIV (deterministic so getString(key) can still look up the right entry without leaking the plaintext key), while values use randomized AES-256-GCM. Both the key and value encryption keys are wrapped by the Keystore master key via Tink's keyset, and the encrypted keyset itself lives in its own prefs file. On disk you see Base64-encoded ciphertext for both the XML key and the value:

<map>
  <string name="Afh2k...(SIV-encrypted key)">  Hk9...(GCM ct: nonce|ciphertext|tag)  </string>
</map>

The hardware-backed guarantee comes from the Keystore daemon (keystore2/Keymaster TEE): the app sends ciphertext to the TEE for unwrap and gets back the usable key only inside that trust boundary on StrongBox/TEE devices. On devices without hardware backing the master key is software-protected, so "key never leaves hardware" is conditional on device capability — worth stating explicitly in an interview.

Biometrics

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "I always use Jetpack's BiometricPrompt — FingerprintManager is deprecated and flaky on modern devices. There are two modes: authentication-only, where I just learn the user passed and then trust my own logic, and crypto-bound, where I gate an actual Keystore key behind the biometric so nothing decrypts unless auth genuinely succeeded. The crypto-bound mode is the strong one because authentication-only can be bypassed by a compromised app that just skips the check. The key gotcha is setInvalidatedByBiometricEnrollment(true) — without it, an attacker who enrolls a new fingerprint after stealing the device can unlock your key."

Definition

The BiometricPrompt API in the Jetpack Biometric library gives you a single, unified interface for fingerprint, face, and iris authentication. It is the right API to use — the older FingerprintManager is deprecated and broken on many Android 10+ devices.

Two modes

  1. Authentication only (no Keystore key): verify the user is present; you handle what happens after.
  2. Crypto-bound authentication: tie a Keystore key to biometric auth — the key is only unlocked after biometric passes.

Authentication only

val executor = ContextCompat.getMainExecutor(this)
val biometricPrompt = BiometricPrompt(this, executor, object : BiometricPrompt.AuthenticationCallback() {
    override fun onAuthenticationSucceeded(result: BiometricPrompt.AuthenticationResult) {
        // User authenticated — proceed
        unlockFeature()
    }
    override fun onAuthenticationError(errorCode: Int, errString: CharSequence) {
        // Permanent error (lockout, no hardware, etc.)
        showError(errString.toString())
    }
    override fun onAuthenticationFailed() {
        // Single attempt failed (wrong finger) — prompt stays open automatically
    }
})

val promptInfo = BiometricPrompt.PromptInfo.Builder()
    .setTitle("Authenticate")
    .setSubtitle("Use your biometric to access the app")
    .setNegativeButtonText("Use PIN instead")
    .setAllowedAuthenticators(
        BiometricManager.Authenticators.BIOMETRIC_STRONG or
        BiometricManager.Authenticators.DEVICE_CREDENTIAL // API 30+
    )
    .build()

biometricPrompt.authenticate(promptInfo)

Crypto-bound biometric — strongest pattern

// Step 1: Generate a key that requires per-use biometric auth
fun generateBiometricKey(alias: String) {
    val keyGenerator = KeyGenerator.getInstance(KeyProperties.KEY_ALGORITHM_AES, "AndroidKeyStore")
    keyGenerator.init(
        KeyGenParameterSpec.Builder(alias, KeyProperties.PURPOSE_ENCRYPT or KeyProperties.PURPOSE_DECRYPT)
            .setBlockModes(KeyProperties.BLOCK_MODE_GCM)
            .setEncryptionPaddings(KeyProperties.ENCRYPTION_PADDING_NONE)
            .setUserAuthenticationRequired(true)
            .setUserAuthenticationValidityDurationSeconds(-1) // per-use, not time-window
            .setInvalidatedByBiometricEnrollment(true)
            .build()
    )
    keyGenerator.generateKey()
}

// Step 2: Create a Cipher initialized with the key — this triggers biometric prompt
fun getCipher(alias: String): Cipher {
    val keyStore = KeyStore.getInstance("AndroidKeyStore").apply { load(null) }
    val secretKey = keyStore.getKey(alias, null) as SecretKey
    val cipher = Cipher.getInstance("AES/GCM/NoPadding")
    cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, secretKey) // This doesn't fail yet
    return cipher
}

// Step 3: Show biometric prompt with the crypto object
fun authenticateWithCrypto(cipher: Cipher) {
    val cryptoObject = BiometricPrompt.CryptoObject(cipher)
    biometricPrompt.authenticate(promptInfo, cryptoObject)
    // In onAuthenticationSucceeded, result.cryptoObject?.cipher is the unlocked cipher
}

Checking biometric availability

val biometricManager = BiometricManager.from(context)
when (biometricManager.canAuthenticate(BiometricManager.Authenticators.BIOMETRIC_STRONG)) {
    BiometricManager.BIOMETRIC_SUCCESS -> { /* available */ }
    BiometricManager.BIOMETRIC_ERROR_NO_HARDWARE -> { /* no biometric hardware */ }
    BiometricManager.BIOMETRIC_ERROR_HW_UNAVAILABLE -> { /* temporarily unavailable */ }
    BiometricManager.BIOMETRIC_ERROR_NONE_ENROLLED -> {
        // Prompt user to enroll
        val enrollIntent = Intent(Settings.ACTION_BIOMETRIC_ENROLL)
        startActivity(enrollIntent)
    }
}

Failure modes

  • Using deprecated FingerprintManager — broken on many Android 10+ devices.
  • Not handling BIOMETRIC_ERROR_LOCKOUT and BIOMETRIC_ERROR_LOCKOUT_PERMANENT — user gets locked out with no path forward.
  • Using time-based auth validity (setUserAuthenticationValidityDurationSeconds(30)) for sensitive operations — a compromised app could use the unlocked window.
  • Ignoring setInvalidatedByBiometricEnrollment(true) — a new biometric added by an attacker (after stealing the device) would give them access.

Under the hood

The reason crypto-bound auth is cryptographically meaningful is that the authorization gate lives inside the TEE/Keymaster, not in your app's Java/Kotlin code. When you call cipher.init() on a key created with setUserAuthenticationRequired(true), Keymaster marks the key operation as "needs auth" but doesn't fail yet — it allocates an operation handle. The biometric sensor's hardware (running in its own trusted environment) produces a signed Hardware Auth Token (HAT) on a successful match. BiometricPrompt hands that HAT to Keymaster, which verifies the token's HMAC and timestamp before allowing doFinal(). With validity duration -1 (per-use), Keymaster ties the HAT to that specific operation handle, so the unlocked cipher can be used exactly once. setInvalidatedByBiometricEnrollment(true) works because the key is bound to the current biometric enrollment's secure ID (SID); enrolling a new fingerprint rotates that SID, permanently invalidating the key — that's why your decrypt() throws KeyPermanentlyInvalidatedException and the getToken() catch returns null.

sensor match (TEE) ──► signed HAT (HMAC + timestamp + SID)
        │
        ▼
BiometricPrompt ──► Keymaster verifies HAT ──► authorizes cipher.doFinal()
        │                                            │
   new enrollment ──► biometric SID rotates ──► key tied to old SID is dead

TLS

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "TLS encrypts everything in transit, and from API 28 Android blocks cleartext by default, so I almost never opt back in. I configure trust declaratively through the Network Security Config rather than touching socket code — I keep only system CAs in the base config and push user-CA trust into debug-overrides so Charles works in debug but production stays locked down. The classic interview trap is the trust-all TrustManager: people paste one in to silence a handshake error and it silently disables all certificate validation, which is strictly worse than no TLS because it looks secure."

Definition

Transport Layer Security (TLS) encrypts all data in transit between your app and your servers. Android enforces it by default from API 28 onwards — cleartext traffic is blocked unless you explicitly opt in, which you should almost never do in production.

Network Security Config

Android's Network Security Config (XML) lets you declaratively configure TLS behavior without code changes.

<!-- res/xml/network_security_config.xml -->
<network-security-config>
    <!-- Production: require TLS, no cleartext, no user CAs -->
    <base-config cleartextTrafficPermitted="false">
        <trust-anchors>
            <certificates src="system" />
            <!-- Do NOT include: <certificates src="user" /> in production -->
        </trust-anchors>
    </base-config>

    <!-- Debug-only: allow user-installed CAs for proxy tools like Charles -->
    <debug-overrides>
        <trust-anchors>
            <certificates src="system" />
            <certificates src="user" />
        </trust-anchors>
    </debug-overrides>

    <!-- Allow cleartext for specific domains (legacy API, avoid in new code) -->
    <domain-config cleartextTrafficPermitted="true">
        <domain includeSubdomains="false">legacy.internal.api.com</domain>
    </domain-config>
</network-security-config>
<!-- AndroidManifest.xml -->
<application
    android:networkSecurityConfig="@xml/network_security_config"
    ...>

Key defaults by API level

API Default cleartext User CAs trusted
< 24PermittedYes
24–27PermittedNo (debug builds: yes)
28+Not permittedNo

Retrofit + OkHttp TLS

// Retrofit respects the system TLS config automatically.
// Override TLS version/cipher suites if you need stricter control:
val tlsSpecs = ConnectionSpec.Builder(ConnectionSpec.MODERN_TLS)
    .tlsVersions(TlsVersion.TLS_1_3, TlsVersion.TLS_1_2)
    .cipherSuites(
        CipherSuite.TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384,
        CipherSuite.TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256,
        CipherSuite.TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256,
        CipherSuite.TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
    )
    .build()

val client = OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .connectionSpecs(listOf(tlsSpecs))
    .build()

Failure modes

  • cleartextTrafficPermitted="true" in production Network Security Config → credentials sent in plaintext.
  • <certificates src="user" /> in production config → man-in-the-middle trivially possible with a user-installed CA (the exact scenario proxy tools exploit).
  • Calling setSSLSocketFactory with a trust-all TrustManager → completely disables certificate validation.
// NEVER DO THIS — it defeats all TLS security
val trustAll = object : X509TrustManager {
    override fun checkClientTrusted(chain: Array<X509Certificate>, authType: String) {}
    override fun checkServerTrusted(chain: Array<X509Certificate>, authType: String) {}
    override fun getAcceptedIssuers(): Array<X509Certificate> = emptyArray()
}

Under the hood

The Network Security Config isn't enforced by some background daemon — at process start the framework parses your XML into an ApplicationConfig, and the platform's default SSLContext/TrustManagerFactory is initialized with a NetworkSecurityTrustManager that consults that config. So when OkHttp does a handshake through the default SSLSocketFactory, the platform X509TrustManager.checkServerTrusted() walks the presented certificate chain up to a configured trust anchor, checking signatures, validity dates, and basic-constraints/key-usage extensions. Cleartext enforcement is a separate hook: NetworkSecurityPolicy.isCleartextTrafficPermitted() is queried by the HTTP stack (and URL/OkHttp) before opening a plaintext socket, and from API 28 the default verdict is false. The trust-all TrustManager is dangerous precisely because it replaces that platform trust manager with one whose checkServerTrusted is empty — no exception thrown means "valid," so the handshake completes against any certificate including an attacker's self-signed one.

handshake ──► platform X509TrustManager.checkServerTrusted(chain, authType)
                 │  walk chain → match a trust anchor from NSC
                 │  verify signatures + validity + extensions
                 └─ throws CertificateException on failure  (empty override = always "trusted")
plaintext open ──► NetworkSecurityPolicy.isCleartextTrafficPermitted(host)  (false by default on 28+)

Certificate Pinning

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "Pinning makes the app reject any cert that doesn't match a public key I've shipped, even if a trusted CA signed it — so it defends against a rogue or compromised CA, which standard TLS can't. I pin the SPKI hash, not the leaf cert, so it survives renewal as long as the key pair is reused, and I always ship a backup pin plus an expiration date. The big operational gotcha is rotation: if you push a new cert without a backup pin already in the field, every un-updated user loses connectivity and you can't fix it remotely — that's the failure mode that turns pinning into a self-inflicted outage."

Definition

Certificate pinning makes your app reject any TLS certificate that doesn't match a specific public key or certificate you've embedded in the app — even if that certificate was signed by a trusted CA. The key insight is that it defends against scenarios where the CA itself is compromised, rogue, or coerced: a nation-state MITM, a rogue CA issuing a fraudulent cert for your domain, or a corporate proxy intercepting traffic.

How it works

Instead of trusting the entire CA chain, you embed a hash of the server's public key (or certificate) in your app. At connection time, you compare the server's presented public key against your pinned hash.

Network Security Config pinning (recommended)

<!-- res/xml/network_security_config.xml -->
<network-security-config>
    <domain-config>
        <domain includeSubdomains="true">api.yourapp.com</domain>
        <pin-set expiration="2027-01-01">
            <!-- SHA-256 hash of the Subject Public Key Info (SPKI) -->
            <!-- Primary pin (current certificate) -->
            <pin digest="SHA-256">abc123...base64hash...</pin>
            <!-- Backup pin (next certificate, ready for rotation) -->
            <pin digest="SHA-256">def456...base64hash...</pin>
        </pin-set>
    </domain-config>
</network-security-config>

Getting the pin value:

# Extract SPKI hash from a certificate
openssl x509 -in cert.pem -pubkey -noout | \
  openssl pkey -pubin -outform DER | \
  openssl dgst -sha256 -binary | \
  openssl enc -base64

OkHttp CertificatePinner (programmatic)

val certificatePinner = CertificatePinner.Builder()
    .add("api.yourapp.com", "sha256/abc123...base64...")  // primary
    .add("api.yourapp.com", "sha256/def456...base64...")  // backup
    .build()

val client = OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .certificatePinner(certificatePinner)
    .build()

Pin rotation strategy

Pin rotation is the hardest operational challenge with certificate pinning. If you deploy a new certificate without a backup pin already shipped in the app, users on old versions lose connectivity to your server, and you have to support the old pins until the whole userbase has updated.

Best practice:

  1. Always include a backup pin — the next certificate's SPKI hash — so you can rotate without a blackout window.
  2. Set an expiration date in Network Security Config — after expiry, pinning is disabled and the app falls back to standard CA validation, which prevents a permanent hard lockout for old app versions that can't be updated.
  3. Pin the SPKI (the public key hash) rather than the full certificate — that way the pin survives certificate renewal as long as the same key pair is reused.

When to use certificate pinning

  • Financial apps, health apps, any app handling highly sensitive data where a rogue CA attack is a realistic threat.
  • Apps that communicate with a small number of known, controlled API endpoints.
  • Do NOT pin if: your API is behind a CDN that rotates certificates frequently, or if you can't guarantee app updates before certificate expiry.

Trade-offs

Benefit Cost
Defeats rogue CA / MITM attacksCertificate rotation can hard-break old app versions
Visible in code reviewBlocks legitimate corporate TLS inspection proxies
Works with Network Security Config (no code)Harder to test — requires debug bypass

Debug bypass for testing with Charles/mitmproxy

<debug-overrides>
    <!-- In debug: disable pinning so you can inspect traffic -->
    <trust-anchors>
        <certificates src="system" />
        <certificates src="user" />
    </trust-anchors>
</debug-overrides>

The <debug-overrides> block only applies to debuggable="true" builds — pinning remains enforced in production.

Failure modes

  • Pinning only the leaf certificate (not SPKI) → broken at every certificate renewal.
  • No backup pin → any certificate rotation causes connection failures.
  • No expiry date → old unpatchable app versions are permanently broken.
  • Pinning in an app with a very long tail of old versions → operational nightmare.

Under the hood

A pin is a Base64-encoded SHA-256 digest of the certificate's SubjectPublicKeyInfo (SPKI) — the DER-encoded structure holding the algorithm identifier plus the raw public key, not the whole certificate. Pinning happens after normal chain validation, not instead of it: OkHttp's CertificatePinner (and the platform's NSC pinning path) first lets the standard TrustManager verify the chain to a trusted anchor, then iterates every certificate in the verified chain, computes sha256(cert.publicKey.encoded), and checks whether any of them matches any configured pin. That "any cert in chain" behavior is why you can pin an intermediate or root rather than the leaf and survive leaf rotation. Because the hash is over the public key, reusing the same key pair across renewals keeps the pin valid. The NSC expiration attribute is checked against the current date at parse/connection time; once past it, the pin-set is simply ignored and validation falls back to CA trust — a deliberate safety valve so an un-updatable build isn't bricked forever.

// Conceptually, per connection after chain validation succeeds:
for (cert in verifiedChain) {
    val spkiHash = sha256(cert.publicKey.encoded) // DER SubjectPublicKeyInfo
    if (configuredPins.contains("sha256/" + base64(spkiHash))) return // pass
}
throw SSLPeerUnverifiedException("Certificate pinning failure")

Rooted Device Limitations

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "Root gives a user-space process UID 0, which breaks the core Android assumption that the app sandbox boundary is inviolable — so file permissions, in-process secrets, and SSL pinning all become bypassable with tools like Frida. My honest position is that you can't fully secure an app against a rooted device the attacker physically owns; the goal is to raise cost, not achieve impossibility. So I layer defenses: hardware-isolated keys via StrongBox so even root can't extract key material, server-verifiable attestation through the Play Integrity API, and root detection used to fail gracefully and log server-side — never as a hard barrier I pretend is unbreakable."

Definition

A rooted Android device makes UID 0 (root) access available to user-space processes. Root breaks the foundational assumption of the Android security model — that the app UID boundary is inviolable — which means every defence you've built on top of that boundary becomes weaker or irrelevant.

What root access enables (threat model)

Attack Mechanism
Read private filesRoot bypasses filesystem permissions
Extract Keystore keysOn devices without StrongBox, root can access the Keystore daemon's memory or storage
Read process memoryRoot can ptrace your app process and dump the heap
Modify app code at runtimeFrida/JDWP hooking, method swizzling
Bypass SSL pinningFrida scripts to hook OkHttp's certificate pinner
Disable ProGuard obfuscation effectJadx/apktool decompile the APK

What you can do (and their limits)

1. Detect root (defense in depth, not a hard barrier)

// Using RootBeer library (or implement manually)
val rootBeer = RootBeer(context)
if (rootBeer.isRooted) {
    // Warn the user or limit functionality
    // Do NOT silently stop working — that's a bad UX with no explanation
}

Manual checks (can each be individually bypassed by a determined attacker):

fun isDeviceRooted(): Boolean {
    // Check 1: su binary present
    val suPaths = listOf("/system/bin/su", "/system/xbin/su", "/sbin/su")
    if (suPaths.any { File(it).exists() }) return true

    // Check 2: Test Tags (build props on production ROMs)
    if (Build.TAGS?.contains("test-keys") == true) return true

    // Check 3: Can we execute su?
    return try {
        Runtime.getRuntime().exec(arrayOf("/system/xbin/su", "-c", "id"))
        true
    } catch (e: IOException) {
        false
    }
}

2. Use StrongBox-backed keys

On Pixel and other StrongBox-equipped devices, keys are in a separate secure element — root on the application processor cannot extract them.

3. Integrity checks: Google Play Integrity API

val integrityManager = IntegrityManagerFactory.create(context)
val request = StandardIntegrityManager.StandardIntegrityTokenRequest.builder()
    .setRequestHash(requestHash)
    .build()
integrityManager.requestIntegrityToken(request)
    .addOnSuccessListener { response ->
        // Send response.token() to your backend for verification
        // Backend verifies: device integrity, app integrity, account details
    }

The Play Integrity API verdict distinguishes: MEETS_DEVICE_INTEGRITY, MEETS_BASIC_INTEGRITY, NO_INTEGRITY.

4. SafetyNet Attestation (deprecated — prefer Play Integrity)

SafetyNet was deprecated in June 2023. Existing integrations continue to work until further notice, but migrate to Play Integrity.

Honest interview answer on the limits

"No mobile app can be fully secured against a rooted device with physical access and unlimited time — that's just the reality of running on hardware you don't control. The goal of root detection isn't to make attack impossible; it's to raise the cost. So the right layered approach is: use Keystore keys, preferably StrongBox-backed, so the key material is hardware-isolated even from a root process; use the Play Integrity API to get a server-verifiable attestation of device and app state; and do root detection to fail gracefully — warn the user and log the event server-side — rather than pretending you can stop a determined attacker."

Under the hood

Root detection is fundamentally a client-side signal that the client itself can lie about, which is why server-side attestation matters. The Play Integrity verdict is meaningful because it's rooted in hardware the app can't forge: the device produces a token signed by a key whose chain ultimately attests back to a Google-provisioned hardware-backed key in the TEE/StrongBox, and that token is encrypted/signed such that only Google's servers (or your backend after Google decodes it) can validate it. That's the structural difference from RootBeer — isRooted returns a boolean your own process computes, so a Frida hook can simply patch the method to return false. Likewise StrongBox raises the bar because Keymaster runs in a physically separate secure element with its own CPU and storage; the application-processor root can ptrace your app and dump heap, but it never sees the key bytes because crypto operations execute inside that element and only inputs/outputs cross the boundary. The takeaway interviewers want: trust must terminate on the server against a hardware root of trust, because anything evaluated purely in-process is bypassable on a rooted device.

in-process check (RootBeer.isRooted)  ──► attacker hooks method → returns false   (untrusted)
Play Integrity ──► TEE/StrongBox-signed token ──► your backend verifies via Google  (trusted)
StrongBox key ──► crypto runs in separate secure element; only I/O crosses boundary  (key bytes never exposed)

Avoiding Hardcoded Secrets

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "My baseline assumption is that anything shipped inside the APK is public — a jadx decompile recovers every string literal in minutes, including values in BuildConfig and res/values/. So real secrets like API keys, server credentials, or symmetric keys can't live in the binary at all; they belong behind a backend proxy or get delivered at runtime over authenticated TLS and stored in EncryptedSharedPreferences. The gotcha interviewers love is the obfuscation myth: R8 renames identifiers but leaves string constants intact, so it does nothing to hide a secret."

Definition

Hardcoded secrets are API keys, tokens, passwords, or cryptographic keys embedded directly in source code, resource files, or compiled bytecode. The problem is not theoretical — Android APKs are trivially decompilable, and any string literal in your code is recoverable in minutes.

Why it's a problem

Android APKs are trivially decompilable with tools like jadx, apktool, or even online services. Any string in your code, BuildConfig, or res/values/ is recoverable from the APK in minutes — even with ProGuard/R8 obfuscation applied, because R8 renames identifiers but does not encrypt string literals.

What counts as a secret

  • API keys for third-party services (Firebase, Maps, Stripe).
  • Server-side credentials.
  • Cryptographic keys (symmetric keys, private keys).
  • Hardcoded passwords or salts that are meaningful without context.

What does NOT need protection

  • Public keys (by definition public).
  • API keys for client-side-only services designed to be public (like a public Maps embed key with domain restrictions) — though even these should be restricted on the server side.

Mitigations

Approach Use case
Backend proxyThe mobile app calls your backend, which holds the API key and proxies to the third-party service. The mobile app never sees the key.
Runtime key deliveryKey is fetched from your server at runtime (over TLS + authenticated) and stored in EncryptedSharedPreferences. Never in the APK.
Firebase Remote Config / AWS SSMKey is stored server-side and fetched at runtime.
Android KeystoreFor keys generated on-device — they never exist outside the device, so there's nothing to hardcode.
Restricted API keysSome services (Google Maps) allow domain/package/certificate restrictions on the key. Even if extracted, the key is unusable from another app or server.

ProGuard/R8 does NOT protect secrets

A common misconception is that obfuscation hides secrets. R8 renames identifiers but leaves string literals intact, so jadx will find "sk_live_abc123" in your code regardless of how thoroughly you've obfuscated everything else.

Detecting hardcoded secrets in code review

# Search for common patterns
grep -rn "api_key\|apikey\|secret\|password\|passwd\|token" app/src/ --include="*.kt" --include="*.java"

# Tools: truffleHog, gitleaks, GitHub secret scanning

Build-time injection (acceptable for non-sensitive config)

// build.gradle.kts — value comes from environment variable, not committed
android {
    buildTypes {
        release {
            buildConfigField("String", "API_BASE_URL", "\"${System.getenv("API_BASE_URL")}\"")
        }
    }
}

This is acceptable for non-secret config values (base URLs, feature flag service URLs). Still visible in the APK via BuildConfig, but not a secret per se. Never use this pattern for API keys or tokens.

Under the hood

A string literal in Kotlin/Java is compiled into the class file's constant pool as a CONSTANT_Utf8_info entry referenced by a CONSTANT_String_info; at the use site the compiler emits an ldc bytecode that loads that constant by index. R8 operates on this bytecode — it rewrites the name pool (class/method/field identifiers) and prunes dead code, but the UTF-8 constant pool entries holding your literal bytes are left verbatim because the program's behavior depends on them. BuildConfig fields compile to static final fields whose initializers are also constant-pool literals (or inlined ldcs). A decompiler like jadx simply walks the constant pool and reconstructs the literals, which is why obfuscation never hides a secret. Even runtime XOR/Base64 "encoding" only adds a trivially reversible transform that an attacker can replay by calling the same decode routine via Frida.

const-string v0, "sk_live_abc123"   # dex/smali: literal lives in the string_id pool
# R8 may rename the enclosing class to a.b.c, but "sk_live_abc123" is untouched

Logging Sensitive Data

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "Logcat is a shared, unencrypted ring buffer, so my rule is that secrets, tokens, and PII never get written to it — not even in debug, because debug logs leak through ADB and through crash SDKs that snapshot recent Logcat lines. In release I strip Log.d/Log.v with R8's assumenosideeffects and route everything through a Timber tree that scrubs before it ships anything to Crashlytics or Sentry. The subtle gotcha is toString() on a data class — the auto-generated one prints every property, so a token field silently lands in your logs unless you override it."

Definition

Android's Logcat is a system-wide, unencrypted log buffer. Any app with READ_LOGS permission — or root — can read every line in it, and crash-reporting SDKs routinely capture recent log output and ship it to their servers. That means sensitive data written to Logcat doesn't just sit on the device; it can travel off it.

The problem

Before API 19, any app could read Logcat. From API 19 onwards, only apps with READ_LOGS — a signature-level permission granted to some system apps — or root can read other apps' logs. But that still leaves three real exposure paths. First, developer devices with ADB enabled expose the entire Logcat to anyone with USB access. Second, crash reporting SDKs like Sentry and Firebase Crashlytics may capture recent Logcat output and send it to their servers. And third, some OEM apps ship with READ_LOGS, so production Logcat is not private even without root.

Rules

// NEVER LOG:
Log.d("Auth", "Token: $authToken")              // token in log
Log.d("User", "Password: $password")             // password
Log.d("Profile", "SSN: ${user.ssn}")             // PII
Log.d("Payment", "Card: ${card.number}")         // card number

// OK IN DEBUG, NEVER IN RELEASE:
if (BuildConfig.DEBUG) {
    Log.d("Network", "Response: $responseBody")  // may contain PII
}

// SAFE:
Log.d("Auth", "Token refreshed successfully")    // no token value
Log.d("Network", "Request failed with code: $code")
Log.e("Payment", "Payment failed: ${error.code}")

Using ProGuard/R8 to strip debug logs

# Strip Log.d and Log.v calls in release builds
-assumenosideeffects class android.util.Log {
    public static int d(...);
    public static int v(...);
}

Timber (logging library) pattern

// Plant debug tree only in debug builds
if (BuildConfig.DEBUG) {
    Timber.plant(Timber.DebugTree())
} else {
    Timber.plant(CrashReportingTree()) // custom tree that filters PII
}

class CrashReportingTree : Timber.Tree() {
    override fun log(priority: Int, tag: String?, message: String, t: Throwable?) {
        if (priority < Log.WARN) return // only warn+ in production
        // Scrub before sending to crash reporter
        val scrubbed = message.replace(TOKEN_REGEX, "[TOKEN]")
        Sentry.captureMessage(scrubbed)
    }
}

Crash reporter configuration

Configure your crash reporting SDK to exclude certain fields:

// Sentry example — scrub sensitive breadcrumbs
SentryAndroid.init(context) { options ->
    options.beforeBreadcrumb = BeforeBreadcrumbCallback { breadcrumb, _ ->
        if (breadcrumb.category == "auth") null // drop auth breadcrumbs
        else breadcrumb
    }
    options.beforeSend = BeforeSendCallback { event, _ ->
        // Strip request bodies from network events
        event.request?.data = null
        event
    }
}

Failure modes

  • Debug logging left in release builds (ProGuard didn't strip it, or ProGuard not configured).
  • Exception messages containing sensitive data being sent to crash reporters.
  • Using toString() on data classes that include token fields in the generated output.
// Data class: toString() includes all fields — be careful
data class UserSession(
    val userId: String,
    val token: String // this will appear in any Log.d("Session", session.toString())
)

// Safer: override toString to exclude sensitive fields
data class UserSession(
    val userId: String,
    @Transient val token: String
) {
    override fun toString() = "UserSession(userId=$userId, token=[REDACTED])"
}

Under the hood

android.util.Log.d(...) ultimately calls into native __android_log_write, which writes the record into the kernel-backed logd daemon's circular buffers (the main, system, crash, etc. ring buffers) over a socket — a single shared, plaintext store with no per-app encryption; READ_LOGS (a signature|privileged permission) or root lets a reader drain those buffers. The R8 strip works because -assumenosideeffects tells the optimizer that Log.d/Log.v produce no observable effect, so it deletes the invocation and the bytecode that builds its arguments — the entire string-concatenation invokedynamic/StringBuilder chain for the message is pruned as dead code, so the literal pieces never make it into the release dex. The data class trap comes from the compiler auto-synthesizing toString(): it emits a method that appends every val/var declared in the primary constructor (via StringBuilder), so a token property is interpolated by default unless you override toString() — note that @Transient alone affects serialization, not the generated toString().

Log.d(tag, "Token: " + token)
   └─ liblog: __android_log_write() ──socket──► logd ──► /dev/socket per-buffer ring (plaintext)
                                                          ↑ drained by `adb logcat`, READ_LOGS holders, crash SDKs

Interview Q&A Master List

13.1 Security Basics

Q: How do you secure an exported component?

"There are three layers. First, don't export unless you genuinely have to — set android:exported='false' or remove intent-filters from anything that's internal to your app. Second, if it must be exported, require a signature-level custom permission so only apps signed with the same key as yours can call it. And third, treat every piece of Intent data that arrives as untrusted input: whitelist expected actions, sanitize extras, and reject anything with an unexpected shape. I also avoid doing any privileged work in response to externally-triggered Intents without first validating the caller's identity."

Q: What is intent spoofing?

"Intent spoofing is when a malicious app sends a crafted Intent to one of your exported components, either impersonating a legitimate caller or injecting malicious data to trigger behaviour you didn't intend. The root of the problem is that Android Intents carry no built-in caller authentication — any app on the device can send any Intent to any exported component. So the defence has three parts: don't export components unnecessarily, require signature-level permissions on components that must be exported, and treat every Intent extra as untrusted user input regardless of what action string it declares."

Q: Why avoid exposing file paths directly (file:// URIs)?

"There are two reasons. First, from API 24 onwards, passing a file:// URI to another app via an Intent throws FileUriExposedException — it literally crashes the app. And second, more fundamentally, a file:// URI reveals the absolute filesystem path to a private file, so any app that sees that Intent now knows where your app stores its data. FileProvider solves both problems at once: it generates a content:// URI that the OS routes through your ContentProvider, granting the receiving app temporary read access without ever exposing the underlying path. The other app calls ContentResolver.openInputStream() and gets the bytes — it never learns where those bytes came from on disk."

Q: How do you validate deep links?

"There are four steps. First, use App Links — HTTPS with android:autoVerify='true' and an assetlinks.json file — so only your app handles your domain's URLs. Custom schemes are a problem because any app can register the same scheme and intercept your links. Second, even with App Links in place, validate the scheme and host in code before you act on the link, because App Links can be bypassed on some older devices. Third, whitelist known paths and reject anything unexpected. And fourth, sanitize and range-check all query parameters as untrusted input. For OAuth deep links there's an extra step: always validate the state parameter against the one you generated before launching the flow, or you're open to CSRF."

Q: What is PendingIntent mutability and why does it matter?

"FLAG_IMMUTABLE prevents the recipient of a PendingIntent from modifying the wrapped Intent's action, component, or extras. The vulnerability with a mutable PendingIntent is that if you leave the action or component unspecified, the receiver can fill in whatever it wants — and it executes under your app's identity and your app's permissions, not theirs. That's a privilege escalation. Since API 31, omitting both flags entirely throws an IllegalArgumentException, so you have to be explicit. My rule is to default to FLAG_IMMUTABLE everywhere, and only reach for FLAG_MUTABLE in the specific cases where a system framework genuinely needs to fill in fields — for example, inline reply notifications."

13.2 Data Security

Q: Where do you store auth tokens?

"I store auth tokens in EncryptedSharedPreferences, which uses AES-256-GCM for values and AES-256-SIV for keys, with the master key living in the Android Keystore. On supported hardware that key never leaves the secure element. For extremely sensitive operations — like a private signing key — I go one level lower and use the Keystore directly: only ciphertext and the IV go to disk, and the raw key material never exists outside the Keystore. The things I never do are plain SharedPreferences — its XML is exposed in ADB backups on pre-Marshmallow devices — external storage, or any form of hardcoded value."

Q: Can you fully secure secrets in a mobile app?

"No, not fully. A mobile app runs on hardware you don't control, in the user's hands. With physical access and a rooted device, an attacker with enough time can extract almost anything from user space — they can read process memory, bypass TLS pinning with Frida, and on devices without StrongBox they can potentially access Keystore key material too. So the goal is not to make attack impossible; it's to raise the cost high enough that it's not worth it. You do that by using hardware-backed Keystore keys — preferably StrongBox-backed — so the key material is isolated even from root, by never hardcoding secrets anywhere in the APK, by using the Play Integrity API to detect compromised device states at the server level, and by architecting your backend so that a compromised client has a limited blast radius: short-lived tokens, scope-limited keys, and server-side rate limiting."

Q: What is Android Keystore and how does it work?

"Android Keystore is a system service that stores cryptographic keys in hardware-isolated storage — ideally a TEE, which is a Trusted Execution Environment within the main SoC, or a StrongBox, which is a dedicated secure element on a separate chip. Keys are bound to the app's UID, so another app can't use yours. The defining property is that key material never leaves the secure hardware in plaintext — every cryptographic operation happens inside the Keystore service, not in your process. From your code's perspective you just reference a key by alias and call standard JCE APIs like KeyGenerator and Cipher; the implementation quietly routes those operations to the hardware. You can optionally bind a key to biometric authentication, a time-based validity window, or a user presence check. Keys survive app updates but are wiped on uninstall, factory reset, and — if you set setInvalidatedByBiometricEnrollment(true) — whenever new biometrics are enrolled."

Q: When should you use certificate pinning?

"I use it in high-value apps where a rogue or compromised CA is a realistic threat — financial, health, or any app handling highly sensitive data. The conditions I need before pinning are: I control the API endpoints so I know the certificate in advance, the API doesn't rotate certificates frequently, and I can guarantee app updates before the pin expiry date. The operational discipline around it is non-negotiable. There are three rules. First, always include a backup pin for the next certificate's SPKI hash, so you can rotate without breaking users. Second, set an expiration date in Network Security Config so old app versions that can't be updated fail open — back to standard CA validation — rather than being permanently broken. Third, pin the public key hash, the SPKI, rather than the full certificate, so key reuse across renewals doesn't invalidate your pin. The cases where I wouldn't pin: APIs behind a CDN with frequent certificate rotation, or any situation where I can't control when the certificate changes."

Q: What is the difference between EncryptedSharedPreferences and using the Keystore directly?

"EncryptedSharedPreferences is a high-level drop-in replacement for SharedPreferences. It uses the Keystore to hold a master key, which in turn wraps a data encryption key that's stored alongside the prefs file. From your code's perspective, all the cipher, IV, and key management is abstracted away — you just call putString and getString like normal. The ciphertext ends up in an XML file on internal storage, protected by UID isolation plus AES-256 encryption. Using the Keystore directly means generating your own AES key, calling Cipher.init() yourself, managing the IV, and storing the ciphertext wherever you choose. The trade-off is that you get much more control: you can require biometric authentication per encryption operation, request StrongBox backing, or use an asymmetric key pair — but you're writing substantially more boilerplate. For most token storage scenarios, EncryptedSharedPreferences is the right level of abstraction. The Keystore-directly approach makes sense when you need per-operation biometric binding or you're handling something unusually sensitive."

14.1 Startup Performance

Cold Start

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "A cold start is the worst case: the process doesn't exist, so the system has to fork it from zygote, run my Application class, then build and render the first Activity. Everything in Application.onCreate() is on the critical path because the main thread is blocked until it returns. The nuance interviewers probe is the difference between TTID — the first frame drawn — and TTFD, which is when the screen is actually usable; I report the latter with reportFullyDrawn() so my metrics reflect real perceived performance, not just a skeleton."

Definition: A cold start is what happens when the app process does not exist in memory at all and the system has to spin up a brand-new process from scratch.

How it works:

  1. The system forks a new process from zygote (the pre-forked Android runtime).
  2. The app's Application class is instantiated and Application.onCreate() runs.
  3. The target Activity is created: onCreate() → onStart() → onResume().
  4. The first frame is rendered and delivered to SurfaceFlinger.

Timeline breakdown:

  • Time To Initial Display (TTID): Time until the first frame is drawn. This is what Displayed in logcat measures.
  • Time To Full Display (TTFD): Time until the app's content is fully loaded and interactive (can be reported with reportFullyDrawn()).

Under the hood

The zygote process is started by init at boot and preloads the core framework classes and shared resources, then sits blocked in a select/socket loop. When ActivityManagerService needs a new app, it asks zygote to fork() — the child inherits the already-warmed heap via copy-on-write memory pages, which is why apps don't pay to reload android.* classes. After the fork, ActivityThread.main() sets up the main Looper, calls bindApplication (which instantiates your Application), then drives the activity lifecycle through the H handler. The "Displayed" log is emitted by ActivityManagerService when it receives the first dispatchWindowsDrawn callback from the window's ViewRootImpl after the first Choreographer frame completes.

init → zygote (preloaded classes, blocked on socket)
         │ fork() + COW pages
         ▼
ActivityThread.main() → Looper.prepareMainLooper()
         │ bindApplication → new Application(); onCreate()
         ▼
handleLaunchActivity → Activity onCreate/onStart/onResume
         │ ViewRootImpl.performTraversals → first Choreographer frame
         ▼
dispatchWindowsDrawn → AMS logs "Displayed"

Android implications:

  • Cold start is measured from when the user taps the launcher icon to when the first frame appears.
  • The system displays a splash screen window (preview window) immediately from windowBackground theme attribute, providing visual feedback before any app code runs.
  • All Dagger component initialization, third-party SDK initialization, and database schema migrations that run in Application.onCreate() add directly to cold start time.
  • Pre-Android 12, apps controlled the splash screen entirely. Android 12+ enforces a system-managed splash screen.

Optimizing cold start:

  • Defer initialization that is not needed immediately (lazy init, background threads).
  • Use App Startup library to sequence and parallelize initializer dependencies.
  • Use Baseline Profiles so the ART JIT compiler has pre-compiled hot paths.
  • Avoid disk I/O or network calls on the main thread during startup.
  • Minimize the depth and breadth of the Dagger object graph that is constructed eagerly.

Measuring cold start:

# Force a cold start by killing the process first
adb shell am force-stop com.example.app
adb shell am start-activity -W com.example.app/.MainActivity

# Output:
# ThisTime: 847
# TotalTime: 1203
# WaitTime: 1210
  • ThisTime: Time for the last activity to start.
  • TotalTime: Time from process creation to onResume() of the first activity.
  • WaitTime: Total time including the system overhead before am start returns.

Also watch logcat for:

I/ActivityManager: Displayed com.example.app/.MainActivity: +1s203ms

Warm Start

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "A warm start is when the process is still alive but the Activity was destroyed — so Application.onCreate() is skipped, but the Activity gets fully recreated from onCreate through onResume, restoring any saved Bundle. It's typically two to three times faster than cold because class loading and the app graph are already warm. The gotcha is that it lulls you into assuming your in-memory state is always there; in production a user can always hit a true cold start after process death, so my code has to render correctly from null or empty initial state."

Definition: A warm start is when the app process is already alive in memory, but the Activity itself was destroyed — for example, the user navigated away and the system reclaimed it, or the user killed the Activity without killing the whole process.

How it works:

  • The Application object already exists — Application.onCreate() is NOT called again.
  • The system recreates the Activity from scratch: onCreate() → onStart() → onResume().
  • Saved instance state (Bundle) is restored if available.

Under the hood

In a warm start the process's main Looper is still running and the JVM has already loaded and verified the relevant classes, so there's no zygote fork or class-loading cost. ActivityManagerService simply schedules a new LaunchActivityItem on the existing ActivityThread's H handler. The saved Bundle was captured earlier in onSaveInstanceState (which serializes via Parcel into native memory held by the system_server's ActivityRecord, not your process), and it's handed back into onCreate/onRestoreInstanceState. Because that state lives in system_server, it survives the Activity object being garbage-collected — but it does NOT survive the process being killed, since the ActivityRecord is also torn down.

Android implications:

  • Warm starts are typically 2–3x faster than cold starts because process + class loading is already done.
  • Any initialization in Application.onCreate() is not repeated, but Activity.onCreate() still runs.
  • Retained ViewModel instances survive warm starts (across configuration changes), but do NOT survive process death — which triggers a cold start.

Common warm-start failure mode: Assuming ViewModel data is always populated because warm start is common during development. In production, users can always encounter a cold start; code must handle null/empty initial state gracefully.

Hot Start

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "A hot start is the best case — both the process and the Activity are still in memory, the app was just backgrounded, so the system only runs onRestart → onStart → onResume and brings the existing window forward. No object creation happens, so it's usually under a hundred milliseconds and isn't really an optimization target. What I do watch for is staleness: in-memory caches can be old if the user was gone a while, and memory pressure while backgrounded can get the process killed, silently demoting the next launch to a cold start."

Definition: A hot start is the best case — the app process and the Activity both already exist in memory, and the user has simply backgrounded the app and come back.

How it works:

  • The system simply brings the existing Activity to the foreground: onRestart() → onStart() → onResume().
  • No new object creation occurs for the Application or Activity.

Under the hood

On a hot start the Activity's Window, ViewRootImpl, and the whole decor view hierarchy are still attached and the rendered surface is still allocated in SurfaceFlinger — nothing needs re-inflation or re-measure unless something changed. The system_server's WindowManagerService just changes the window's visibility and z-order, and the existing Surface's buffers can often be composited straight away. The lifecycle callbacks fire through the same H handler, but no performTraversals re-layout is forced, which is why the cost is dominated by callback dispatch rather than rendering work.

Android implications:

  • Hot starts are extremely fast (< 100 ms typically) and are not a meaningful startup optimization target.
  • The primary concern for hot starts is state freshness: data cached in memory may be stale if the user was gone for a long time.
  • Memory pressure while backgrounded can cause the system to kill the process and degrade the next start to cold.

Application.onCreate()

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "Application.onCreate() runs exactly once when the process is created, and the main thread is blocked until it returns — so every millisecond here is paid on every cold start. The discipline is to only do work that genuinely must be ready before any code runs, like crash reporting, and defer everything else: no disk reads, no network, no eager Dagger graph. The trap interviewers love is multi-process apps — onCreate runs once per process, so a background :remote process for push or Bluetooth will redundantly build your whole UI graph unless you guard it by checking the process name."

Definition: Application.onCreate() is the single entry point that runs once when the app process is first created. It's the place every library, SDK, and framework gravitates toward for global initialization, which is exactly what makes it the most important location for startup optimization.

What happens here (and why it matters):

  • The main thread is blocked until Application.onCreate() returns.
  • Everything inside it adds directly to cold start time.
  • This is the most impactful single location for startup optimization.

What MUST happen in Application.onCreate():

  • Crash reporting initialization (Crashlytics, Sentry) — needs to be active before any crash can occur.
  • Strict mode setup (debug builds only).
  • Process-name-specific initialization (multi-process apps must guard with ProcessUtils.getProcessName() to avoid initializing UI dependencies in background processes).

What should NOT happen in Application.onCreate():

  • Database schema migration or opening database connections.
  • SharedPreferences.getSharedPreferences() calls (triggers disk read on main thread).
  • Network calls of any kind.
  • Heavy Dagger graph construction (e.g., constructing a component that transitively initializes dozens of dependencies).
  • Analytics SDK full initialization if it can be deferred.
  • Image loading library disk cache setup (Glide/Coil manage this lazily).
  • Feature flag synchronization from network.

Multi-process trap: In apps with :remote or other background processes (e.g., push notification services, Bluetooth services), Application.onCreate() runs once per process. If you initialize your Dagger component unconditionally, you're paying full initialization cost in every process. Guard with:

class MyApplication : Application() {
    override fun onCreate() {
        super.onCreate()
        if (isMainProcess()) {
            initializeMainProcessComponents()
        }
        // crash reporting is OK for all processes
        initializeCrashReporting()
    }

    private fun isMainProcess(): Boolean =
        packageName == getProcessName()
}

Under the hood

Application.onCreate() is invoked synchronously by ActivityThread.handleBindApplication(), which runs as message BIND_APPLICATION on the main Looper before any Activity launch message is processed. Crucially, ContentProvider.onCreate() for every provider declared in the manifest runs even earlier — between Application instantiation (the constructor and attachBaseContext) and Application.onCreate() — which is exactly the hook auto-init libraries exploit. Each process gets its own forked copy of the runtime, so static initializers and the Application singleton are per-process; getProcessName() reads the process name the system assigned at fork time (backed by ActivityThread.currentProcessName() on API 28+, or /proc/self/cmdline historically).

ActivityThread.handleBindApplication():
   makeApplication()        → new Application(); attachBaseContext()
   installContentProviders() → every <provider>.onCreate()   ← auto-init runs here
   mInstrumentation.callApplicationOnCreate(app) → onCreate()  ← main thread blocked
   ... only now can ActivityThread process LAUNCH_ACTIVITY ...

Lazy Initialization

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "Lazy initialization means I defer constructing an expensive object until the first access, so I keep it off the startup critical path. In Kotlin by lazy is thread-safe by default — it synchronizes the first read — and I can drop to LazyThreadSafetyMode.NONE for single-threaded access to skip that locking. The nuance is that lazy doesn't make the cost disappear, it just moves it; if that first access lands on the main thread during a user interaction it becomes jank or even an ANR, so for things I know I'll need I preload them on a background thread after startup."

Definition: Lazy initialization means deferring object construction or expensive operations until the first time they are actually needed, rather than paying the cost upfront at startup.

How it works in Kotlin:

// Property-level lazy — thread-safe by default (SYNCHRONIZED mode)
val database: AppDatabase by lazy {
    Room.databaseBuilder(context, AppDatabase::class.java, "app.db").build()
}

// LazyThreadSafetyMode.NONE — fastest, only safe if accessed from one thread
val cache: LruCache<String, Bitmap> by lazy(LazyThreadSafetyMode.NONE) {
    LruCache(maxSize)
}

Dagger lazy injection:

// Dagger provides Lazy<T> — the object is constructed on first .get() call
@Inject lateinit var expensiveService: Lazy<AnalyticsService>

fun trackEvent(event: String) {
    expensiveService.get().track(event)  // constructed only here
}

Under the hood

by lazy desugars to a synthetic backing field holding a Lazy<T> instance — by default SynchronizedLazyImpl. Its value getter checks a field against a sentinel (UNINITIALIZED_VALUE); on a miss it acquires a lock (double-checked locking) and runs your initializer lambda exactly once, then caches the result so subsequent reads are a plain field read. LazyThreadSafetyMode.NONE uses UnsafeLazyImpl, which is just an unsynchronized field check with no lock and no volatile — fast, but two threads racing can both run the initializer and see torn state. Dagger's Lazy<T> is a different mechanism: it generates a DoubleCheck provider wrapper that memoizes the result of the underlying Provider.get() factory, also via double-checked locking.

// Conceptually, what SynchronizedLazyImpl.value does:
val v1 = _value
if (v1 !== UNINITIALIZED) return v1 as T   // fast path: already set
return synchronized(lock) {
    if (_value === UNINITIALIZED) { _value = initializer() }
    _value as T
}

Android implications:

  • by lazy is ideal for singletons that are expensive to construct but used infrequently.
  • The trade-off: the first access has the full construction cost. If this happens on the main thread during a user interaction, it causes jank. Move first access to a background thread or preload on a background thread after startup.
  • Avoid lazy init for objects required immediately on every cold start — the cost is identical, just deferred.

Failure modes:

  • Lazy init on main thread during first user interaction causing dropped frames or ANR.
  • Thread-safety issues with LazyThreadSafetyMode.NONE when multiple threads access the same lazy property.
  • Circular initialization: lazy A depends on lazy B which depends on lazy A.

App Startup Library

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "App Startup is the Jetpack library that replaces the old per-library ContentProvider auto-init trick with a single shared InitializationProvider. I write Initializer<T> classes that declare their dependencies, and the library topologically sorts them into a DAG and runs them in order. The key trade-off interviewers want me to name is that everything still runs on the main thread before the first frame by default — so it's about ordering and de-duplicating ContentProviders, not about moving work off the critical path; anything not needed at first frame I'd lazily initialize instead."

Definition: The App Startup library (androidx.startup) is a Jetpack library that gives you a structured, dependency-aware way to initialize components at startup, replacing the scattered ContentProvider initialization tricks that libraries historically relied on.

Background — the ContentProvider trick: Many libraries (WorkManager, Firebase, etc.) historically used a ContentProvider to auto-initialize without requiring app code. A ContentProvider with android:initOrder runs before Application.onCreate(). The problem: each ContentProvider is a separate process boundary hook, they run sequentially, and they bloat startup time invisibly.

How App Startup works:

  1. A single InitializationProvider (one ContentProvider total, shared across all initializers) is registered in the manifest.
  2. You define Initializer<T> classes for each component.
  3. Each initializer declares its dependencies via dependencies(), forming a DAG.
  4. The library topologically sorts the DAG and runs initializers in order, on the main thread by default.
class WorkManagerInitializer : Initializer<WorkManager> {
    override fun create(context: Context): WorkManager {
        WorkManager.initialize(
            context,
            Configuration.Builder()
                .setMinimumLoggingLevel(Log.ERROR)
                .build()
        )
        return WorkManager.getInstance(context)
    }

    override fun dependencies(): List<Class<out Initializer<*>>> = emptyList()
}

class AnalyticsInitializer : Initializer<Analytics> {
    override fun create(context: Context): Analytics {
        // depends on WorkManager being ready
        return Analytics.init(context)
    }

    override fun dependencies() = listOf(WorkManagerInitializer::class.java)
}

Manifest registration:

<provider
    android:name="androidx.startup.InitializationProvider"
    android:authorities="${applicationId}.androidx-startup"
    android:exported="false"
    tools:node="merge">
    <meta-data
        android:name="com.example.WorkManagerInitializer"
        android:value="androidx.startup" />
    <!-- AnalyticsInitializer is discovered transitively via dependencies() -->
</provider>

Lazy/manual initialization: Remove the <meta-data> entry and call manually:

AppInitializer.getInstance(context)
    .initializeComponent(WorkManagerInitializer::class.java)

Trade-offs:

  • Pro: Centralizes and makes startup dependencies explicit and auditable.
  • Pro: Eliminates redundant ContentProviders.
  • Con: All initializers still run on the main thread by default; async initializers require careful handling.
  • Con: Dependency cycles produce a runtime exception at startup.

Under the hood

InitializationProvider is an ordinary ContentProvider, so the framework calls its onCreate() during ActivityThread.installContentProviders() — before Application.onCreate(). In that callback AppInitializer.discoverAndInitialize() reads the <meta-data> entries from the provider's ProviderInfo via PackageManager, then for each entry recursively resolves dependencies(), doing a depth-first traversal while tracking an "initializing" set to detect cycles (which throw IllegalStateException). Results are memoized in a mInitialized map keyed by initializer class, so a dependency shared by several initializers is only constructed once. Because the whole walk happens on the provider's onCreate on the main thread, the DAG is effectively executed sequentially in topological order — there is no built-in threading.

installContentProviders()
   InitializationProvider.onCreate()
      AppInitializer.discoverAndInitialize()
         read <meta-data> → list of Initializer classes
         for each: doInitialize(clazz, initializing=set)
            if clazz in initializing → throw (cycle)
            for dep in dependencies(): doInitialize(dep, ...)
            result = initializer.create(context)   // memoized in mInitialized

Android implications:

  • Use to replace library ContentProvider auto-init patterns (disable with tools:node="remove" in manifest merger).
  • Prefer lazy initialization over eager App Startup for anything not needed at first frame.

Baseline Profiles

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "Baseline Profiles are AOT compilation hints I ship in the APK that tell ART to natively compile my hot startup paths the moment the app installs, so I skip the JIT warm-up that normally makes the first few launches sluggish. I write a Macrobenchmark that drives the critical path, it captures which methods and classes matter, and ProfileInstaller applies it on device. The gotcha interviewers love is that the profile is useless without the profileinstaller dependency, and it goes stale as code changes — so I regenerate it in CI on a cadence."

Definition: Baseline Profiles are pre-compiled ART profiles that you ship inside your APK or AAB. The key idea is that they let the system AOT-compile your hot code paths on install, so you get native-speed execution from the very first launch instead of waiting for the JIT compiler to warm up over several runs.

Background — ART compilation modes:

  • Interpreted mode: Bytecode run directly. Slowest but requires no compilation time.
  • JIT (Just-In-Time): Code is profiled at runtime; hot methods are compiled to native. After ~10 minutes of use, the system compiles the profile in the background. This means new installs are slow for the first few app starts.
  • AOT (Ahead-Of-Time): Code compiled to native before execution. Fastest at runtime but compilation takes time and space.

Baseline Profiles give you AOT compilation of critical paths on first launch, eliminating the JIT warm-up period.

How to create a Baseline Profile:

  1. Add the androidx.benchmark:benchmark-macro and androidx.profileinstaller:profileinstaller dependencies.
  2. Write a BaselineProfileGenerator (a Macrobenchmark test) that exercises your startup path:
@RunWith(AndroidJUnit4::class)
class BaselineProfileGenerator {
    @get:Rule
    val rule = BaselineProfileRule()

    @Test
    fun generate() = rule.collect(
        packageName = "com.example.app",
        profileBlock = {
            // navigate the critical startup path
            pressHome()
            startActivityAndWait()
            // interact with the home screen
            device.findObject(By.text("Search")).click()
            waitForIdle()
        }
    )
}
  1. Run the test on a rooted device or emulator — it produces a baseline-prof.txt in src/main/.
  2. The profile is packaged into the APK and read by the ProfileInstaller library on device.

AGP integration (AGP 8.x):

// build.gradle.kts
android {
    defaultConfig {
        // enables ProfileInstaller to install profile at first run
    }
}

The Baseline Profile plugin (com.android.tools.baselineprofile) automates generation and inclusion.

Measured impact: Google reports 30–40% startup improvement for apps with comprehensive Baseline Profiles. The improvement is most visible on cold starts on lower-end devices.

Trade-offs:

  • Pro: Dramatic cold start improvement, especially on first run post-install.
  • Pro: Works at the library level too — Jetpack libraries ship their own baseline profiles.
  • Con: Requires a connected rooted device for profile generation (CI setup is non-trivial).
  • Con: Profiles go stale if code changes significantly — need periodic regeneration.
  • Con: APK size increases slightly.

Failure mode: Forgetting to add profileinstaller dependency — the profile ships in the APK but is never installed on the device.

Under the hood

The human-readable baseline-prof.txt is a list of method and class descriptors in the HRF (Human-Readable Format), e.g. HSPLcom/example/MyClass;->myMethod(I)V, where the leading flags mean Hot, Startup, and Post-startup. AGP compiles this into a binary .prof/.profm file embedded under assets/dexopt/ in the APK. On first run, ProfileInstaller copies that profile into ART's reference profile location (/data/misc/profiles/ref/<pkg>). ART's dex2oat then performs AOT compilation of exactly those flagged methods into the .odex/.art files, rather than waiting for the runtime interpreter+JIT to discover them across many sessions. Without the embedded profile, ART starts cold: methods run interpreted, the JIT samples execution counts, and only after thresholds are crossed (and during idle bg-dexopt maintenance) does it compile them — which is why the first several launches are slow.

baseline-prof.txt (HRF)        AGP packaging              device, first run
  HSPLcom/app/Foo;->bar()  ──>  assets/dexopt/baseline.prof  ──>  ProfileInstaller
                                + baseline.profm                    copies to ref/
                                                                          │
                                                                    dex2oat AOT-compiles
                                                                    flagged methods -> .art/.odex

Splash Screen

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "Since Android 12 the system owns the splash screen — it draws your themed icon over a window background on every cold and warm start, and dismisses it the instant your first frame is ready. I use the AndroidX core-splashscreen library so the behavior backports to API 23, and installSplashScreen() must run before super.onCreate(). The thing interviewers probe is setKeepOnScreenCondition — it's evaluated every single frame on the main thread, so it has to be a cheap StateFlow read, never a blocking call, and it must eventually return false or the app looks frozen."

Definition: The splash screen is the initial visual shown while the app loads. Starting with Android 12, the system enforces a standardized splash screen API rather than letting apps roll their own.

Pre-Android 12 (legacy):

  • Apps set windowBackground on the launch theme to a drawable/color, giving the appearance of instant launch.
  • The "splash screen" was actually the window background visible before the Activity drew its first frame.
  • Common pattern: theme switch — launch with SplashTheme (sets windowBackground), then setTheme(R.style.AppTheme) in onCreate() before setContentView().

Android 12+ SplashScreen API:

  • The system always shows a splash screen on cold and warm starts.
  • Composed of: icon (adaptive icon), icon background, window background.
  • The splash screen is dismissed when the app draws its first frame (or when you call splashScreen.setKeepOnScreenCondition { true } to hold it longer).

Jetpack SplashScreen library (androidx.core:core-splashscreen) — backports to API 23:

// In Activity.onCreate(), BEFORE super.onCreate()
val splashScreen = installSplashScreen()

// Keep splash visible until data is ready
splashScreen.setKeepOnScreenCondition {
    viewModel.isLoading.value
}

// Animate the exit
splashScreen.setOnExitAnimationListener { splashScreenView ->
    val slideUp = ObjectAnimator.ofFloat(
        splashScreenView.view, View.TRANSLATION_Y, 0f, -splashScreenView.view.height.toFloat()
    )
    slideUp.doOnEnd { splashScreenView.remove() }
    slideUp.start()
}

Theme setup:

<style name="Theme.App.Starting" parent="Theme.SplashScreen">
    <item name="windowSplashScreenBackground">@color/colors_background_white</item>
    <item name="windowSplashScreenAnimatedIcon">@drawable/ic_launcher_foreground</item>
    <item name="windowSplashScreenAnimationDuration">300</item>
    <item name="postSplashScreenTheme">@style/Theme.App</item>
</style>

Under the hood

The system splash is not a separate Activity — it's a window the framework adds in the same window as your starting Activity, using the attributes resolved from your launch theme (windowSplashScreenBackground, windowSplashScreenAnimatedIcon, etc.). The WindowManager/StartingSurface machinery in system_server constructs this "starting window" before your process even finishes drawing, which is why it appears instantly. installSplashScreen() must run before super.onCreate() because it swaps your Activity's theme from Theme.App.Starting to postSplashScreenTheme and registers the keep-on-screen predicate; after setContentView, the framework hooks the ViewTreeObserver.OnPreDrawListener on the content root. On each frame the pre-draw listener evaluates your keepOnScreenCondition — returning true consumes the draw (returns false from the listener so the frame is suspended), and once it finally returns false the listener removes itself and the exit animation runs. That per-frame evaluation is exactly why the condition must be O(1).

cold start
  ├─ system_server adds starting window (theme attrs) ── shown immediately
  ├─ app process: onCreate -> installSplashScreen() swaps theme + sets predicate
  ├─ setContentView -> OnPreDrawListener attached to decor/content root
  └─ every frame: keepOnScreenCondition?  true -> suspend draw
                                          false -> remove listener, exit anim, draw

Android implications:

  • setKeepOnScreenCondition is checked on every frame; keep it cheap (read a StateFlow value, not a blocking call).
  • The splash screen duration should be minimized — it's loading time from the user's perspective.
  • Do not use the splash screen to hide a slow startup; use it to bridge the inevitable gap.
  • On Android 12+, showing a custom splash screen Activity before the system splash screen will result in a double-splash flicker.

Failure modes:

  • Forgetting installSplashScreen() before super.onCreate() — the splash screen is dismissed immediately.
  • setKeepOnScreenCondition that never returns false — app appears frozen.
  • Custom animated icon not respecting adaptive icon safe zone — icon appears clipped.

Dependency Graph Initialization

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "Dependency graph init is the cost of building every object that has to exist before the first user interaction — and with Dagger, calling DaggerAppComponent.create() eagerly constructs all your unscoped singletons, including any that do I/O in their constructors. My playbook is to keep the singleton component truly global, defer feature subcomponents until those features open, and wrap expensive singletons in Lazy<T> so they're built on first access. The subtle gotcha is transitive I/O hiding in constructors — like a SharedPreferences inject that silently parses an XML file off disk on the main thread — so I instrument each initializer with Trace.beginSection to find them."

Definition: Dependency graph initialization is the cost of constructing all the objects and their interdependencies that have to exist before the app can serve its first user interaction.

The problem: Dependency injection frameworks like Dagger construct an entire object graph eagerly when you call DaggerAppComponent.create(). If the component includes dozens of singletons — each with their own @Inject constructor doing I/O or computation — the graph construction cost is paid at startup.

Strategies:

  1. Scoped components: Don't build the entire graph in Application.onCreate(). Use a SingletonComponent with only truly global singletons, and defer feature-scoped components (booking, search) until those features are accessed.
