"I work through this in seven steps. First, reproduce — I identify the user flow, run it in a debug build with StrictMode enabled, and attach Android Studio Profiler to trigger the scenario. Second, pull the ANR trace: either adb pull /data/anr/ if I have root, or adb bugreport and extract the anr_*.txt from the zip. Third, find the main thread — I search for "main" or tid=1 and look at the topmost non-framework frame in my own code.

Fourth, identify the blocking pattern. There are four signatures I look for: if the main thread is Blocked with waiting to lock <0x...> held by thread N, that's lock contention — I then look up thread N in the same file to see what it's doing. If the main thread is in Native state at epoll_wait or nativePollOnce, it's actually idle, which means the ANR was probably a slow Binder call rather than a pure CPU block. If I see a frame at Object.wait(), the main thread is waiting for a signal from another thread — potential deadlock or a runaway background operation. And if I see a frame directly in my own code doing disk or network I/O, that's just a missing withContext(Dispatchers.IO).

Fifth, I scan all the other threads looking for any that are BLOCKED and hold the lock the main thread is waiting for. Sixth, I fix — move blocking work off the main thread, reduce lock scope, or restructure to avoid contention. And seventh, I verify with Macrobenchmark on the specific interaction path that triggered the ANR, and add a StrictMode or tracing check so a regression would be caught before it ships again."

Q: What is the difference between a crash and an ANR?

"The core distinction is cause and timing. A crash is an unhandled exception — a NullPointerException, an OutOfMemoryError, or a native signal — and the process dies immediately. An ANR is not a crash; the process is still running, but the main thread is blocked so long that the system decides the app has stopped responding.

From the user's perspective: a crash closes the app instantly with an 'App has stopped' dialog. An ANR freezes the app, and after 5 seconds the user sees 'App is not responding' with a choice to wait or close. Crucially, if the main thread unblocks before the user acts, an ANR can self-resolve — a crash never can.

For diagnosis: crashes go to Crashlytics via the FATAL EXCEPTION logcat tag, and the stack trace points to the throw site. ANRs go into /data/anr/ traces and Android Vitals, and the stack trace points to whatever blocking call the main thread is stuck on. They need different debugging strategies."

Aspect Crash ANR
CauseUnhandled exception (e.g., NullPointerException, OutOfMemoryError) or native signalMain thread blocked for too long (I/O, lock, Binder)
User experienceApp closes immediately with "App has stopped" dialogApp freezes; after 5s user sees "App not responding" dialog
System behaviorProcess is killedSystem kills the process after the dialog is dismissed (or user waits)
Diagnosis toolCrashlytics, logcat FATAL EXCEPTIONANR traces (/data/anr/), Android Vitals ANR dashboard
Stack trace locationAt the exception throw siteAt the blocking call on the main thread
RecoverabilityNone — process is deadUser can "Wait" and app may recover if blocking clears

Q: How do you prioritize production stability issues?

"I use a seven-factor framework. First, impact — users affected times frequency. A crash hitting 10,000 users a day is always higher priority than one hitting 10, regardless of how easy either is to fix. Second, bad behavior thresholds: Android Vitals flags ANR rate above 0.47% and crash rate above 1.09% as bad behavior, and those directly hurt your Play Store ranking — anything above the threshold is immediate. Third, recency: a crash that appears for the first time in the latest release is a P0 because it's a regression and you have a clear rollback option. An old crash with a flat rate is lower urgency. Fourth, Crashlytics velocity alerts — a sudden spike on an existing issue means a new trigger just appeared, whether a new OS version, a new device model, or a user behavior change. Fifth, business impact: a crash in the checkout or payment flow is P0 regardless of volume, because it directly blocks revenue. A crash in the settings screen can wait. Sixth, reproducibility: an issue I can reproduce locally is cheaper to fix than one that only shows up on obscure devices in the field — give reproducible issues a priority boost. And seventh, user feedback correlation: if app store reviews start mentioning a specific crash, cross-reference with Crashlytics — that signal often surfaces issues before the volume numbers look alarming.

In practice that maps to:"

Practical prioritization matrix:

P0 (fix immediately): new regression, checkout/payment crash, ANR > threshold
P1 (this sprint): high-volume crash (> 1000 affected users/day), ANR cluster
P2 (next sprint): medium-volume crash, non-critical flow
P3 (backlog): rare crash (< 10/day), device-specific, already mitigated

15.1 Android App Architecture Design

Senior and staff design interviews are not about memorizing a pattern. They are about showing that you can drive decisions across the full stack of a feature — from network protocol to UI rendering, from data persistence to security model, from rollout strategy to monitoring.

Use this framework for every design:

Architecture → Modules → State Management → Data Flow → Offline Strategy →
Error Handling → Threading → Caching → Security → Performance → Testing →
Monitoring → Rollout

Worked Designs

Chat App

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "For a chat client I make Room the single source of truth and treat the WebSocket as just another writer into it — a process-scoped ChatSessionManager owns the socket, and every incoming frame gets persisted, so the UI is always a reactive read off the DB via Paging. Sends are optimistic: I insert with status=PENDING immediately, then reconcile to SENT/DELIVERED/READ as ACKs come back. The nuance an interviewer probes is reliability on a flaky network — that's why pending sends live in Room and a WorkManager job drains the queue on reconnect, and why I batch incoming frames before writing to avoid DB thrash."

Scenario: Design the Android client for a consumer chat application (think WhatsApp/Signal scale). Real-time messaging, media sharing, read receipts, message status, group chats.

Architecture

MVVM with a single-direction data flow per conversation screen. Each open conversation has its own ConversationViewModel. A global ChatSessionManager (singleton, process-scoped) owns the WebSocket lifecycle. Repository layer mediates between the remote (WebSocket/REST) and local (Room) sources.

UI (Compose ConversationScreen)
   ↑ UiState
   ViewModel (ConversationViewModel)
   ↑ Flow<List<Message>>
   Repository (MessageRepository)
   ↑                   ↑
Room (MessageDao)   WebSocket / REST

Modules

:app                          — entry, DI wiring
:feature:chat                 — conversation list + open chat screens
:feature:media                — media picker, upload, preview
:data:chat                    — MessageRepository, ConversationRepository
:data:network                 — WebSocketClient, ChatApiService
:data:db                      — Room DB, DAOs
:domain:chat                  — Message, Conversation domain models, use cases
:core:crypto                  — end-to-end encryption utilities
:core:push                    — FCM token registration, notification routing
:core:ui                      — shared Compose components (Bubble, Avatar, etc.)

State Management

ConversationViewModel exposes a single StateFlow<ConversationUiState>. That state includes:

  • messages: List<MessageUiModel> (paginated, sorted by timestamp)
  • typingIndicators: Set<UserId>
  • sendStatus: SendStatus (idle / sending / failed)
  • scrollToPosition: Int?

Side-effects (scroll triggers, attachment picker opening) use SharedFlow<ConversationEvent>.

Data Flow

  1. App opens → ChatSessionManager.connect() opens a persistent WebSocket.
  2. Incoming frame decoded → MessageRepository.handleIncoming(frame) → persisted to Room → Room

emits new Flow<List<Message>> → ViewModel picks up → UI re-renders.

  1. User sends message → ViewModel calls SendMessageUseCase → message inserted into Room with

status=PENDING → Room emission updates UI immediately (optimistic) → background coroutine sends over WebSocket → on ACK update status=SENT → on server push update status=DELIVERED / status=READ.

  1. Pagination: ViewModel uses Pager + PagingSource backed by `MessageDao.getMessages(threadId,

limit, offset)`. Load older messages on scroll-to-top.

Offline Strategy

  • Messages typed while offline are inserted into Room with status=PENDING.
  • A WorkManager PeriodicWorkRequest (PendingMessageSyncWorker) processes the queue when

connectivity is restored.

  • Conversation list and last messages are always served from Room; staleness is acceptable

because the WebSocket reconciles on reconnect.

  • Media uploads are queued via WorkManager with NetworkType.CONNECTED constraint.

Error Handling

  • WebSocket disconnection: exponential back-off reconnect (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s, cap at 60s).

ChatSessionManager emits ConnectionState (CONNECTED / RECONNECTING / OFFLINE) into a StateFlow; the UI shows a subtle banner.

  • Send failure: the PENDING message stays in the local DB. UI shows a retry icon. User can

tap to retry or swipe to cancel.

  • Media upload failure: WorkManager retries up to 3 times; on final failure emit an event toast.
  • Decryption failure: show a placeholder "This message could not be decrypted" rather than

crashing.

Threading

  • WebSocket callbacks arrive on an IO dispatcher thread. Parsing and DB writes are on

Dispatchers.IO. ViewModel collects on Dispatchers.Main.

  • Media compression is on Dispatchers.Default (CPU-bound).
  • Never block the main thread; use launch(Dispatchers.IO) for all persistence.
  • Use structured concurrency: ConversationViewModel creates its own `CoroutineScope(

SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Main) cancelled in onCleared()`.

Caching

  • Room is the single source of truth. No in-memory cache for messages — paging handles this.
  • Avatar/profile images: Coil's disk cache (LRU, 50 MB limit). HTTP Cache-Control headers

drive eviction. Coil uses an in-memory LRU for recently seen avatars.

  • Attachments (images, videos): cached on disk under getCacheDir()/attachments/, max 200 MB

with LRU eviction managed by a custom AttachmentCacheManager.

Security

  • End-to-end encryption: Signal Protocol (libsignal-client). Keys stored in Android Keystore.
  • Message DB encrypted via SQLCipher; the SQLCipher key is stored in Keystore and only accessible

with user auth (biometric/pin).

  • TLS pinning on the WebSocket and REST endpoints.
  • No message content in notifications on locked screen (show "New message" only); configurable

per user setting.

  • Media sent to S3 via pre-signed URLs; the URL is only valid for 24 hours.
  • Prevent screenshots in sensitive screens using FLAG_SECURE.

Performance

  • LazyColumn for message list; use key { message.id } for stable recomposition.
  • Avatar Composables use remember { painter } to avoid re-loading on every recompose.
  • Diff in PagingData uses DiffUtil keyed on message ID; only changed items re-render.
  • Use stateIn(SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5000)) to avoid re-fetching from DB during

screen rotation.

  • Incoming WebSocket frames are batched (100ms debounce) before triggering DB writes to avoid

thrashing.

Testing

  • MessageRepository unit tested with FakeMessageDao (in-memory) and FakeWebSocketClient.
  • ConversationViewModel tested with MainCoroutineTestRule and fake repository.
  • SendMessageUseCase unit tested independently with mocked repository.
  • UI tests with Espresso/Compose test: verify message appears in list after sendMessage(),

verify retry button appears on simulated network failure.

  • WorkManager tested with TestWorkerBuilder.

Monitoring

  • Sentry: capture ConversationCrash events; tag with conversationId (not participant names).
  • Custom metric: message_send_latency_ms from user tap to status=SENT; tracked via DataDog.
  • connection_drop_rate = drops per session, alerted if > 2%.
  • Media upload success rate (target > 99%).
  • pending_message_count gauge: rising queue means sync worker is broken.

Rollout

  1. Ship behind AB flag chat_v2_enabled.
  2. 1% → 5% → 20% → 100% rollout over two weeks.
  3. Monitor crash-free rate, message delivery rate, latency p95.
  4. Kill-switch: flag off returns users to previous chat implementation.

Under the hood

The "persistent" WebSocket is a single TCP connection upgraded from an HTTP/1.1 Upgrade: websocket handshake; OkHttp's WebSocket runs frame reading on a dedicated reader thread and writes through a queue, so callbacks (onMessage) come off that I/O thread, never the main thread. The optimistic-send "instant UI" works because Room's Flow-returning DAO query registers an InvalidationTracker observer on the underlying SQLite tables — on any write, SQLite update hooks mark the table version dirty, the tracker re-runs the query on the IO executor, and re-emits, which is why a local INSERT repaints the list before the network round-trip completes.

tap "send"  → INSERT row(status=PENDING)   ──┐ (same DB txn commits)
                                             ├─► InvalidationTracker fires
LazyColumn repaints (PENDING bubble) ◄───────┘     re-runs SELECT, emits
   ... background coroutine: ws.send(frame)
   ACK frame on reader thread → UPDATE status=SENT → tracker fires again → repaint

Delivery reliability under process death rests on WorkManager persisting the WorkSpec to its own Room DB and registering a JobScheduler job; the OS, not the app, re-invokes the worker after a kill or reboot, which is why a PENDING queue survives where a plain coroutine would not.

Offline-First Feed

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "An offline-first feed is a strict local-first loop: the UI only ever reads from Room through Paging, and the only thing allowed to write network data into Room is a WorkManager sync job. That separation is the whole design — reads never touch the network, so the feed is instantly available offline, and writes are atomic upserts guarded by a transaction. The gotcha interviewers chase is staleness and resumability: I keep a feed_sync_meta row with the last cursor and timestamp so sync resumes where it left off and the UI can honestly say 'cached from X minutes ago' instead of pretending it's live."

Scenario: Design a social/news feed that works fully offline. Think Twitter timeline, Reddit feed, or an internal news app with periodic content.

Architecture

Repository pattern with Room as the single source of truth. The UI always reads from local DB. A FeedSyncManager (tied to WorkManager) is the only component that writes from network to DB. This is a strict local-first pattern.

UI (Compose FeedScreen)
   ↑ PagingData<FeedItemUiModel>
   FeedViewModel
   ↑ PagingSource (Room)
   FeedRepository
          ↑ write only
   FeedSyncManager (WorkManager PeriodicWork)
          ↑
   FeedApiService (Retrofit)

Modules

:feature:feed          — FeedScreen, FeedViewModel
:data:feed             — FeedRepository, FeedSyncManager
:data:db               — FeedItemEntity, FeedDao
:data:network          — FeedApiService, NetworkMonitor
:domain:feed           — FeedItem domain model, GetFeedUseCase
:core:sync             — BaseSyncWorker, SyncResult, retry policy

State Management

ViewModel exposes:

  • PagingData<FeedItemUiModel> via Pager backed by FeedDao.getFeedItems().
  • feedStatus: StateFlow<FeedStatus> (SYNCED / SYNCING / STALE / ERROR) — this comes from a

metadata table feed_sync_meta (last sync timestamp, sync result).

  • Pull-to-refresh triggers FeedRepository.requestSync() which starts an expedited WorkManager

request.

Data Flow

Read path: FeedDao → PagingSource → PagingData → ViewModel → Compose LazyColumn. Write path: FeedSyncWorker.doWork() calls FeedApiService.getFeed(cursor), maps to entities, calls FeedDao.upsertAll(entities), updates feed_sync_meta. The DB write wakes up the PagingSource observer automatically.

Offline Strategy

  • Feed is always readable — Room has all previously fetched items.
  • NetworkMonitor (wraps ConnectivityManager.NetworkCallback) emits isOnline: StateFlow<Bool>.
  • When offline: show a banner "Showing cached content from X minutes ago". Use

feed_sync_meta.lastSyncTimestamp for the time.

  • WorkManager constraint NetworkType.CONNECTED — sync only happens with connectivity.
  • Pagination cursor stored in feed_sync_meta so sync resumes from last known position after

re-connect.

  • Read articles are stored; user can explicitly save articles for permanent offline.

Error Handling

  • Network error during sync: WorkManager returns Result.retry() with exponential back-off.

After 3 retries, Result.failure() updates feed_sync_meta.lastSyncStatus = ERROR. UI shows "Could not refresh" with a retry button.

  • Partial sync: if the API returns 50 items but fails mid-write, use a DB transaction

(@Transaction) to ensure atomicity — all or nothing.

  • Parse error for a single item: skip that item, log to Sentry, continue.

Threading

  • All DB reads via Dispatchers.IO (Room automatically uses IO dispatcher for suspending

functions).

  • WorkManager doWork() is called on a background thread pool; no extra dispatchers needed.
  • ViewModel collects PagingData on Dispatchers.Main.

Caching

  • Room IS the cache. No additional in-memory layer.
  • Image caching: Coil with disk cache; staleWhileRevalidate header support.
  • Cache eviction: a nightly CleanupWorker deletes FeedItemEntity rows older than 7 days,

except those marked saved = true.

  • Article body (HTML/markdown): stored in a separate article_body table with its own 24-hour

TTL.

Security

  • API auth via bearer token (stored in EncryptedSharedPreferences).
  • HTTPS-only; certificate pinning in OkHttp interceptor.
  • Saved articles: no PII in local DB (user IDs stored as hashed tokens).

Performance

  • PagingSource with pageSize = 20, prefetchDistance = 5.
  • Pager cached in ViewModel with cachedIn(viewModelScope) so rotation does not re-fetch.
  • Images: use AsyncImage with crossfade, avoid loading full-res in feed (request thumbnail

variant from CDN with ?w=400).

  • DB indices on FeedItemEntity: index on (timestamp DESC) for the main sort, index on

(saved, timestamp) for saved filter.

Testing

  • FeedSyncWorker tested with TestWorkerBuilder and a FakeFeedApiService.
  • FeedRepository tested with an in-memory Room DB.
  • FeedViewModel tested with TestCoroutineDispatcher and fake repository.
  • UI: screenshot tests of feed in CACHED state vs SYNCING state.

Monitoring

  • feed_sync_success_rate per WorkManager run.
  • feed_load_time_ms from screen open to first item visible.
  • stale_content_shown_rate — how often users see cached content older than 1 hour.

Rollout

  • Feature flag offline_first_feed_enabled.
  • Shadow mode: new sync path runs alongside old network-then-cache path; compare outputs.
  • Gradual rollout; watch stale_content_shown_rate and crash rate.

Under the hood

Paging 3's RemoteMediator formalizes exactly this two-path design: the PagingSource reads only from Room, while the mediator's load() runs the network fetch and upserts, so the list and the network are decoupled by the database. upsertAll inside a @Transaction compiles to a single SQLite transaction (BEGIN … COMMIT); Room's InvalidationTracker defers its table-invalidation notification until the transaction commits, so observers never see the half-written 50-item batch — that's what makes "all or nothing" actually atomic for the reader, not just the writer. WorkManager.enqueueUniquePeriodicWork with KEEP means a duplicate enqueue is a no-op rather than a second job, preventing overlapping syncs that would race on the cursor.

RemoteMediator.load(REFRESH/APPEND)
   → api.getFeed(cursor)
   → db.withTransaction { dao.upsertAll(items); meta.update(cursor, ts) }  // one COMMIT
   → InvalidationTracker fires AFTER commit → PagingSource invalidated
   → Pager generates a fresh PagingSource → LazyColumn diffs & repaints

The NetworkType.CONNECTED constraint is enforced by the OS JobScheduler, which only dispatches the job once a validated network is available — the worker code never polls connectivity itself.

Video Streaming App

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "A streaming client is really an orchestration problem around ExoPlayer: I wrap it in a single controller, feed it a MediaItem with the manifest and DRM config, and let ExoPlayer do HLS/DASH adaptive bitrate and buffering internally — my job is the state machine, resume position, and downloads. The thing interviewers push on is ExoPlayer's threading and DRM: all player calls have to be on the application thread it was created on, and offline playback means fetching and persisting a Widevine offline license keyed to the downloaded segments, then checking its expiry on app open before you let the user hit play."

Scenario: Design an Android client for a video streaming service (Netflix/YouTube scale). Browse catalog, search, play video, download for offline.

Architecture

Feature-modular MVVM. ExoPlayer is the media engine, wrapped in a VideoPlayerController singleton. Download management via DownloadManager (ExoPlayer's download module) backed by WorkManager.

Modules

:feature:home          — catalog browse
:feature:player        — playback screen + mini-player
:feature:downloads     — download list, download management
:feature:search        — search screen
:data:catalog          — CatalogRepository (GraphQL + Room)
:data:playback         — PlaybackSessionRepository, DRM license fetching
:data:download         — DownloadRepository (ExoPlayer DownloadManager + Room)
:core:player           — VideoPlayerController, ExoPlayer factory, DRM
:core:analytics        — playback telemetry (QoE events)

State Management

PlayerViewModel exposes:

  • playbackState: StateFlow<PlaybackState> (IDLE / BUFFERING / PLAYING / PAUSED / ENDED / ERROR)
  • currentPosition: StateFlow<Long> (updated every 500ms via ExoPlayer.addListener)
  • videoMetadata: StateFlow<VideoMetadata>
  • qualityLevel: StateFlow<Quality> (for adaptive bitrate display)

Data Flow

  1. User taps video → PlayerViewModel.loadVideo(videoId) → PlaybackSessionRepository

fetches manifest URL + DRM license URL → construct MediaItem with DRM config → hand to ExoPlayer.

  1. ExoPlayer handles HLS/DASH ABR internally.
  2. Player listener events → StateFlow updates → UI reacts.
  3. Resume position: on pause/stop, persist (videoId, position) to Room → on next open, seek

to that position.

Offline Strategy

  • ExoPlayer DownloadManager with SegmentDownloader for HLS/DASH.
  • Download request added via DownloadService (foreground service required by ExoPlayer).
  • DRM offline license fetched and stored alongside segments.
  • DownloadRepository exposes Flow<List<DownloadState>> backed by ExoPlayer's DownloadIndex

(SQLite-backed).

  • Expired downloads: check license expiry on app open; prompt user to re-download if needed.

Error Handling

  • Playback error → PlaybackException from ExoPlayer → map to user-friendly error + retry button.
  • DRM license fetch failure: surface "Content not available in your region / retry".
  • Download failure: WorkManager retry; notify user with NotificationCompat progress notification.
  • Network interruption mid-playback: ExoPlayer buffers 30s; auto-resumes when connectivity

returns; show "Reconnecting..." indicator after 5s buffer exhausted.

Threading

  • ExoPlayer must run on main thread. All ExoPlayer calls from Dispatchers.Main.
  • Manifest/license fetches: OkHttp on IO dispatcher.
  • Download: ExoPlayer DownloadService runs in its own process with foreground service

notification.

Caching

  • SimpleCache (ExoPlayer) for in-memory HLS segment cache (100 MB default).
  • LeastRecentlyUsedCacheEvictor with configurable max size.
  • Catalog metadata: Room with 24-hour TTL via catalog_meta.fetchedAt column.
  • Thumbnails: Coil disk cache.

Security

  • Widevine DRM (L1 on supported hardware, L3 fallback).
  • FLAG_SECURE on player Activity to prevent screen recording.
  • Offline DRM licenses: keystore-backed encrypted storage via ExoPlayer's DefaultDrmSessionManager.
  • API tokens in EncryptedSharedPreferences.
  • Certificate pinning for CDN and license server endpoints.

Performance

  • Thumbnail loading: use low-resolution variants from CDN; full-res only on detail screen.
  • Pre-fetch next episode: when 80% through current episode, start buffering next episode's first

30s in background (ConcatenatingMediaSource).

  • ABR: ExoPlayer AdaptiveTrackSelection with custom DefaultBandwidthMeter calibrated to

streaming profile.

  • Reduce startup latency: pre-warm ExoPlayer instance on app cold start.

Testing

  • VideoPlayerController unit tested with FakeExoPlayer (ExoPlayer test utilities).
  • PlaybackSessionRepository mocked with MockK; test DRM license fetch path.
  • Integration test: mock API server + ExoPlayer playing test HLS stream.
  • Manual QA checklist: seek behavior, background playback, download flow, resume after kill.

Monitoring

  • QoE metrics: startup time, buffering ratio, average bitrate, error rate per stream.
  • video_start_failure_rate alerted if > 0.5%.
  • rebuffering_ratio alerted if > 2%.
  • Download success rate (target > 98%).
  • Crash-free rate on Player Activity (target > 99.9%).

Rollout

  • ExoPlayer version upgrades: shadow A/B, compare QoE metrics before full rollout.
  • New DRM configuration: 1% → 5% → 20% with crash rate monitoring at each step.

Under the hood

ExoPlayer is an internal pipeline of MediaSource → Renderer → LoadControl, driven by an internal playback thread; the public Player object is a façade that asserts you call it from the thread that created it (Player.getApplicationLooper()) — violating that throws, which is why "main thread only" is enforced, not advisory. Adaptive bitrate is the TrackSelection layer polling the BandwidthMeter's sliding-window throughput estimate before each chunk and choosing the highest-bitrate variant whose download it predicts will finish before the buffer drains. Widevine DRM runs through the platform MediaDrm API into a hardware TEE (L1) or software (L3); an offline license is a persisted key set whose opaque key-set ID is stored alongside the downloaded segments, and Widevine itself enforces the license's embedded expiry — the app's "check on open" is just to fail gracefully before the secure decoder rejects the keys.

chunk boundary reached
  → BandwidthMeter.getBitrateEstimate()
  → AdaptiveTrackSelection picks variant (with hysteresis to avoid flip-flop)
  → MediaSource loads next segment → SampleQueue → MediaCodec (secure, via MediaDrm) → Surface

Payments Flow

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "For payments, correctness beats UX everywhere: card data never touches my servers — the PCI SDK tokenizes it and I only ever handle the token — and I never do optimistic UI on the actual charge, only on the steps around it. The single most important mechanism is the client-generated idempotency key persisted in Room: every confirm request carries it, so a retry, a timeout, or a crash-then-relaunch can re-query by that key instead of risking a double charge. That's the trap interviewers set — 'the network drops right after you hit Pay' — and the answer is never assume failure; reconcile by idempotency key."

Scenario: Design a payments flow in an Android app — add card, select payment method, confirm purchase. Security and reliability are paramount.

Architecture

A dedicated PaymentsActivity hosts a single-flow NavHost. Each step is a Compose screen. PaymentViewModel is scoped to the Activity (not individual screens) to maintain state across steps. All payment data handling is strictly in the data:payments module behind an interface.

PaymentsActivity (NavHost)
  ├── SelectPaymentMethodScreen
  ├── AddCardScreen (delegates to PCI-compliant SDK)
  ├── ConfirmPurchaseScreen
  └── PaymentResultScreen

PaymentViewModel (Activity-scoped)
   ↑ PaymentUiState
   PaymentRepository
   ↑
   PaymentApiService (Retrofit)
   StripeSDK / BraintreeSDK (PCI-compliant card tokenization)

Modules

:feature:payments       — UI screens, PaymentViewModel, navigation
:data:payments          — PaymentRepository, PaymentApiService
:domain:payments        — PaymentMethod, Order, PaymentResult domain models
:core:security          — BiometricHelper, EncryptedPreferences

State Management

PaymentUiState is a sealed class:

  • SelectingMethod(methods: List<PaymentMethod>)
  • AddingCard
  • Confirming(orderSummary: OrderSummary, selectedMethod: PaymentMethod)
  • Processing
  • Success(receipt: Receipt)
  • Failure(error: PaymentError)

One-way flow: state emitted from ViewModel → UI renders. User action → ViewModel event → new state. No state stored in individual screen Composables.

Data Flow

  1. Screen opens → PaymentViewModel.loadPaymentMethods() → REST call → StateFlow updated.
  2. User selects saved card → proceed to Confirm step.
  3. User adds new card → Stripe SDK tokenizes (card number never leaves the SDK) → token returned

to app → sent to backend for association with account.

  1. User taps "Pay" → PaymentViewModel.confirmPayment(orderId, methodToken) → REST call →

idempotency key sent with request → result updates state.

Offline Strategy

Payments must NOT proceed offline. If NetworkMonitor.isOnline == false:

  • Disable "Pay" button.
  • Show "No internet connection — payment not processed."
  • Queue no payment attempts offline (risk of double-charge).

Error Handling

  • Network timeout: show "Something went wrong" + retry. Do NOT assume payment succeeded.
  • Idempotency keys: every payment request includes a UUID generated client-side and stored in

Room. If the same request is retried, the same key is sent — backend deduplicates.

  • Card declined: show specific error from backend (insufficient funds, expired card, etc.).
  • 3DS challenge: launch a Chrome Custom Tab for the challenge URL; handle redirect back to app

via deep link.

  • Crash during payment: on next app open, query backend with the idempotency key to determine

payment status. Never assume a crash means failure.

Threading

  • All payment API calls on Dispatchers.IO.
  • Stripe SDK operations on the thread Stripe requires (usually main thread for their UI components).
  • Never make payment calls on main thread.

Caching

  • Payment methods list: cached in Room for 15 minutes. Show stale data with "Refresh" button.
  • Never cache raw card data.
  • Order summary: not cached — always fresh from backend to prevent stale price display.

Security

  • PCI DSS: card data never touches app servers — Stripe/Braintree SDK handles tokenization.
  • Biometric confirmation before payment: BiometricPrompt required for purchases > threshold.
  • FLAG_SECURE on payment Activity — no screenshots, no recents thumbnail.
  • No card numbers in logs, analytics, crash reports.
  • Token storage: payment method tokens in EncryptedSharedPreferences.
  • Jailbreak/root detection: warn user, optionally block (policy decision).
  • Certificate pinning on payment API endpoints.
  • Tamper detection: use SafetyNet/Play Integrity API before confirming payment.

Performance

  • Payment method list pre-fetched when user enters checkout funnel (not just when they tap the

payment button).

  • Optimistic UI only for non-payment steps; never for the actual charge (wait for server ACK).

Testing

  • PaymentRepository tested with mock Retrofit + idempotency key verification.
  • PaymentViewModel state machine tested exhaustively: every transition.
  • Stripe SDK integration: use Stripe test mode with test card numbers.
  • Test double-submit prevention by rapid-tapping the Pay button.
  • Test network drop at the exact moment of payment confirmation.

Monitoring

  • Payment success rate (target > 99.5%).
  • payment_start_to_success_latency_ms p95.
  • Idempotency key collision rate (should be ~0).
  • 3DS challenge completion rate.
  • Alert on any payment error spike (> 1% error rate triggers page).

Rollout

  • Never ship payment changes without QA sign-off on test mode + staging environment.
  • Shadow mode: run new payment path alongside old for 24 hours, compare success rates.
  • Feature flag with instant kill-switch.
  • Gradual rollout: 1% for 48 hours minimum, watching payment error rate.

Under the hood

The idempotency guarantee is fundamentally a server contract, but the client mechanics matter: the UUID is generated and committed to Room before the network call leaves the device, so even if the process is killed mid-request the key survives the cold start and the same key is replayed. The backend stores (idempotency_key → result) and on a duplicate returns the original recorded outcome rather than charging again — so the network drop after "Pay" is safe because the client re-asks "what happened to key X?" rather than re-submitting a fresh charge. FLAG_SECURE is enforced by SurfaceFlinger / the display compositor at the system level: it sets the surface's secure flag so the framework excludes it from screenshots, screen recordings, and the Recents thumbnail snapshot — the app does nothing per-frame. The 3DS round-trip via Chrome Custom Tabs hands control to a real browser process (so cookies and the issuer's session are shared), and the issuer redirects to your registered deep-link scheme, which the OS resolves back to your Activity via an intent filter.

Pay tapped → UUID v4 → Room.insert(paymentAttempt, key)  // committed first
          → POST /charge  Idempotency-Key: <key>
   timeout/crash ──► relaunch ──► GET /charge?key=<key> ──► authoritative status

Ride Tracking App

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "A ride app is a strict trip state machine fed by a real-time channel: one TripViewModel owns a sealed TripUiState and the server pushes location, ETA, and status events over WebSocket or MQTT that drive legal transitions only — I reject and log any skip. Two mechanisms make it feel right: a foreground service keeps the socket alive when the app is backgrounded so the trip survives, and I animate the map marker between 1 Hz updates with a ValueAnimator so it glides instead of teleporting. The gotcha interviewers love is reconnect correctness — on reconnect I REST-poll the current trip to reconcile any events I missed while the socket was down, because the live channel alone isn't a reliable source of truth across drops."

Scenario: Design the Android client for a ride-hailing app. Real-time driver location, ETA, fare calculation, trip state machine.

Architecture

Feature-modular MVVM. Real-time location updates via WebSocket (or MQTT). Google Maps SDK for rendering. TripViewModel is the single owner of trip state throughout the trip lifecycle.

Modules

:feature:booking        — search, request ride
:feature:tracking       — in-trip screen, driver location, ETA
:feature:history        — past trips
:data:trip              — TripRepository, TripApiService, WebSocketClient
:data:location          — UserLocationManager (FusedLocationProvider)
:core:maps              — MapRenderer, RouteDrawer, MarkerManager
:core:realtime          — WebSocket/MQTT client abstraction

State Management

TripViewModel exposes TripUiState:

sealed class TripUiState {
    object Idle : TripUiState()
    data class Searching(val params: RideParams) : TripUiState()
    data class DriverAssigned(val driver: DriverInfo, val eta: Duration) : TripUiState()
    data class DriverEnRoute(val driverLocation: LatLng, val eta: Duration) : TripUiState()
    data class InTrip(val driverLocation: LatLng, val route: Route) : TripUiState()
    data class Completed(val receipt: Receipt) : TripUiState()
    data class Cancelled(val reason: String) : TripUiState()
}

Trip state transitions are strict (no direct Idle → InTrip skip). Any unrecognized transition is logged and treated as an error.

Data Flow

  1. User requests ride → REST call → returns tripId.
  2. WebSocket subscribe to trip/{tripId}/updates channel.
  3. Server pushes DriverLocationUpdate, EtaUpdate, TripStatusChange events.
  4. TripRepository.handleTripEvent(event) → updates StateFlow<TripState> → ViewModel

observes → UI re-renders map marker + ETA.

  1. Driver location: smooth marker animation using ObjectAnimator on LatLng (ValueAnimator

interpolating between last position and new position over 1s).

Offline Strategy

  • Active trip: if connection drops, display last known driver location with "Reconnecting..."

overlay. Reconnect loop with back-off.

  • On reconnect: REST poll for current trip state to reconcile with missed WebSocket events.
  • App backgrounded during trip: use a ForegroundService with a persistent notification

showing driver ETA. The service keeps the WebSocket alive.

  • Historical trips: fully cached in Room; always available offline.

Error Handling

  • Trip match timeout: "No drivers available. Try again?" after 120s.
  • WebSocket disconnect: automatic reconnect with exponential back-off; foreground service

prevents process death.

  • GPS unavailability: fall back to network location; show "Low accuracy" indicator.
  • Fare dispute: local trip data (start time, route, distance) stored in Room for reference.

Threading

  • WebSocket messages on IO dispatcher.
  • Map rendering happens on main thread (Google Maps SDK requirement).
  • FusedLocationProviderClient callbacks on main thread → post to IO for processing.
  • Marker animation: ObjectAnimator on main thread (required).

Caching

  • Current trip state persisted to Room (in case of process death + restore).
  • Map tiles: Google Maps SDK handles tile caching internally.
  • Driver profile/photo: Coil disk cache.
  • Route polyline: stored in Room as encoded polyline string for process restore.

Security

  • Trip ID is a server-generated UUID; not guessable.
  • Location data sent to server only when user has an active trip (not background always-on).
  • Driver/passenger location shared only with each other during active trip.
  • Payment: same PCI approach as payments flow.

Performance

  • Driver location updates at 1Hz; map marker animation fills in the gap between updates.
  • Reduce map re-renders: only call marker.position = newLatLng when distance > 10m.
  • Route polyline: use encoded polyline format; decode on device.
  • Minimize WebSocket frame size: use binary encoding (protobuf) for location updates.

Testing

  • TripRepository unit tested with fake WebSocket client, verify state transitions.
  • TripViewModel unit tested: every state transition scenario.
  • Location smoothing algorithm unit tested with known coordinate sequences.
  • Integration test: mock WebSocket server, simulate trip from request to completion.

Monitoring

  • WebSocket connection uptime per active trip (target > 99%).
  • Location update latency (time from driver device to rider screen).
  • Trip state consistency (detect cases where UI state diverges from server state).
  • Foreground service kill rate (canary for battery optimization issues).

Rollout

  • Test on diverse device set (budget Android, Android 8-14) — foreground service behavior

varies by OEM.

  • Battery impact monitoring via device profiling in beta.

Under the hood

MQTT is usually preferred over a raw WebSocket here because it adds QoS levels and a persistent session: with QoS 1 and cleanSession=false, the broker buffers undelivered messages for a disconnected client and replays them on reconnect, which is the protocol-level version of the "REST reconcile" fallback. The marker glide is ValueAnimator driven by the Choreographer: the platform Choreographer posts a FrameCallback on each VSYNC (~16.6 ms at 60 Hz), the animator computes a fraction along its interpolator, and the listener lerps between old and new LatLng — so the visual 60 fps motion is decoupled from the 1 Hz data rate. The foreground service survives backgrounding because, once startForeground() posts its notification, the OS raises the process's oom_adj priority so the low-memory killer treats it like a visible app rather than a cached background process.

1 Hz data:   P0 ............ P1 ............ P2
VSYNC 60Hz:  | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | |   ← Choreographer frame callbacks
marker x:    P0→──lerp(t)──→P1 (ValueAnimator over ~1s)  → marker.position each frame

Large E-Commerce App

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "A large e-commerce app is a multi-module, feature-first build where each feature owns its ViewModel, repository, and UI, and shared infra lives in :core modules — that's what lets many teams ship in parallel without stepping on each other. The interesting state decision is the cart: it's a process-scoped singleton because the badge must be consistent everywhere, whereas every screen otherwise gets its own scoped ViewModel. The nuances interviewers chase are freshness and reliability — price and inventory get short TTLs and a re-check on resume because stale prices are a real bug, and checkout uses idempotency keys and never goes offline, while browsing and cart stay Room-backed and offline-friendly."

Scenario: Design an Android app for a large e-commerce platform (Amazon/eBay scale). Catalog browsing, search, product detail, cart, checkout, order tracking.

Architecture

Multi-module, feature-first. Each feature is a Gradle module with its own ViewModel, Repository, and UI. Shared infrastructure (network, DB, auth, analytics) in :core modules. App module wires DI. Bottom navigation drives top-level feature switching.

Modules

:app                    — Activity, NavGraph, DI component
:feature:home           — personalized home feed
:feature:search         — search, filters, SERP
:feature:pdp            — product detail page
:feature:cart           — cart management
:feature:checkout       — checkout flow (address, payment, confirmation)
:feature:orders         — order list + tracking
:feature:account        — profile, saved addresses, payment methods
:data:catalog           — CatalogRepository (REST + Room)
:data:cart              — CartRepository (Room only, server-synced on session start)
:data:orders            — OrderRepository
:data:user              — UserRepository, AuthManager
:core:network           — OkHttp, Retrofit, interceptors, token refresh
:core:db                — Room DB, type converters
:core:analytics         — FEM/analytics event tracking
:core:ui                — MezzanineTheme, shared composables
:core:ab                — A/B flag wrapper

State Management

  • Cart: CartViewModel is a process-scoped singleton (via @ActivityRetainedScoped or a

Application-level singleton) — the cart badge must be consistent across all features.

  • Each feature screen has its own scoped ViewModel.
  • UiState sealed classes per screen. SharedFlow<UiEvent> for one-time effects (navigation,

toasts).

Data Flow

  • Catalog: REST → Room cache → ViewModel. TTL-based invalidation.
  • Cart: local Room as source of truth. Server sync on session open and on checkout. Conflict

resolution: last-write-wins for quantity changes.

  • Checkout: no local state — each step calls REST (address validate, payment tokenize, order

submit). Idempotency keys for order submission.

  • Order tracking: WebSocket for live status; REST for history.

Offline Strategy

  • Browse catalog: served from Room if freshness window allows.
  • Cart: always readable offline (Room). Sync queued for connectivity restore.
  • Checkout: requires connectivity (no offline checkout).
  • Search: no offline (always live).
  • Saved items / wishlist: Room-backed, fully offline.

Error Handling

  • Add to cart failure: optimistic local insert, server sync in background; rollback on server

reject (e.g., item out of stock).

  • Checkout failure: show specific error (address invalid, card declined, out of stock at time

of checkout). Never double-submit (idempotency key).

  • Product unavailable: redirect from PDP to "Item no longer available" screen.
  • Search failure: show last cached results with staleness indicator.

Threading

  • All network and DB on Dispatchers.IO.
  • Image decoding on Dispatchers.Default.
  • Main thread only for UI.
  • Use supervisorScope in ViewModel so one parallel fetch failing doesn't cancel siblings.

Caching

  • Product images: CDN-served, Coil disk cache (100 MB).
  • Product metadata: Room with TTL (price changes frequently — 15-min TTL; description — 24 hours).
  • Search results: in-memory cache (last 5 queries, 5-min TTL).
  • Cart: Room, always fresh locally.
  • Home feed: Room with TTL-based refresh.

Security

  • Auth: OAuth2 + token refresh via Authenticator interceptor. Tokens in EncryptedSharedPreferences.
  • Payment data: never stored, handled via PCI-compliant tokenization SDK.
  • Deep link validation: all incoming deep links validated against known URL patterns before

navigation.

  • Certificate pinning on all first-party API endpoints.

Performance

  • PDP images: lazy-load below fold; preload primary image.
  • SERP: LazyColumn + Pager; 20 items per page.
  • Price and inventory freshness: poll on PDP appear (not on navigate, use ON_RESUME check).
  • App startup: defer non-critical initializations (analytics, AB config) behind App.onCreate()

via Initializer with dependency ordering.

  • Baseline profile for critical flows (home, SERP, PDP, checkout).

Testing

  • Each module tested in isolation (feature module does not depend on other feature modules).
  • Integration: full checkout flow tested with mock API server.
  • Performance: Macrobenchmark for startup and SERP scroll.
  • Visual regression: screenshot tests for PDP and cart with Percy.

Monitoring

  • Add-to-cart success rate.
  • Checkout funnel drop-off per step.
  • Search latency p95.
  • Home feed load time.
  • Crash-free sessions (target > 99.9%).
  • ANR rate (target < 0.1%).

Rollout

  • Feature flags on every major new feature.
  • Checkout changes: dark launch with shadow traffic; compare order success rates.
  • Performance changes: Macrobenchmark CI gate; reject PRs that regress startup by > 5%.

Under the hood

The "process-scoped singleton cart" relies on the ViewModelStore lifecycle: a normal viewModels() ViewModel is keyed in the Activity/Fragment's ViewModelStore and dies with it, whereas an @ActivityRetainedScoped (Hilt) or app-singleton instance is held in a store that outlives configuration changes and screen transitions — that shared instance is literally why the badge stays consistent across features. The App Startup Initializer with dependency ordering builds a topological sort of dependencies() and runs initializers lazily through a single InitializationProvider (a manifest-merged ContentProvider), which collapses many libraries' separate auto-init ContentProviders into one and cuts cold-start ApplicationInfo provider instantiation. Baseline Profiles ship a baseline-prof.txt listing hot methods/classes; at install time ART's dex2oat AOT-compiles exactly those into native code, so the critical flows skip JIT warm-up on first run.

App Startup graph:   Analytics → depends → Logging
                     ABConfig  → depends → Network
   InitializationProvider.onCreate() → topo-sort → init Logging, Network, then Analytics, ABConfig

Modular Super-App

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "A super-app is many feature verticals in one host, so the core idea is Dynamic Feature Modules that download on demand plus hard isolation: features never import each other — they talk only through a :core:navigation contract, shared :core:data repositories, and an event bus, and I enforce no cross-feature edges with Dependency Guard. That isolation is what lets independent teams ship without breaking each other. The thing interviewers probe is the failure and ownership model: DFM install can fail so you need a graceful 'feature unavailable' fallback, and shared :core modules need a platform-team owner with required review, otherwise the contract erodes."

Scenario: Design an Android super-app (WeChat/Grab style) where multiple mini-apps or feature verticals live in one host app. Multiple teams, independent deployment where possible.

Architecture

Dynamic Feature Modules (DFMs) for feature verticals. A central :core:navigation module defines the navigation contract (DeepLinkHandler, FeatureLauncher). Features communicate only through this contract, never by direct dependency.

:app (host)
   ├── :feature:payments (DFM)
   ├── :feature:food-delivery (DFM)
   ├── :feature:ride (DFM)
   ├── :feature:health (DFM)
   ├── :core:navigation          — NavRouter, FeatureLauncher interface
   ├── :core:auth                — shared session, login
   ├── :core:analytics           — shared analytics
   ├── :core:network             — shared OkHttp, token handling
   ├── :core:db                  — shared Room DB (multi-module entities)
   ├── :core:design              — shared Compose design system
   └── :core:di                  — DI entry points per feature

Module Communication

  • Features do NOT import each other. Communication through:
    1. Navigation: FeatureLauncher.launch(FeatureRoute.Food.Menu) — registered at runtime.
    2. Shared data: via shared :core:data repositories (user, session, cart).
    3. Events: AppEventBus (in :core:events) for loose coupling (e.g., user logged out →

all features clear local state).

  • No circular dependencies enforced by Gradle build rules (+ Dependency Guard plugin).

State Management

  • Per-feature: each DFM has its own ViewModel graph.
  • Cross-feature: AppSessionState in :core:auth holds user identity, accessible by all.
  • Cart: CrossFeatureCartRepository in :core:data (e.g., food + grocery share a cart concept).

Multi-Team Workflow

  • Each team owns one or more DFMs.
  • Shared modules (:core:*) have a designated platform team as owners; changes require review

from that team.

  • API contracts between modules defined as interfaces in :api:* modules; implementations in

:impl:* modules. Teams program to interfaces.

  • Dependency Guard enforces that :feature:A cannot depend on :feature:B transitively.

Offline Strategy

Each DFM defines its own offline policy. Platform team provides:

  • NetworkMonitor in :core:network.
  • Standard BaseSyncWorker in :core:sync.
  • Room DB scaffolding in :core:db.

Teams adopt the standard or document their deviation.

Error Handling

  • DFM install failure: show "Feature unavailable, please update the app" dialog; fall back

gracefully.

  • Cross-feature navigation failure: FeatureLauncher returns an error; host shows error screen.
  • Auth expiry: AppEventBus.emit(Event.AuthExpired) → all features clear state → host launches

login flow.

Threading

  • Shared CoroutineDispatchers instance provided by :core:di — ensures consistent dispatcher

configuration and easy swapping in tests.

Security

  • Each DFM declares permissions it needs; host enforces at install time.
  • Feature isolation: each DFM's sensitive data lives in its own namespace within the shared Room DB

(table prefix, separate encrypted keys per feature if needed).

  • DFM signature verification before install (Play DFM handles this; for sideloaded builds, verify

manually).

Performance

  • DFM download on demand: only when user first navigates to that feature.
  • Baseline profile covers the host shell + most common feature (e.g., ride, food).
  • Startup: only :core:* initialized at startup; feature-specific init deferred to first use.

Testing

  • Each DFM tested in isolation via its own test module.
  • Contract tests: :api:* interfaces tested with a standard compliance suite all implementations

must pass.

  • Integration: test harness FakeFeatureLauncher for host-feature integration tests.
  • Lint checks for cross-module import violations.

Monitoring

  • DFM install success rate per feature.
  • Cross-feature navigation latency.
  • Per-feature crash-free session rate (segmented by DFM version).

Rollout

  • Each DFM has its own version code. Teams can ship DFM updates via Play without full app release.
  • Feature flags in :core:ab enable/disable features in the host's navigation registry without

a code change.

Under the hood

A DFM is a separate com.android.dynamic-feature module that is not in the base APK; SplitInstallManager requests it from Play, which streams a split APK and the framework SplitCompat merges its dex, resources, and native libs into the already-running process classloader at runtime — that's why the feature's classes aren't on the classpath until install, and why direct cross-feature imports can't compile against a DFM. The enforced "no cross-feature dependency" runs through FeatureLauncher resolving routes reflectively/by registry at runtime rather than by a compile-time edge, so Dependency Guard can keep the Gradle dependency graph acyclic. The shared AppEventBus is typically a hot MutableSharedFlow (or replay-0 broadcast) so a single emit(AuthExpired) fans out to every collecting feature without any feature knowing the others exist.

user taps "Food"  → SplitInstallManager.startInstall(food)
   → Play streams split APK → SplitCompat installs dex/resources into running classloader
   → FeatureLauncher.launch(Food.Menu) resolves route from runtime registry → Activity/destination

Real-Time Collaborative App

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "Collaborative editing is event sourcing: the document is a stream of operations, not a blob. I apply local edits optimistically, enqueue them, and send them; the server merges with OT or CRDT and broadcasts canonical ops back, and I transform my pending local ops against incoming remote ops before applying. The hard part interviewers focus on is convergence across offline and reconnect — I persist the operation queue in Room so edits survive process death, replay them with a version vector on reconnect, and the whole reason for OT/CRDT is that concurrent edits must converge to the same document regardless of arrival order, with last-write-wins only as a degraded fallback."

Scenario: Design a real-time collaborative editing app (Google Docs/Figma style). Multiple users editing a shared document simultaneously on Android.

Architecture

MVVM + event sourcing. The document is represented as a sequence of operations (OT or CRDT). Local operations are applied immediately (optimistic), sent to server, and server broadcasts merged operations to all clients.

Modules

:feature:editor         — EditorScreen, EditorViewModel, Compose rich text editor
:data:document          — DocumentRepository, OperationQueue, WebSocket channel
:domain:collab          — Operation, Document, ConflictResolver (OT/CRDT logic)
:core:realtime          — WebSocketClient, ReconnectManager
:core:presence          — CollaboratorPresence (cursors, selection state)

State Management

EditorViewModel exposes:

  • documentState: StateFlow<DocumentContent> — the current rendered content.
  • collaborators: StateFlow<List<CollaboratorPresence>> — other users' cursors.
  • syncState: StateFlow<SyncState> (SYNCED / PENDING / CONFLICTED / OFFLINE).

Data Flow

  1. User makes edit → LocalOperation created → applied to local document immediately (optimistic

→ documentState updates) → enqueued in OperationQueue.

  1. OperationQueue.flush() sends operations over WebSocket.
  2. Server applies OT/CRDT, broadcasts merged operation to all clients.
  3. Remote operation received → ConflictResolver.transform(localPending, remoteOp) → apply to

local document → update state.

  1. On full sync (reconnect): fetch full document snapshot from REST; replay pending local ops on top.

Offline Strategy

  • Continue editing offline; operations buffered in OperationQueue (Room-backed for persistence

across process death).

  • On reconnect: send buffered operations in order with version vector for server-side OT.
  • Show "Editing offline" badge; other collaborators' changes not visible until reconnect.

Error Handling

  • Conflict resolution failure: fall back to "last write wins" at field granularity with a toast

"Some of your changes may have been overridden."

  • Persistent sync failure: prompt user to save a local copy and try again.
  • WebSocket disconnect: foreground service keeps connection alive while editing; app background

pauses collaboration session after 30s.

Threading

  • WebSocket on IO dispatcher.
  • OT/CRDT conflict resolution on Dispatchers.Default (CPU-bound).
  • UI updates on Dispatchers.Main.
  • Operations are sequential (use Channel with UNLIMITED capacity to serialize them).

Caching

  • Document snapshots: Room. Fetch on first open; subsequent opens use local + delta sync.
  • Collaborator presence: in-memory only (ephemeral).

Security

  • Document access control enforced server-side; client trusts server's rejection.
  • Operations signed with session token to prevent forgery.
  • End-to-end encryption option for private documents (keys exchanged out-of-band).

Performance

  • Rich text rendering: avoid re-rendering unchanged paragraphs. Use Compose key {} at paragraph

level.

  • Presence cursors: debounce cursor position sends (50ms) to reduce WebSocket traffic.
  • Operation batch: batch up to 10 ops or 100ms into one WebSocket frame.

Testing

  • ConflictResolver unit tested extensively with known OT scenarios (concurrent inserts, deletes,

reorders).

  • OperationQueue tested for correct ordering and replay behavior.
  • Integration test: two DocumentRepository instances on a fake WebSocket server, verify eventual

consistency.

Monitoring

  • Operation round-trip time (client send → server broadcast → client receive).
  • Conflict resolution rate.
  • Sync failure rate.
  • Presence latency (cursor position latency).

Rollout

  • Beta with controlled set of collaborative documents.
  • Monitor conflict rate; high conflict rate may indicate OT implementation bugs.

Under the hood

OT and CRDT solve the same convergence problem differently. OT keeps operations as positional edits (e.g., insert(pos=5,"x")) and runs a transform(opA, opB) function so a concurrent insert before your position shifts your index — correctness depends on the server imposing a total order and every client transforming against the same sequence, which is why a version vector accompanies replayed ops. A CRDT instead gives every character a globally unique, densely-orderable identifier (a position between two neighbors), so concurrent inserts commute by construction and merge needs no central transform — at the cost of per-character metadata. The Channel(UNLIMITED) serializes edits because a channel is a FIFO queue with a single consuming coroutine, guaranteeing operations are applied in send order even though producers run on different dispatchers.

local:  "ABC"  insert(1,"X")  → "AXBC"  (enqueued, version v3)
remote: insert(0,"Z")  arrives → transform(insert(1,"X"), insert(0,"Z")) ⇒ insert(2,"X")
apply remote then transformed local → both clients converge to "ZAXBC"

SDK Used by Many Apps

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "An SDK embedded in dozens of host apps has to be a good guest: zero opinion about the host's architecture, minimal transitive dependencies, a tiny public surface, and — most importantly — it must never crash the host, so every public method is wrapped and bad init drops the SDK into a safe no-op mode. The mechanism that makes it well-behaved is deferral: init() does no network and almost no I/O, events just append to an in-memory buffer, and flushing happens on a background scope by size/time/lifecycle triggers with Room-backed retry. The nuances interviewers probe are dependency conflicts and API stability — shade or make OkHttp optional, keep public types ProGuard-safe with @Keep, and treat every public method as semver debt."

Scenario: You are designing an Android SDK that will be embedded in dozens of third-party apps. The SDK provides analytics, identity, or feature-flag capabilities.

Architecture

The SDK is a library module (AAR). It must have zero opinion about the host app's architecture. No forced DI framework. Minimal transitive dependencies. Exposes a simple public API surface.

Design Principles

  1. No forced dependencies: Do not pull in Hilt, Dagger, or large libraries. Use manual DI

internally. If using OkHttp, shade it (jarjar) or make it optional.

  1. Single entry point: MySDK.init(context, config) — one call to start.
  2. Thread-safe: All public methods safe to call from any thread. Internally uses a

dedicated CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.IO) that the host can optionally replace.

  1. No crash propagation: Catch all exceptions internally; never let SDK bugs crash the host app.

Log internally, report to own backend silently.

  1. Minimal permissions: Only request permissions the SDK absolutely needs; document them.
  2. ProGuard-friendly: Ship a proguard-rules.pro file. Annotate public API with @Keep.
  3. Small binary size: Every KB counts when embedding in a host app. Use R8 full-mode.

Modules (internal)

sdk-api/          — public interfaces + data classes (no implementation)
sdk-core/         — SdkCore, initialization, config
sdk-network/      — SdkHttpClient (shaded OkHttp or HttpURLConnection)
sdk-storage/      — SdkPreferences, SdkDatabase (scoped, named with SDK prefix)
sdk-analytics/    — event batching, flush scheduler

Public API Surface

// Keep it minimal. Every method added is API debt.
object MySDK {
    fun init(context: Context, apiKey: String, config: SdkConfig = SdkConfig())
    fun logEvent(name: String, properties: Map<String, Any> = emptyMap())
    fun identify(userId: String)
    fun reset()
    fun setLogLevel(level: SdkLogLevel) // debug only
}

State Management

SDK maintains internal state in a thread-safe AtomicReference<SdkState>. Public state is exposed via a simple callback interface (not Kotlin Flow — host apps may be Java or non-coroutine).

Data Flow

  1. Host calls logEvent() → event queued in in-memory CircularBuffer.
  2. Flush triggered by: buffer full (100 events), time interval (30s), app going to background.
  3. Flush sends batched events to SDK backend via HTTP POST with retry.
  4. On failure: events persisted to SdkDatabase (Room, SDK-namespaced); retried next flush.

Offline Strategy

All events queued in Room until connectivity available. WorkManager optional (do not force it). SDK can use ConnectivityManager and schedule its own flush on network available via ConnectivityManager.registerNetworkCallback.

Error Handling

  • Wrap every public method in try/catch; log internally; never throw to caller.
  • If initialization fails (e.g., invalid API key), put SDK in NO-OP mode — all calls are safe

no-ops. Never crash.

  • If backend rejects events (400): drop them (don't fill up disk). If 500: retry.

Security

  • API key validated on backend; not embedded in SDK binary.
  • Event data: no PII by default; document clearly what the SDK collects.
  • Certificate pinning: opt-in only (host apps may have their own pinning; forcing SDK pinning

causes conflicts).

  • No reflection access into host app.

Performance

  • SDK startup: < 10ms in init(). No network calls in init(). Defer all I/O.
  • Event logging: < 1ms per call (just a queue append).
  • Flush on IO thread; never block the calling thread.
  • SDK memory: < 5 MB RSS overhead.
  • No StrictMode violations in init().

Testing

  • SDK tested as a standalone module (no host app in tests).
  • Unit tests for event queuing, batching, flush logic.
  • Integration tests against a mock HTTP server.
  • Compatibility test matrix: API 21–34, AGP versions, Kotlin/Java host apps.
  • Binary size test: fail build if AAR exceeds size budget.

Monitoring (SDK's own telemetry)

  • SDK health endpoint: reports SDK version, init success rate, event delivery rate.
  • SDK crash reporting: SDK-internal Sentry project (separate from host's Sentry).

Rollout

  • Semantic versioning. MAJOR version for breaking public API changes.
  • Changelog for every release.
  • Minimum 30-day deprecation notice before removing public API.
  • Ship beta releases (1.2.0-beta01) for host app partners to validate before stable release.
  • Provide a migration guide for every MAJOR version bump.

Under the hood

"Shading" OkHttp means running a tool like the Gradle Shadow plugin / jarjar that rewrites the bytecode's package references from okhttp3.* to com.mysdk.shaded.okhttp3.* and relocates the class files, so the SDK's HTTP stack can't conflict with a different OkHttp version the host already ships — the JVM treats them as entirely distinct classes by fully-qualified name. @Keep is consumed by R8 as a keep rule so the class/method survives tree-shaking and isn't renamed in the host's own minification pass, which would otherwise break reflective or public-API access. The "init must not throw" guarantee leans on a single AtomicReference<SdkState> for lock-free compare-and-set transitions (e.g., UNINITIALIZED → READY or → NO_OP), so concurrent calls from any host thread observe a consistent state without a lock, and a failed init atomically lands in NO_OP where every public method short-circuits.

host classpath:  okhttp3.OkHttpClient            (host's version, untouched)
SDK (shaded):    com.mysdk.shaded.okhttp3.OkHttpClient   ← different FQN, no conflict

init() → CAS(state, UNINITIALIZED → READY)   on failure → CAS(... → NO_OP)
logEvent() → if state==NO_OP return; else buffer.append(e)   // never throws upward

Multi-Process App

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "Multi-process is the answer when a background operation must outlive the UI — a music player or VPN — so I run a foreground service in its own :remote process that owns the authoritative state, and the UI process talks to it over AIDL. The key consequence is that the two processes have separate heaps, so I can't share in-memory objects; I bridge AIDL callbacks into a StateFlow for the UI. The traps interviewers set are the Binder limits and threading: AIDL callbacks arrive on a binder thread pool not the main thread, a transaction over roughly 1 MB throws TransactionTooLarge, and a RemoteException means the binder died so you must reconnect — never pass a bitmap through Binder, pass a URI."

Scenario: Design an Android app that uses multiple processes — e.g., an app with a persistent background service (music player, VPN, location tracker) that must survive the main process being killed.

Architecture

Main process: UI + ViewModel + normal app logic. Service process (:remote): foreground service owning the long-running operation. Communication via AIDL (for structured IPC) or Messenger (for simple message passing). Alternatively, broadcast intents for fire-and-forget signaling.

When Multi-Process is Warranted

  • The background operation must outlive the UI process.
  • The operation uses significant memory and you want the OS to manage its lifecycle separately

(lower OOM priority for the service process).

  • You are implementing an accessibility service, input method, or VPN — which Android mandates

run in separate processes.

Modules

:app                    — UI, main process
:service                — MusicPlayerService (separate process), foreground notification
:ipc-api                — AIDL interfaces, Parcelable data classes (shared by both processes)
:core:notification      — NotificationBuilder (used by service process)

State Management

  • Service process owns the authoritative state (e.g., PlaybackState).
  • UI process subscribes to state changes via AIDL callback interface.
  • PlaybackServiceConnection in the UI process wraps ServiceConnection and exposes a

StateFlow<PlaybackState> by bridging AIDL callbacks to coroutine channels.

IPC Data Flow

UI Process                     Service Process
PlaybackControls               MusicPlayerService
   │ AIDL call (play/pause)         │
   └──────────────────────────────► │
                                    │ updates state
   ◄────────────────────────────────┘
   AIDL callback (PlaybackStateChanged)

Offline Strategy

The service process does not depend on network for playback of downloaded content. Network for streaming handled within the service process independently.

Error Handling

  • Service process crash: ServiceConnection.onServiceDisconnected() fires → UI shows

"Service disconnected, reconnecting..." → rebind with exponential back-off.

  • AIDL RemoteException: wrap all AIDL calls in try/catch. RemoteException = binder dead.

Trigger reconnect.

  • Process OOM kill of UI while service alive: service continues playing; notification controls

remain functional.

Threading

  • AIDL binder callbacks arrive on a binder thread pool (not main thread). Marshal to main thread

or appropriate dispatcher before UI updates.

  • Service process: Dispatchers.IO for all I/O, Dispatchers.Main for Service lifecycle

methods.

Caching

  • Shared data between processes: do NOT use in-memory cache (separate heap). Use:
    • ContentProvider for structured data.
    • SharedPreferences (multi-process mode is deprecated; prefer a DB-backed ContentProvider

or AIDL for live state).

  • Room with WRITE_AHEAD_LOGGING mode (WAL) is safe for multi-process read (one writer, many

readers).

Security

  • AIDL service should check caller's UID (Binder.getCallingUid()) to reject unauthorized clients.
  • Use android:process to set a custom process name; the process has the same UID as the app

(unless using sharedUserId which is deprecated).

  • Parcelable data: validate all incoming Parcelable data in the service process (treat as

untrusted if the IPC is exposed to other apps).

Performance

  • Minimize IPC frequency: batch state updates rather than calling AIDL per frame.
  • Large data (e.g., album art bitmap): do NOT pass through Binder (1 MB Binder transaction limit).

Pass a URI; UI process loads separately.

  • Service process memory: profile separately; it has its own heap.

Testing

  • AIDL interfaces tested with a mock binder in unit tests.
  • Integration: instrumented test that binds to the service, sends commands, verifies state

callbacks.

  • Simulate UI process death while service is running; verify graceful recovery.

Monitoring

  • Binder transaction failure rate.
  • Service crash rate (separate from UI crash rate).
  • RemoteException frequency.
  • Service foreground notification persistence (OEM-specific issues).

Rollout

  • Foreground service behavior varies dramatically by OEM (Samsung, Xiaomi, Huawei kill services

aggressively). Test on top 10 OEM device configurations before release.

  • Gradual rollout; monitor service crash rate per device brand.

Under the hood

AIDL compiles into a Stub/Proxy pair: the generated Stub.onTransact() runs in the service process and the Proxy in the caller marshals arguments into a Parcel, then transact() makes a binder_transaction ioctl into the kernel's binder driver. The driver copies the parcel into the target process via a shared mmap'd buffer (binder_alloc) and dispatches it on a thread from the binder thread pool — which is exactly why callbacks don't land on the main thread. The ~1 MB ceiling is the per-process binder transaction buffer the driver maps at process start (BINDER_VM_SIZE), shared across all in-flight transactions; exceeding it throws TransactionTooLargeException, so bitmaps go by URI instead. Room's WAL mode lets concurrent readers proceed against the last committed snapshot while a single writer appends to the -wal file, which is what makes one-writer/many-readers safe across processes where the deprecated MODE_MULTI_PROCESS SharedPreferences is not.

UI proc:   Proxy.play() → writeToParcel → ioctl(BINDER_WRITE_READ)
kernel:    binder driver copies parcel into target's mmap buffer (cap ~1MB)
svc proc:  binder thread → Stub.onTransact(TRANSACTION_play) → MusicPlayerService.play()
           state change → callback.onStateChanged()  (arrives on UI's binder thread, not main)

Interview Angles — Architecture

"Design a scalable Android app architecture"

"I'd anchor the whole thing on eight principles. First, feature modules with clear ownership boundaries — each team owns its module and you enforce that with Dependency Guard. Second, unidirectional data flow with MVVM or MVI, so the UI is purely a function of state and there are no hidden side-channel updates. Third, the Repository pattern as the single gatekeeper between data sources and business logic — the ViewModel never talks directly to the network or the database. Fourth, define contracts as interfaces between layers and depend on abstractions, not concretions, so you can swap implementations and test in isolation. Fifth, Compose with StateFlow for the UI layer — reactive and lifecycle-safe. Sixth, WorkManager for any background work that must complete reliably, even if the process is killed. Seventh, Baseline Profiles measured with Macrobenchmark so performance is a tracked metric, not a guess. And eighth, monitoring from day one: crash-free session rate, ANR rate, and the business metrics that actually matter for your feature."

"How would you migrate legacy MVP to MVVM/Compose?"

"The approach is incremental, feature by feature — never rewrite everything at once. There are six steps. First, identify a small, well-tested screen as the pilot so you have a contained blast radius. Second, add a ViewModel alongside the existing Presenter and move the state there, keeping the Presenter delegating to the ViewModel temporarily so nothing breaks. Third, replace the Fragment's XML with a Compose screen inside an AndroidViewBinding stub, then remove the stub once it's stable. Fourth, retire the Presenter once the screen is fully ViewModel-driven — at that point it's dead code. Fifth, measure code coverage, crash rate, and rendering frame times before and after per screen so you can prove the migration is paying off. And sixth, get team buy-in early with a concrete before/after comparison on the pilot screen — once they see the difference, the rest of the migration is much easier to drive."

"How would you introduce modularization gradually?"

"I'd do it in six steps, ordered by risk and impact. First, extract the :core modules — networking, database, and UI tokens — because they have no upward dependencies and immediately unlock parallel builds for everything that depends on them. Second, start writing all new features as :feature:X modules from day one; no rework of existing code yet. Third, introduce Dependency Guard and module ownership rules so the new model is enforced automatically, not just by convention. Fourth, extract existing features one at a time, starting with the most isolated ones that touch the fewest shared files. Fifth, be deliberate about api versus implementation dependencies to prevent transitive leakage from bleeding your module boundaries. And sixth, measure build time at every step with Gradle build scans — if a module extraction doesn't move the needle on compile scope, question whether it was worth the overhead."

"How do you handle offline mode?"

"My framework has five pieces. First, Room as the single source of truth — the UI always reads from the local database, never directly from the network. Second, the Repository decides whether to serve local or remote data based on a freshness policy, so that decision is centralized and not scattered across the codebase. Third, a NetworkMonitor wrapping ConnectivityManager that exposes an isOnline: StateFlow<Boolean> in :core:network, so any component can react to connectivity changes. Fourth, WorkManager for background sync with a NetworkType.CONNECTED constraint, so writes queue up and flush automatically when connectivity returns. Fifth, the UI reflects sync state explicitly — SYNCED, STALE, or OFFLINE — so users always know what they're looking at. And the one thing I always call out separately is conflict resolution, because the right strategy varies: for most data it's last-write-wins, for collaborative data you need a merge strategy, and for some things you have to prompt the user."

"How do you support multiple teams in the same codebase?"

"There are seven things I'd put in place. First, module ownership with CODEOWNERS so every module has a designated team responsible for it. Second, :api modules that define public contracts and :impl modules that are private to the owning team, so teams program to interfaces and never depend on each other's internals. Third, no cross-feature direct dependencies — all cross-feature navigation goes through :core:navigation, which keeps features genuinely isolated. Fourth, shared infrastructure in :core:* owned by a platform team, with any changes requiring a platform team review. Fifth, the Dependency Guard plugin to automatically enforce that no circular or cross-feature imports sneak in. Sixth, module-level lint rules so each team can have their own code-style preferences without polluting the whole codebase. And seventh, parallel builds per feature module so teams aren't blocking each other on the critical path at compile time."

15.2 Trade-Off Thinking

For every comparison, run through the same five questions: what problem does it solve, what are the benefits, what are the costs, when would I use it, and when would I avoid it.

MVVM vs MVI

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "MVVM and MVI are both unidirectional, but they differ in how state is shaped. MVVM is the pragmatic default — ViewModel exposes state, survives config changes, maps cleanly to StateFlow and Compose — and it's where I start. MVI tightens that into a single immutable UiState produced by a pure reducer from explicit Intent actions, which buys you consistency and replayable, testable state for complex flows. The nuance I'd flag is the failure mode of each: MVVM's separate StateFlows can drift out of sync, while MVI's cost is boilerplate and over-engineering on simple screens — so I upgrade to MVI only when interacting state fields make the ViewModel hard to reason about."

MVVM (Model-View-ViewModel)

  1. Problem it solves: Separates UI rendering from business logic; ViewModel survives config changes.
  2. Benefits:
    • Simpler mental model; most Android developers familiar with it.
    • Less boilerplate for straightforward screens.
    • StateFlow + SharedFlow maps naturally to Compose.
    • Well supported by Android Jetpack; viewModels() delegation, SavedStateHandle.
  3. Costs:
    • Multiple state fields (separate StateFlows) can get out of sync if not careful.
    • Side effects (navigation, toasts) require extra SharedFlow<Event> pattern.
    • Bidirectional data binding (if used with XML) causes hidden coupling.
  4. When to use: Most CRUD screens, standard forms, list-detail flows. When team is familiar with MVVM and the feature complexity is low-to-medium.
  5. When to avoid: Screens with complex, interdependent state where multiple events must be processed in strict order. Large screens where state fields proliferate and become hard to track.

MVI (Model-View-Intent)

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "MVI's whole point is a single source of truth for the screen: one immutable state, all changes flowing through a pure reduce(state, action) -> state function, and side effects pushed out to a separate effect channel. That purity is why it's so testable and why time-travel and action replay are even possible.
