The trade-off an interviewer will press is that it's heavier — sealed Intent hierarchies, a reducer, an effects channel — so on a trivial list-with-loading screen it's over-engineering; I reach for it on payment flows, multi-step wizards, and editors where interdependent state genuinely needs a state machine."
  1. Problem it solves: Strict unidirectional data flow; all state changes are explicit and testable; time-travel debugging possible.
  2. Benefits:
    • Single sealed UiState class — state is always consistent (no partial updates).
    • All events are explicit Intent/Action objects — easy to log, replay, test.
    • Reducer function is pure: reduce(currentState, action) → newState. Easy to unit test.
    • Easier to reason about complex state machines (payments, multi-step flows).
  3. Costs:
    • More boilerplate: Intent sealed class, Reducer, Effect channel.
    • Slight learning curve for teams unfamiliar with the pattern.
    • Can be over-engineering for simple screens.
  4. When to use: Complex screens with many interdependent state fields; payment flows; multi-step wizards; collaborative editors; any feature that benefits from action logging/replay.
  5. When to avoid: Simple screens (a list with a loading state). When team has no MVI experience and delivery timeline is short.

The rule of thumb is: start with MVVM, and upgrade to MVI when the ViewModel becomes hard to reason about because multiple state fields are interacting with each other.

Under the hood

The two patterns differ mechanically in how Compose recomposition is driven. In MVVM with N separate StateFlows, each collectAsStateWithLifecycle() is an independent snapshot State object; Compose's snapshot system tracks reads per-Composable, so an update to one flow recomposes only readers of that flow — efficient, but the screen can momentarily render an inconsistent combination of fields because the emissions aren't atomic. MVI funnels everything into one StateFlow<UiState>: the reducer runs state.copy(...) to produce a new immutable instance, StateFlow does an equals() distinct-until-changed check and emits once, so the UI always sees a single coherent snapshot. The reducer being pure is what makes replay real — fold(initialState, actions, ::reduce) deterministically reconstructs any state from the action log.

// MVI core loop — single coherent emission per action
intents
  .scan(initialState) { state, action -> reduce(state, action) } // pure, no side effects
  .distinctUntilChanged()
  .collect { uiState -> /* one consistent snapshot → Compose recomposes once */ }
// side effects (nav, toast) emitted separately so they don't re-fire on recomposition

Compose vs XML Views

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "Compose is declarative — the UI is a function of state and the runtime reconciles changes for you — whereas XML is imperative: you inflate a view tree once and then mutate it by hand, which is where most stale-UI bugs come from. For all new screens I default to Compose because of less boilerplate, first-class animation/theming, and a smart recomposition model. The nuance interviewers want is knowing the seams: Compose still needs AndroidView for SurfaceView-based things like maps, camera, and video, and performance hinges on understanding stability, remember, and derivedStateOf so you don't recompose more than necessary."

Compose

  1. Problem it solves: Declarative UI — UI is a function of state; no manual view synchronization.
  2. Benefits:
    • Less boilerplate: no ViewBinding, no notifyDataSetChanged().
    • Animations and theming are first-class.
    • Easier testing via Compose test APIs (onNodeWithText, performClick).
    • Strong recomposition model — Compose only re-renders what changed.
    • Single language (Kotlin) for both logic and UI.
  3. Costs:
    • Learning curve for teams trained in XML.
    • Compose compiler adds to build time.
    • Some edge cases in performance require understanding recomposition (stability, remember, derivedStateOf).
    • Interop with existing XML views adds complexity (but works via AndroidView/ComposeView).
  4. When to use: All new screens. Teams building greenfield apps or migrating screen by screen.
  5. When to avoid: Screens that use complex custom View subclasses not yet Compose-compatible; teams under tight deadline with no Compose experience; SurfaceView-based features (maps, cameras, video — use AndroidView).

XML Views

  1. Problem it solves: Standard declarative UI layout with view hierarchy inflated at runtime.
  2. Benefits: Large existing ecosystem; every Android developer knows it. Mature tooling (Layout Inspector, Layout Editor).
  3. Costs: Manual synchronization between UI and data model; boilerplate ViewBinding; adapter pattern required for lists; poor animation ergonomics.
  4. When to use: Only when maintaining existing XML code or when a specific custom view is not yet Compose-portable.
  5. When to avoid: Any new screen or feature.

Under the hood

The Compose compiler plugin rewrites every @Composable function to take a hidden $composer parameter and a $changed bitmask, and wraps the body in composer.startRestartGroup()/endRestartGroup(). Each group's emitted nodes and remembered values are stored as "slots" in a gap-buffer data structure called the slot table; on recomposition the runtime compares parameters via the $changed mask and the stability inference, and skips re-executing any restartable group whose inputs are unchanged — that's the "only re-render what changed" claim, concretely. XML instead inflates into a heap-allocated View tree once via LayoutInflater (reflection/<merge>-aware XML parsing), and every later change is a direct field mutation plus invalidate()/requestLayout() that you trigger manually. AndroidView is needed for SurfaceView/TextureView because those punch a separate hardware compositor layer that Compose's own draw pass can't synthesize.

Compose:  state changes → invalidated group marked → recompose runs ONLY that group
          → slot table updated → Layout/Draw nodes diffed → minimal redraw
XML:      inflate tree once → you call view.setText(...) + invalidate()/requestLayout() by hand

Room vs Raw SQLite

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "Room is a compile-time abstraction over SQLite: annotation processing verifies my SQL against the schema at build time, generates the boilerplate, and gives me Flow and coroutine support plus a real migration system. Raw SQLite is just the low-level API — no type safety, manual cursors, hand-rolled migrations. I use Room almost always for structured data; I'd only drop to raw SQLite in an SDK where pulling in Room's footprint and KSP is unacceptable. The gotcha worth naming is that Room is still SQLite underneath — exotic SQL like window functions or CTEs may need @RawQuery, and migrations are on me; a missing migration throws at open time, not at compile time."

Room

  1. Problem it solves: Type-safe compile-time verified SQL on Android without boilerplate.
  2. Benefits:
    • @Entity, @Dao, @Query — SQL verified at compile time, not runtime.
    • Built-in coroutine and Flow support.
    • Database migrations with Migration objects; version checked at open.
    • @TypeConverter for custom types.
    • Easy to test with in-memory Room DB.
  3. Costs:
    • Kapt/KSP annotation processing adds build time.
    • Some complex SQL (window functions, CTEs) requires raw query workarounds.
    • Adds ~200 KB to APK.
  4. When to use: Almost always. Any structured local data storage in an Android app.
  5. When to avoid: Extremely simple key-value storage (use DataStore instead). Embedding a database in an SDK where you want to minimize transitive dependencies. Apps that require complex SQL features Room doesn't cleanly support (rare).

Raw SQLite

  1. Problem it solves: Direct low-level database access.
  2. Benefits: No dependencies, no annotation processing.
  3. Costs: No type safety, no compile-time query verification, manual cursor management, no built-in migration system, no reactive support.
  4. When to use: SDK where pulling Room is unacceptable. Very simple use case (one table, five columns).
  5. When to avoid: Any app with non-trivial data model.

Under the hood

Room's KSP/kapt processor parses each @Query string at compile time, opens the schema you declared via @Entity, and actually validates column names and types against it — a typo'd column fails the build, which is the entire value proposition. It then generates a *_Impl DAO that binds parameters to a compiled SupportSQLiteStatement and walks the resulting Cursor into your data class, so there's no reflection at runtime — just generated cursor.getString(columnIndex) calls. Reactive queries register an InvalidationTracker observer that uses SQLite's per-table update hooks: writes bump a versioned trigger table, the tracker re-runs affected queries on the query executor and re-emits the Flow. Migrations are validated by a stored schema hash in room_master_table; on open, if the on-disk user_version differs and no matching Migration is registered, Room throws IllegalStateException — that's the runtime (not compile-time) failure to call out.

build time:  @Query("SELECT name FROM user WHERE id=:id")
             → KSP validates name/id against @Entity schema → generates UserDao_Impl
runtime:     UserDao_Impl binds :id → SupportSQLiteStatement → Cursor → User(...)
open time:   on-disk user_version != expected && no Migration → IllegalStateException

WorkManager vs Foreground Service

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "WorkManager and a foreground service answer different questions. WorkManager is for guaranteed, deferrable work — uploads, syncs, cleanup — that must eventually finish across process death and reboots, with constraint-based scheduling and backoff, but it's not real-time: periodic work has a 15-minute floor. A foreground service is for work that's running right now and the user is aware of — playback, navigation, live location — with a mandatory persistent notification. The nuance interviewers like is that they compose: a long upload can be an expedited WorkManager job that uses setForeground() to show a notification, and on Android 14 you must declare the foreground service type or the OS rejects it."

WorkManager

  1. Problem it solves: Guaranteed deferred background work that survives process death and device reboots.
  2. Benefits:
    • Constraint-based scheduling (network, battery, storage).
    • Chaining, parallelism, backoff built-in.
    • Works across all Android versions (no doze/battery optimization issues).
    • Progress observation via WorkInfo LiveData/Flow.
    • Expedited work requests for near-immediate execution.
  3. Costs:
    • Not for real-time or low-latency work (15-minute minimum interval for periodic).
    • No user-visible progress notification built-in (you add it manually).
    • Debugging scheduled work is harder (use WorkManager.getWorkInfosForUniqueWork()).
  4. When to use: Uploads, syncs, cleanup jobs, notification scheduling, any work that must complete "eventually" but not immediately.
  5. When to avoid: Work that needs to run immediately and continuously (use foreground service). Work where sub-second latency matters.

Foreground Service

  1. Problem it solves: Long-running operations that the user is aware of and that must not be interrupted.
  2. Benefits:
    • Runs indefinitely while foregrounded (persistent notification).
    • User-visible progress.
    • Required for real-time operations (location, media playback, calls, downloads).
  3. Costs:
    • Must show a persistent notification (Android 8+).
    • Foreground service types required (Android 14+) — must declare type in manifest.
    • OEM battery optimizations can kill even foreground services on some devices.
    • More complex lifecycle management.
  4. When to use: Music/podcast playback, navigation, ongoing call, real-time location tracking, file download/upload requiring user progress.
  5. When to avoid: Short background tasks (use WorkManager or coroutines). Anything that doesn't need to be running while the user is actively watching.

Under the hood

WorkManager persists each request as a WorkSpec row in its own Room database and then delegates to a platform scheduler — JobScheduler on API 23+ (and AlarmManager + a BroadcastReceiver on older versions). Because the schedule lives in the OS and the spec lives on disk, work survives both process death and reboot (a boot BroadcastReceiver reschedules pending specs). The "15-minute minimum" for periodic work is a JobScheduler constraint, and expedited work maps to a JobScheduler expedited job (or a short-lived foreground service on older APIs) that the OS runs out of the normal deferral window but still subject to quota. A foreground service is a different contract entirely: startForeground(id, notification) must be called within ~5 seconds of start or the system throws ForegroundServiceDidNotStartInTimeException; on Android 14+ the call must match a <service android:foregroundServiceType> declaration and a runtime-granted permission, and the elevated process importance (oom_adj) is what protects it from the low-memory killer.

WorkManager.enqueue → WorkSpec row in Room → JobScheduler.schedule(jobInfo + constraints)
   (process killed / reboot) → OS / boot receiver re-dispatches → Worker.doWork() on a thread pool

startForegroundService() → must call startForeground() < ~5s
   → notification posted + FGS type checked (API 34) → process importance raised → survives LMK

Coroutines vs RxJava

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "I default to coroutines for all new Kotlin code — they give me structured concurrency, so a scope ties async work to a lifecycle and cancellation propagates automatically, and the code reads sequentially instead of as nested callbacks. RxJava still wins when I'm in a Java module or need exotic operators with no Flow equivalent, but those cases are rare. The gotcha an interviewer probes is that coroutines aren't free of leaks — if you launch on a scope you don't cancel, like GlobalScope, the work outlives the component, which is exactly the disposal problem RxJava had."

Coroutines

  1. Problem it solves: Asynchronous and concurrent programming without callback hell; structured concurrency.
  2. Benefits:
    • Sequential-looking code for async operations (no nesting).
    • Structured concurrency: CoroutineScope ties coroutine lifetime to component lifecycle.
    • Cancellation propagates automatically.
    • First-class Kotlin support: suspend, async/await, Flow.
    • Smaller runtime overhead than RxJava.
    • Official Google/Jetpack recommendation.
  3. Costs:
    • Requires Kotlin. Java code cannot call suspend functions directly.
    • Flow is less feature-rich than RxJava Observable for exotic operators.
    • Debugging: coroutine stack traces less readable (use -Dkotlinx.coroutines.debug).
  4. When to use: All new async code. Any Kotlin codebase.
  5. When to avoid: When the codebase is Java-only (use RxJava). When complex reactive pipelines use operators not in Flow (rarely true).

RxJava

  1. Problem it solves: Reactive programming model: compose streams of events with rich operators.
  2. Benefits:
    • Rich operator set (flatMap, zip, combineLatest, throttle, etc.).
    • Works in Java codebases.
    • Mature ecosystem, large community.
  3. Costs:
    • Steep learning curve.
    • Verbose code.
    • Easy to forget to dispose subscriptions → memory leaks.
    • Heavier runtime than coroutines.
    • No longer the Android-recommended approach.
  4. When to use: Maintaining existing RxJava code. Java-only modules. Complex observable pipelines with operators that have no good coroutine equivalent.
  5. When to avoid: All new Kotlin code. Any greenfield feature.

Under the hood

The compiler rewrites every suspend function via a Continuation-Passing Style transform: it adds a hidden Continuation parameter and turns the function body into a state machine. Each suspension point becomes a label case in a generated invokeSuspend; locals that must survive a suspension are spilled to fields on that state-machine object. When a function suspends, it returns the sentinel COROUTINE_SUSPENDED instead of blocking a thread; the dispatcher resumes by calling resumeWith on the continuation, re-entering invokeSuspend at the saved label. This is why a single thread can host thousands of coroutines — they're heap objects, not OS threads.

suspend fun load(): Data            // source
fun load(cont: Continuation): Any?  // compiled signature
  switch(cont.label) {
    case 0: cont.label = 1; return api.fetch(cont)  // may return COROUTINE_SUSPENDED
    case 1: return parse(cont.result)               // resumed here
  }

By contrast RxJava builds an operator chain of Observable objects at subscribe time; each subscribe() allocates Disposable links you must dispose, and there is no compiler support — the "stream" is a runtime object graph, not a thread-cheap state machine.

Flow vs LiveData

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "Flow is my default because it lives in pure Kotlin modules, has real operators, and StateFlow always holds a current value so there are no missed emissions across config changes. LiveData I only touch in legacy code — it's main-thread-only and tied to the Android framework, so it can't live in a domain module. The nuance interviewers want is collection safety: a cold Flow keeps running in the background unless I collect with repeatOnLifecycle or collectAsStateWithLifecycle, whereas LiveData stops automatically — so Flow trades convenience for control and you can leak if you forget that."

Flow (StateFlow/SharedFlow)

  1. Problem it solves: Reactive data streams that integrate with coroutines and support backpressure.
  2. Benefits:
    • Works outside Android (ViewModel, Repository, even pure Kotlin modules can use Flow).
    • Richer operator set than LiveData (map, filter, combine, flatMapLatest, etc.).
    • StateFlow is always consistent (no "missed emissions" on config change).
    • Better for UI layer with Compose (collectAsStateWithLifecycle).
    • Testable with turbine library.
  3. Costs:
    • Requires explicit lifecycle-aware collection (repeatOnLifecycle or collectAsStateWithLifecycle) — forgetting this leaks.
    • No built-in null-value semantics for initial state (use a nullable or wrapper type).
  4. When to use: All new code. Repository → ViewModel → UI data flow. Any stream that needs operators.
  5. When to avoid: Very simple one-shot data that doesn't change. Cases where LiveData lifecycle integration is already well-tested and working.

LiveData

  1. Problem it solves: Lifecycle-aware observable that automatically stops/resumes with the lifecycle owner.
  2. Benefits:
    • Automatic lifecycle handling (no repeatOnLifecycle needed).
    • Simple API.
  3. Costs:
    • Main thread only (value is always posted to main thread).
    • Weak operator set.
    • Tied to Android framework (not usable in non-Android modules like :domain:).
    • MediatorLiveData is verbose compared to Flow operators.
  4. When to use: Maintaining existing LiveData code.
  5. When to avoid: All new code. Any code in domain/data layers (non-Android modules).

Under the hood

A plain Flow is cold: the lambda passed to flow { } doesn't run until a terminal collect is called, and it re-executes per collector. StateFlow is hot and conflated — it's backed by a single AtomicReference-style slot holding the latest value plus an array of subscriber slots; new collectors immediately receive the current value, and equal consecutive values are dropped via equals, which is why a poorly chosen data class can swallow emissions. Collection suspends the collecting coroutine until cancelled. LiveData, by comparison, keeps an ObserverWrapper per observer and registers a LifecycleObserver; it gates dispatch on whether the owner is at least STARTED, and setValue enforces the main thread while postValue hops through a Runnable posted to the main Handler — and because postValue only stores the last value before the runnable runs, rapid posts can be coalesced and lost.

// StateFlow conflation: only distinct values reach collectors
val state = MutableStateFlow(0)
state.value = 1   // emitted
state.value = 1   // dropped — equals() the current value

Hilt vs Manual DI

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "Hilt is my pick for standard apps because it generates the Dagger component hierarchy already wired to the Android lifecycle — Application, Activity, ViewModel scopes — so I get correct scoping without writing it. Manual DI I reserve for SDKs and pure-Kotlin modules where I can't depend on the framework and want zero annotation processing. The trade-off interviewers care about is build time: Hilt runs through KAPT or KSP, and that annotation processing is usually the single biggest hit to incremental build speed, so on a large modularized app I weigh that cost deliberately."

Hilt

  1. Problem it solves: Boilerplate-free DI on Android using annotation-based code generation on top of Dagger 2.
  2. Benefits:
    • Standard component hierarchy tied to Android lifecycle (Application, Activity, ViewModel, etc.).
    • Less boilerplate than raw Dagger 2.
    • @HiltViewModel integrates ViewModel injection seamlessly.
    • Good documentation and tooling.
    • Testing support: @HiltAndroidTest, @UninstallModules.
  3. Costs:
    • Build time: Hilt/Dagger annotation processing (KAPT/KSP) is the single largest build time contributor.
    • Hard to use outside Android (not suitable for pure Kotlin SDK).
    • Opaque compile errors when DI graph is incomplete.
  4. When to use: All standard Android apps. Greenfield apps. When team is willing to invest in DI setup upfront.
  5. When to avoid: SDKs (no framework dependency). Apps where build time is critical and team is small (consider Koin or manual DI). Apps targeting very low API levels where Hilt adds unexpected overhead.

Manual DI (Pure Kotlin)

  1. Problem it solves: Dependency injection without annotation processing — create factories and pass dependencies by hand.
  2. Benefits:
    • Zero build time overhead.
    • Works in any Kotlin/Java code (SDK, non-Android modules).
    • No magic; easier to reason about.
  3. Costs:
    • Boilerplate: factories, constructor call sites.
    • Scope management is manual (you manage singleton vs scoped vs transient).
    • Hard to maintain at scale (100+ classes).
  4. When to use: SDKs. Small apps. Non-Android modules in a larger project.
  5. When to avoid: Large apps with many injection points — the boilerplate becomes unmanageable.

Under the hood

Hilt/Dagger resolve the entire dependency graph at compile time, not runtime — there is no reflection in the hot path. The annotation processor reads @Inject constructors, @Module/@Provides, and @Binds, then generates Java Factory classes (e.g. MyClass_Factory) and component implementations (DaggerApplicationComponent) that are just nested Provider objects calling constructors directly. Scoping is implemented as DoubleCheck, a double-checked-locking lazy wrapper that caches a single instance per component. Hilt adds a bytecode-transform step that injects boilerplate into your Application/Activity and generates the @InstallIn component wiring. Because it's full graph validation, a missing binding fails the build — that's the source of the "opaque" multi-line Dagger errors.

@Inject MyRepo(api: Api)  ──KAPT/KSP──▶  MyRepo_Factory implements Provider<MyRepo>
                                          get() = MyRepo(apiProvider.get())
@Singleton  ──▶ DoubleCheck.provider(...)  // one instance cached per component

Manual DI, by contrast, is just hand-written constructor calls resolved when the code runs — no generated factories, no graph validation, so a missing dependency is a normal compile error at the call site rather than a processor failure.

Monolith vs Modular Architecture

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "A monolith in a single :app module is fine for a small team and an MVP — one DI graph, no inter-module plumbing. But it doesn't scale: any change recompiles everything and there are no ownership boundaries. I move to modular for multi-team apps and to attack build time, because Gradle can compile independent modules in parallel and skip unchanged ones. The subtlety interviewers push on is that modularization only pays off if the dependency graph is wide and flat — if everything depends on one big :common module, you serialize the build and lose the parallelism you modularized for."

Monolith (Single App Module)

  1. Problem it solves: Simple app structure where all code lives in :app.
  2. Benefits:
    • Simple setup; fast to get started.
    • No inter-module dependency management.
    • Single DI component graph.
  3. Costs:
    • Build time: any change recompiles everything.
    • No ownership boundaries — any team can modify any code.
    • Harder to enforce clean architecture.
    • Difficult to extract to modular later (becomes a big bang rewrite risk).
  4. When to use: Small apps (1 team, <5 engineers). Prototype/MVP. Short-lived apps.
  5. When to avoid: Multi-team codebases. Apps that plan to grow. Apps where build time is already a concern.

Modular Architecture

  1. Problem it solves: Parallel builds, clean ownership boundaries, faster incremental compilation.
  2. Benefits:
    • Build: only changed modules recompile.
    • Ownership: teams own specific modules.
    • Testability: modules tested in isolation.
    • Enables dynamic feature modules.
    • Enforces clean architecture (import rules).
  3. Costs:
    • Complex Gradle setup.
    • Inter-module communication needs explicit contracts (:api modules).
    • Easy to make circular dependencies if not managed.
    • Higher ramp-up for new engineers.
  4. When to use: Any app with > 2 teams. Any app targeting aggressive build time reduction. Any app planning DFMs.
  5. When to avoid: Small teams where the overhead exceeds the benefit.

Under the hood

Gradle models the build as a task DAG (directed acyclic graph). Modules with no dependency edge between them are scheduled onto separate worker threads and built in parallel; a module rebuilds only if its inputs changed or a dependency's public ABI changed. That last point is the real mechanism behind "only changed modules recompile": Kotlin/Gradle compute an ABI fingerprint of each module's public API, and if you change a method body but not its signature, downstream modules read from the build cache and skip recompilation. An :api module exposing only interfaces maximizes this — implementation changes don't perturb the ABI consumers see. A monolith collapses this DAG into one node, so every edit invalidates one giant compilation task with no parallelism and no per-module cache hits.

:feature-a ─┐
:feature-b ─┼─▶ :core-api (interfaces only)   parallel; downstream skips
:feature-c ─┘        ▲                          rebuild on body-only edits
                     │  changing an impl behind :core-api
                  :core-impl  ──── ABI unchanged ⇒ cached

Single Activity vs Multiple Activities

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "Single Activity with a NavController is my default for a linear app — one back stack, shared ViewModel scope across the graph, and cheap Compose transitions. I reach for multiple Activities when features are genuinely independent or need their own task stacks and external entry points, because that's what Android's task model handles correctly. The thing interviewers probe is task and back-stack behavior: NavController only manages an in-process fragment/composable back stack, so deep links and launch modes that need real Android task isolation still want separate Activities."

Single Activity

  1. Problem it solves: One Activity hosts all screens; NavController/NavHost handles navigation within.
  2. Benefits:
    • Shared ViewModel scope across the navigation graph.
    • Smooth transitions (shared element, slide) across all screens.
    • Single back stack managed by NavController.
    • Less Intent boilerplate.
  3. Costs:
    • Complex flows may need navigation sub-graphs.
    • Shared ViewModels can become large if not decomposed.
    • Screen state from deep in the graph may be complex to save/restore.
  4. When to use: Linear, single-flow apps. Apps where cross-screen animation is important. Greenfield apps.
  5. When to avoid: Super-apps where features are completely independent and should have separate task stacks. When entry points from external intents require different Activities for proper Android back-stack behavior.

Multiple Activities

  1. Problem it solves: Each flow or feature has its own Activity with its own task stack and lifecycle.
  2. Benefits:
    • Proper Android task management (each Activity can be a task root).
    • Clear isolation between features.
    • Easier to support multiple deep-link entry points.
  3. Costs:
    • More Intent/Parcelable boilerplate.
    • Harder to share state across Activities.
    • Activity transitions are heavier than Compose navigation transitions.
  4. When to use: Flows with independent entry points. Multi-process apps. Feature modules that should be isolated.
  5. When to avoid: Within a single linear flow (use NavController for that).

Under the hood

An Activity is a system-managed component: launching one sends an Intent to the ActivityManagerService in system_server over Binder, which decides the target task (an affinity-based stack of activities) per the launchMode/taskAffinity flags, then drives the lifecycle via the Instrumentation/ActivityThread on your main thread. That cross-process round-trip plus full lifecycle teardown is why Activity transitions are "heavier." NavController, by contrast, never touches the system: its back stack is a plain in-process list of NavBackStackEntry objects, each owning its own ViewModelStore, SavedStateRegistry, and Lifecycle; "navigation" just swaps the displayed destination and pushes/pops that list. So the system back button and onBackPressed resolve against the OS task stack for Activities but against NavController's list for in-app destinations — which is exactly why deep links that must restore a real Android back stack lean on Activities or explicit TaskStackBuilder.

startActivity(intent) ──Binder──▶ ActivityManagerService (system_server)
                                     resolves task by launchMode/affinity
                                     ◀── schedules lifecycle on ActivityThread

navController.navigate(route)  // in-process: push NavBackStackEntry onto a List

Repository per Feature vs Shared Repository

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "I scope a repository per feature when the data is genuinely owned by that feature — it keeps modules decoupled and trivial to mock. But for anything multiple features read, like user identity, session, or cart, I want a single shared repository so there's one source of truth. The failure mode interviewers want me to name is cache coherence: if two per-feature repositories each cache the same entity, they drift out of sync, and you ship bugs where one screen shows stale data the other already updated."

Repository per Feature

  1. Problem it solves: Each feature owns its data access layer; no shared state.
  2. Benefits:
    • Clear ownership.
    • Feature modules have no cross-module data dependencies.
    • Easier to mock in tests.
  3. Costs:
    • Data duplication: two features may have their own copy of UserProfile data.
    • Cache coherence: two repositories caching the same entity may get out of sync.
  4. When to use: Features with truly independent data (e.g., health feature and food feature in a super-app).
  5. When to avoid: When multiple features display the same data (user profile, cart, session) — you want a single source of truth.

Shared Repository

  1. Problem it solves: Single source of truth for data shared across features (e.g., UserRepository, CartRepository).
  2. Benefits:
    • Cache coherence: all readers see the same state.
    • One network call for shared data.
  3. Costs:
    • Creates a dependency from feature modules to :data:shared — careful with ownership.
  4. When to use: User identity, session, cart — anything that must be consistent across features.
  5. When to avoid: Feature-specific data that no other feature needs.

Under the hood

The "single source of truth" only holds if every reader observes the same in-memory instance. A shared repository typically exposes a hot StateFlow (or Room-backed Flow) over one process-singleton instance — usually @Singleton-scoped in DI — so when a writer mutates state, the conflated flow re-emits and all collectors converge on the new value. Two per-feature repositories, even pointing at the same SQLite tables or network endpoint, each hold their own cache object and their own flow; a write through one doesn't notify the other, so they diverge until something forces a refetch. Room mitigates part of this because its query Flows observe the underlying table's InvalidationTracker and re-emit on any write to that table — meaning two repositories reading via Room queries (not in-memory caches) can stay coherent through the database, but two independent memory caches cannot.

Shared:   write ─▶ MutableStateFlow (one @Singleton) ─▶ re-emits ─▶ all collectors agree
Per-feat: write ─▶ Repo A cache ──╳── Repo B cache (no notification) ⇒ stale reads
Room:     write ─▶ table ─▶ InvalidationTracker ─▶ all query Flows re-run

Domain Layer vs No Domain Layer

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "A domain layer means I push business logic into pure-Kotlin use-case classes that don't touch Android, so the ViewModel just orchestrates and the logic is trivially unit-testable and KMP-shareable. The tradeoff — and the thing interviewers probe — is that on a simple CRUD screen the use case becomes a one-line pass-through to a repository, which is pure ceremony. So I treat it as conditional: add it when logic is genuinely complex, multi-step, or shared across ViewModels, not as a blanket rule."

Domain Layer

  1. Problem it solves: Business logic in pure Kotlin use-case classes, independent of Android framework and UI.
  2. Benefits:
    • Pure Kotlin: no Android imports → fast unit tests, reusable across platforms (KMP).
    • Single responsibility: each use case does one thing.
    • ViewModel is thin: delegates to use cases.
    • Logic testable without mocking Android framework.
  3. Costs:
    • Extra layer → more files, more indirection.
    • For simple screens, use cases are trivial pass-throughs (wasted abstraction).
  4. When to use: Complex business logic (payment rules, eligibility checks, booking constraints). Multi-step transformations. Code shared across multiple ViewModels. KMP targeting.
  5. When to avoid: Simple CRUD screens where the "use case" would just call one repository method.

No Domain Layer

  1. Problem it solves: Simplify architecture for straightforward screens.
  2. Benefits: Less boilerplate; faster to write.
  3. Costs: Business logic bleeds into ViewModel or Repository. Hard to test complex logic in isolation.
  4. When to use: Simple screens. Prototype code.
  5. When to avoid: Any non-trivial business logic. Multi-team codebases where logic ownership matters.

Under the hood

A "use case" carries no special framework magic — there's no androidx.usecase class. The convention is just a single-public-method class, often exposing operator fun invoke(...) so callers can write getUser(id) instead of getUser.execute(id). The compiler lowers that invoke operator to an ordinary virtual method call; the call-site sugar is resolved entirely at compile time. Because the class has no Android imports, its compiled bytecode lands in a module that can target the JVM or, via Kotlin Multiplatform, be recompiled to a .klib and lowered to LLVM IR for native or transpiled to JS — the same source feeds multiple backends. The "purity" that makes it fast to test is literally the absence of any android.jar symbol in the class's constant pool, so JUnit can load it on a desktop JVM without Robolectric's shadow framework or an emulator.

class IsEligibleForBooking(private val repo: PatientRepo) {
    // compiles to a normal method; `eligible(patient)` is invoke() sugar
    operator fun invoke(patient: Patient): Boolean = /* pure logic */
}

Local-First vs Network-First

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "Local-first means the UI reads from a local source of truth — usually Room — so reads are instant and the app works offline, with the network just refreshing the cache in the background. The catch is you've now signed up for staleness and conflict resolution, so I reserve it for data where showing slightly-old data beats showing a spinner. For correctness-critical data like a payment confirmation or live seat availability, I go network-first and fail loudly rather than serve a stale value."

Local-First

  1. Problem it solves: App works offline; UI always responsive (reads from local DB first).
  2. Benefits:
    • Zero latency reads.
    • Works offline by default.
    • User experience consistent regardless of network quality.
  3. Costs:
    • Stale data risk: local data may be outdated.
    • Complex sync and conflict resolution needed.
    • More implementation effort (Room + sync logic).
  4. When to use: Feed apps, todo/note apps, offline-capable enterprise apps. Any feature where showing stale data is better than showing nothing.
  5. When to avoid: Real-time critical data (stock prices, live seat availability). Data that must be fresh for correctness (payment confirmation, order status).

Network-First

  1. Problem it solves: Always show the latest data from the server.
  2. Benefits:
    • Always fresh.
    • No conflict resolution needed.
    • Simpler implementation.
  3. Costs:
    • Fails offline.
    • Higher latency (must wait for network).
  4. When to use: Real-time data (prices, inventory, live scores). Data that is wrong if stale.
  5. When to avoid: Data that changes infrequently. Poor network conditions.

Under the hood

The local-first pattern is mechanically the "single source of truth" Flow: the UI collects a Room @Query returning Flow<List<T>>, and the network only writes into the DB. Room implements that reactive query by registering an InvalidationTracker — an Observer keyed to the queried table names — backed by an UPDATE/INSERT/DELETE trigger on a hidden room_table_modification_log table. When a write commits, the trigger flips a per-table dirty flag; the tracker polls (or is notified) and re-runs the query, re-emitting on the Flow. That's why a background sync write automatically pushes fresh data to a screen that's only reading. Network-first skips this entirely: the repository awaits the suspend HTTP call and maps the response straight to UI state, so cancellation of the calling coroutine (e.g. viewModelScope clearing) propagates a CancellationException through OkHttp's call and there's no cached fallback if it fails.

Network → repo.upsert(rows) → SQLite write → InvalidationTracker fires
        → Room re-runs @Query → Flow re-emits → UI recomposes
(UI never awaits the network on the read path)

Synchronous vs Asynchronous IPC

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "Synchronous AIDL is a blocking transact on a Binder thread — the caller waits for the remote process to return, which is simple but dangerous: if the callee does real work you can ANR, and re-entrant synchronous calls can deadlock the limited Binder thread pool. Asynchronous IPC — oneway methods, callbacks, or Messenger — returns immediately and delivers results later on a Binder thread you marshal back to main. My rule: synchronous only for guaranteed sub-millisecond status queries, async for anything touching I/O or computation."

Synchronous IPC (AIDL blocking call)

  1. Problem it solves: Caller waits for the result from another process; simpler sequential code.
  2. Benefits:
    • Simple to reason about: call returns result.
    • No callback management.
  3. Costs:
    • Blocks the calling thread (which is a binder thread, not main thread — but still counts).
    • Risk of ANR if the callee is slow.
    • Deadlock risk if callee calls back into the caller synchronously.
  4. When to use: Quick IPC calls with guaranteed low latency (< 1ms). Status queries where the caller NEEDS the answer immediately.
  5. When to avoid: Any call that involves I/O or computation in the remote process. Any call from a UI-critical context.

Asynchronous IPC (Messenger, callbacks, AIDL with callback)

  1. Problem it solves: Non-blocking IPC; caller continues while waiting for result.
  2. Benefits:
    • Non-blocking; no ANR risk.
    • Callback arrives on binder thread (can be marshalled to main).
  3. Costs:
    • More complex code (callbacks/channels).
    • State management more complex.
  4. When to use: All IPC involving I/O or computation. State subscription (register callback, receive updates over time).
  5. When to avoid: When synchronous result is required and the call is guaranteed fast.

Under the hood

Every AIDL call bottoms out in IBinder.transact(), which copies the marshalled Parcel across the process boundary through the /dev/binder kernel driver via an ioctl. For a synchronous call the driver blocks the caller's thread and schedules the work on a thread from the callee's Binder thread pool, which is capped (16 by default per process). That cap is exactly why blocking calls are risky: saturate the pool and all IPC into that process stalls. Async is the oneway flag in the .aidl — the generated stub sets FLAG_ONEWAY on the transaction, so transact() returns as soon as the kernel has buffered the Parcel into the target's transaction queue without waiting for a reply. A callback is just a second IBinder (a Stub you pass as a method argument), so the "reply" is a fresh oneway transaction in the reverse direction, landing on one of your Binder threads — which is why you then post it to a Handler to reach the main thread. The Binder transaction buffer is ~1MB shared per process, so oversized Parcels throw TransactionTooLargeException regardless of sync vs async.

sync:  transact(code, data, reply, 0)        → caller thread parks until reply Parcel returns
async: transact(code, data, null, FLAG_ONEWAY) → returns after kernel buffers data

HashMap vs TreeMap

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "HashMap gives me amortized O(1) get/put by bucketing on the key's hashCode, with no ordering guarantee, and that's my default. TreeMap is a red-black tree that keeps keys sorted at O(log n), which I reach for only when I actually need ordered iteration or range queries like headMap/subMap. The Android nuance an interviewer likes is that for small maps I'd prefer ArrayMap, and for Int keys SparseArray, because both avoid the autoboxing and per-entry Node overhead that HashMap pays."

HashMap

  1. Problem it solves: O(1) average-case key lookup, insertion, deletion.
  2. Benefits: Fastest for most lookups; no ordering overhead.
  3. Costs: No ordering; iteration order not guaranteed; worst-case O(n) with hash collisions.
  4. When to use: Lookup/cache tables where insertion order or sorted order is not needed. The default choice for most Maps.
  5. When to avoid: When you need sorted iteration (e.g., range queries, sorted display of entries). When key ordering matters for correctness.

TreeMap

  1. Problem it solves: Sorted key ordering with O(log n) operations.
  2. Benefits: Keys always sorted; supports headMap, tailMap, subMap, firstKey, lastKey.
  3. Costs: O(log n) for all operations vs O(1) for HashMap.
  4. When to use: Range queries. Ordered iteration. Implementing a priority queue-like structure where keys have natural ordering.
  5. When to avoid: Simple lookup where ordering is irrelevant. Hot paths where O(log n) is slower than O(1).

Under the hood

HashMap is an array of buckets (Node[] table) indexed by (table.length - 1) & hash, where hash is the key's hashCode() spread with h ^ (h >>> 16) to mix high bits into the low index. Colliding keys form a singly-linked chain; since Java 8 / ART, a bucket that exceeds 8 entries (TREEIFY_THRESHOLD) and a table of at least 64 converts that chain into a red-black tree, bounding worst-case lookup at O(log n) instead of O(n). It resizes (doubling, LOAD_FACTOR 0.75) by rehashing every entry — a spike that's why presizing matters. TreeMap has no array and no hashing at all: it's a red-black tree of Entry nodes, ordered by the Comparator (or natural Comparable), so every get/put walks ~log₂n levels doing comparisons. That's why firstKey/subMap are cheap for TreeMap (tree traversal) and impossible for HashMap. Android's ArrayMap/SparseArray use a different layout entirely — two parallel arrays (sorted hashes + key/value objects) binary-searched — trading O(log n) lookup for far less memory and zero Node allocation, and SparseArray stores int[] keys directly to skip Integer boxing.

HashMap:  hash = h ^ (h>>>16);  idx = (len-1) & hash;  bucket = chain | RB-tree(if >8)
TreeMap:  root → left/right by compare(key);  balanced red-black, height ~log n

ArrayList vs LinkedList

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "ArrayList is a growable array — O(1) indexed access and great cache locality because elements are contiguous, at the cost of O(n) mid-list inserts that shift the tail. LinkedList is a doubly-linked node chain with O(1) head/tail ops but O(n) indexing and a pointer-chasing cache penalty. On Android LinkedList is almost never the right call — for queue/deque I reach for ArrayDeque, which is a circular array that gets O(1) at both ends without the per-node object overhead."

ArrayList

  1. Problem it solves: Ordered, indexed, random-access list backed by an array.
  2. Benefits:
    • O(1) random access by index.
    • Good cache locality (contiguous memory).
    • Efficient iteration.
  3. Costs:
    • O(n) insertion/deletion in the middle (array shift).
    • Amortized O(1) add-at-end; occasional resize copies.
  4. When to use: The default choice for lists. Any list where you read by index or iterate often. Compose LazyColumn data model.
  5. When to avoid: Frequent insertion/deletion in the middle of large lists.

LinkedList

  1. Problem it solves: O(1) insertion/deletion at head/tail without array resizing.
  2. Benefits: O(1) add/remove at head or tail (as a Deque).
  3. Costs:
    • O(n) random access.
    • High memory overhead: each node has two pointers.
    • Poor cache locality.
  4. When to use: Implementing a queue or deque. Frequent insertion at head (e.g., prepend to a list repeatedly). Producer-consumer buffers where you add to one end and remove from the other.
  5. When to avoid: Any list where you access by index. Any list that will be iterated many times. Any list that will be displayed in a UI (use ArrayList).

In practice, LinkedList is rarely the right answer on Android. ArrayDeque is almost always preferable for queue and deque use cases because of its better cache locality and lower per-element overhead.

Under the hood

ArrayList wraps a single Object[] elementData. get(i) is a bounds check plus one array load. add at the end writes to the next slot until full, then grow() allocates a new array ~1.5× the old size and System.arraycopys everything over — amortized O(1), but each individual resize is O(n) and produces garbage. add(i, x) / remove(i) in the middle do an arraycopy to shift the tail, hence O(n). Because the array is contiguous, iterating it streams sequential memory the CPU prefetcher loves. LinkedList is a chain of Node objects, each holding the element plus prev and next references — so on a 64-bit ART runtime every element costs an extra object header (~16 bytes) plus two references, and get(i) walks the chain from whichever end is closer, dereferencing pointers that scatter across the heap and blow the cache. ArrayDeque sidesteps both: a circular Object[] with head/tail indices that wrap with & (length - 1) (capacity is always a power of two), giving O(1) at both ends with array locality and no node allocation — which is why it beats LinkedList for queues in practice.

ArrayList:  [a][b][c][d][_]   get(i)=O(1) load;  insert mid → arraycopy shift O(n)
LinkedList: a⇄b⇄c⇄d           get(i)=O(n) walk;  +header+2 refs per node, poor locality
ArrayDeque: circular array, head/tail & (len-1)  → O(1) both ends, contiguous

15.3 Legacy Code and Migration

When an interviewer asks about migration, what they are really asking is: can you drive a complex multi-month engineering project without stopping feature work, without breaking production, and while bringing the whole team along? Every answer here needs to demonstrate three things — discipline, incrementalism, and measurement.

Java to Kotlin

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "I treat Java-to-Kotlin as an incremental interop migration, never a big bang — Kotlin and Java compile to the same bytecode and call each other freely, so all new code is Kotlin and legacy files convert opportunistically when I'm already touching them. The trap is platform types: when Kotlin calls un-annotated Java it sees String!, which silently bypasses null checks, so I add @Nullable/@NonNull to the Java first, then convert. I prove it worked by watching the NPE rate in Sentry drop, not just by counting converted files."

Goal: Incrementally replace Java files with idiomatic Kotlin without breaking existing tests or callers.

Approach:

  1. Interop first: Kotlin and Java interop seamlessly. Start calling Kotlin from Java and vice

versa. No big-bang needed.

  1. IntelliJ auto-conversion: Use IntelliJ's "Convert Java file to Kotlin" as a starting point,

then review for idiomatic improvements (null safety, data classes, extension functions).

  1. Prioritize new code: All new files are written in Kotlin. Legacy Java is converted

opportunistically when touching a file for other reasons.

  1. Nullability contracts: Add @NonNull/@Nullable annotations to Java before converting.

Kotlin will respect them and emit correct null-safety checks.

  1. Platform types: Eliminate all ! (platform types) in converted code. Make nullability

explicit.

  1. Kotlin idioms: Replace if (x != null) x.foo() with x?.foo(). Replace getters with

properties. Use data classes where appropriate.

  1. Test coverage before and after: Run existing tests after conversion. Conversion should be

behavior-neutral.

Metrics to prove success:

  • % of files in Kotlin tracked over time.
  • NullPointerException rate in Sentry (should decrease as null safety improves).
  • Code review time per PR (should decrease as Kotlin is more concise).

Common pitfalls:

  • companion object vs top-level functions — prefer top-level unless the function is tied to

a class.

  • @JvmStatic, @JvmOverloads, @JvmField needed when Kotlin code is called from Java.
  • data class copy() misuse — the copy is shallow; mutable references inside are shared.

Under the hood

Both languages compile to JVM bytecode, then ART's dex compiler (d8/r8) lowers it to DEX, which is why interop is free — at the bytecode level a Kotlin class and a Java class are indistinguishable callers. Kotlin's null safety is mostly a compile-time fiction: the type system enforces String vs String?, but for a non-null parameter the compiler also injects a runtime Intrinsics.checkNotNullParameter(arg, "name") guard at the method entry, so a null sneaking in from Java fails fast with a clear message instead of a mysterious NPE later. Platform types (String!) arise because un-annotated Java carries no nullability metadata in its bytecode, so the compiler emits no check and trusts you — that's the silent hole the migration order closes. Annotations like @Nullable are read from the class file (or are recognized JSR-305/androidx.annotation markers) and flip the inferred Kotlin type to String?, forcing safe calls. The @Jvm* annotations are pure codegen directives: @JvmStatic emits a real static method (instead of routing through the synthetic Companion instance field), @JvmField suppresses the getter/setter and exposes a public field, and @JvmOverloads generates one bytecode method per default-parameter combination so Java callers — which have no concept of default arguments — can omit them.

Foo.java (no @Nullable) → bytecode has no null metadata → Kotlin sees String! (no check)
Foo.java (@Nullable)    → metadata in .class           → Kotlin sees String? (safe call forced)
fun f(x: String)        → compiler injects Intrinsics.checkNotNullParameter(x, "x")

XML to Compose

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "I migrate XML to Compose incrementally using the interop layer — ComposeView to drop Compose into an existing Fragment, or AndroidView to embed legacy views inside Compose, so I never have to do a big-bang rewrite. I write all new screens in Compose and pilot one simple, well-tested existing screen first. The gotcha interviewers love is the composition strategy: in a Fragment you must set ViewCompositionStrategy.DisposeOnViewTreeLifecycleDestroyed, otherwise the composition outlives the view and leaks."

Goal: Migrate screens from XML layouts to Jetpack Compose incrementally.

Approach:

  1. Interop layer: Use ComposeView inside an existing XML layout to embed Compose in a

Fragment. Use AndroidView inside Compose to embed XML views in Compose. Either direction works.

  1. Start with new screens: All new screens written in Compose.
  2. Pilot an existing screen: Choose a simple, well-covered screen. Replace its XML with

Compose. Keep the Fragment temporarily; it becomes a thin wrapper hosting ComposeView.

  1. Migrate Fragment to Composable function: Once the screen is Compose, the Fragment is

just a one-liner (setContent { ScreenComposable() }). Eventually the Fragment can be removed if navigation is migrated to NavController.

  1. Theme migration: Ensure MezzanineTheme (or the app's design system) is properly

integrated before migration (colors, typography, shapes).

  1. Remove XML files only after the Compose equivalent is shipped and stable.

Metrics:

  • % of screens in Compose tracked in a migration tracker.
  • Rendering frame times per screen (Compose should improve jank on complex screens).
  • Screenshot test parity (before/after visual comparison).
  • APK size delta (Compose adds ~1.5 MB to APK; acceptable for most apps).

Common pitfalls:

  • Missing LocalLifecycleOwner in Compose-in-Fragment setups (use ViewCompositionStrategy.DisposeOnViewTreeLifecycleDestroyed).
  • remember used incorrectly when rememberSaveable is needed for config change survival.
  • Recomposition storms from unstable lambdas (use remember for callbacks, stable data classes).

Under the hood

ComposeView is itself an AndroidView (a subclass of AbstractComposeView extends ViewGroup). When you call setContent, it lazily creates a Composition backed by a Recomposer running on the AndroidUiDispatcher (which ticks off the Choreographer frame callback). The Compose runtime builds a gap buffer "slot table" of your composables and an applier that emits LayoutNodes — not Android Views — so a Compose subtree renders into a single host View that draws directly onto the RenderNode/Canvas. AndroidView, going the other direction, wraps a real View in a LayoutNode via a ViewFactoryHolder and re-runs the update block on every recomposition that touches a read state. The composition strategy matters because the Composition holds references to the composable lambdas and their captured state; without disposing it on view destruction, the slot table and Recomposer registration keep the Fragment's view tree alive.

setContent { } ──► Composition (slot table) ──► Recomposer (AndroidUiDispatcher)
                                  │
                                  ▼
                          LayoutNode tree ──► RenderNode/Canvas (one host View)
ViewCompositionStrategy.DisposeOnViewTreeLifecycleDestroyed
   └─ observes ViewTreeLifecycleOwner → disposes Composition on DESTROYED

MVP to MVVM/MVI

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "I treat the existing View interface as a ready-made state contract: every showX() call maps to a field in a StateFlow<UiState>. I stand up a ViewModel in parallel, drain the Presenter's logic into it until the Presenter is just a thin bridge, then swap the View interface for a Compose screen and delete the Presenter. The thing interviewers probe is RxJava in the Presenter — I don't rip it out all at once; I bridge with kotlinx-coroutines-rx2 (await()/asFlow()) so I can migrate one subscription at a time."

Goal: Replace Presenter + View interface pattern with ViewModel + StateFlow, without stopping feature work.

Approach:

  1. Identify the Presenter contract: The View interface is already a contract. The Presenter

updates the View. Map each View.showX() call to a corresponding state field.

  1. Create a parallel ViewModel: The ViewModel replicates the Presenter's state logic in a

StateFlow<ScreenUiState>. Both Presenter and ViewModel exist simultaneously.

  1. Thin Presenter → ViewModel delegation: Gradually move logic from Presenter to ViewModel.

Presenter becomes a thin bridge that just calls ViewModel.

  1. Replace View interface with Compose: Once ViewModel has all logic, replace the XML

Fragment with a Compose screen observing ViewModel.uiState.

  1. Delete the Presenter and View interface.

Key challenge — RxJava in Presenter: Presenters often use RxJava. Migrate RxJava subscriptions to coroutines using rxObservable.asFlow() or Single.await() from kotlinx-coroutines-rx2. This lets you migrate incrementally — the interop layer translates.

Metrics:

  • Presenter files remaining (tracked in migration backlog).
  • Test coverage before and after (ViewModel tests should cover same paths as Presenter tests).

Under the hood

A ViewModel survives configuration changes because the ViewModelStore that holds it is retained across Activity recreation: ComponentActivity returns the store in onRetainNonConfigurationInstance(), so the same instance is rehydrated after a rotation rather than garbage-collected. viewModelScope is a lazily-created CoroutineScope whose Job is a SupervisorJob plus Dispatchers.Main.immediate; the framework calls scope.cancel() from clear() (which runs onCleared()), so coroutines die deterministically when the store is finally cleared. The kotlinx-coroutines-rx2 bridge works by adapting Rx's push-based callbacks to coroutine suspension: Single.await() registers a SingleObserver and resumes the suspended continuation in onSuccess/onError, while asFlow() wraps the Observable in a callbackFlow-style cold stream that subscribes on collection and disposes the Disposable on cancellation.

rotation ──► Activity destroyed ──► ViewModelStore retained (NonConfigurationInstance)
          └─► new Activity ──► same ViewModel, same StateFlow value replayed
Single.await(): suspend → SingleObserver.onSuccess(v) → continuation.resume(v)
Observable.asFlow(): collect → subscribe(); cancel → Disposable.dispose()

AsyncTask/RxJava to Coroutines

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "AsyncTask was deprecated in API 30 and the mapping is basically one-to-one — each task becomes a launch { withContext(IO) { } }, with the result handed back on Main automatically. For RxJava I lean on the kotlinx-coroutines-rx2 bridge and migrate leaf utilities first, working inward. The win interviewers want me to name is structured cancellation: instead of manually clearing a CompositeDisposable in onDestroy, the scope cancels in onCleared() and cancellation propagates to every child coroutine for free."

AsyncTask Migration:

AsyncTask is deprecated in API 30 and removed in API 33. Migration is straightforward:

// Before: AsyncTask
class FetchDataTask : AsyncTask<Void, Void, Result>() {
    override fun doInBackground(vararg p0: Void?) = fetchFromNetwork()
    override fun onPostExecute(result: Result) { updateUI(result) }
}

// After: coroutine in lifecycleScope
lifecycleScope.launch {
    val result = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { fetchFromNetwork() }
    updateUI(result) // back on Main
}

The mental model is one-to-one: each AsyncTask becomes one launch { withContext(IO) { } } block.

RxJava Migration:

Use kotlinx-coroutines-rx2 bridge:

  • Single<T>.await() → suspend fun T.
  • Observable<T>.asFlow() → Flow<T>.
  • Completable.await() → suspend fun Unit.

Migrate one subscription at a time. Start with leaf-level utilities that have no callers depending on Observable return types. Work inward.

Disposing subscriptions — moving to structured cancellation: Replace CompositeDisposable.clear() in onDestroy with simply letting the CoroutineScope cancel in onCleared(). Cancellation propagates automatically to all child coroutines.

Under the hood

suspend functions are compiled by the Kotlin compiler into a state machine via CPS (continuation-passing style): each suspension point becomes a label, and the function gets an extra Continuation parameter; locals that must survive a suspension are stored as fields on a generated ContinuationImpl rather than on the JVM stack. withContext(Dispatchers.IO) doesn't spawn a thread per call — it dispatches the continuation onto a shared, elastic thread pool (default 64 threads) and resumes back on the caller's dispatcher when the block returns. Structured cancellation works because every coroutine builder installs a Job into a parent-child tree in the CoroutineContext; cancelling the parent Job flips children to a cancelling state and a CancellationException is thrown at the next suspension point (cooperative cancellation). That's why dropping CompositeDisposable.clear() is safe: onCleared() calls viewModelScope's Job.cancel(), which walks the child Jobs and tears them down without manual bookkeeping.

suspend fun f() { a(); g(); b() }   // g() suspends
   ▼ compiler
class f$Continuation { int label; /* saved locals */ }
   label 0 ─► a(); call g(this) ─► returns COROUTINE_SUSPENDED
   (later) resumeWith(result) ─► label 1 ─► b()
Job tree:  viewModelScope.Job ──┬── launch{}.Job ── cancel propagates down
                                └── launch{}.Job

Introducing Dependency Injection

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "The real first step has nothing to do with Hilt — it's converting classes to constructor injection so they receive dependencies instead of building them, which you can do with zero framework. Then I add Hilt incrementally: @HiltAndroidApp on the Application, @AndroidEntryPoint on Activities and Fragments one at a time, @Inject constructor, and @Provides modules for third-party types. The risk an interviewer flags is that @HiltAndroidApp rewrites Application init and the whole graph is validated at compile time, so a single missing binding fails the build — which is actually the feature, not the bug."

Goal: Add Hilt (or Dagger) to a codebase that uses manual construction (e.g., MyClass(MyDep())).

Approach:

  1. Identify construction sites: Every new MyClass(...) or MyClass(...) in Activities,

Fragments, or ViewModels is a construction site to migrate.

  1. Extract constructor injection: Change classes to receive their dependencies via constructor

rather than constructing them internally. This is the key step and can be done without Hilt.

  1. Add Hilt incrementally:
    • Add @HiltAndroidApp to Application.
    • Add @AndroidEntryPoint to Activities and Fragments one by one.
    • Add @Inject constructor() to classes being injected.
    • Add @Module / @Provides for third-party classes.
  2. Migrate ViewModel injection: Add @HiltViewModel + @Inject constructor(). Remove

ViewModelFactory boilerplate.

  1. Test modules: Add @UninstallModules + fake @TestInstallIn modules for testing.

Risk: Adding @HiltAndroidApp changes Application initialization. Test thoroughly.

Under the hood

Hilt is an annotation processor (Dagger under the hood) that runs at compile time and generates the entire object graph as plain Java code — there is no runtime reflection. @HiltAndroidApp triggers generation of a Hilt_MyApplication base class plus the root ApplicationComponent/SingletonComponent; @AndroidEntryPoint generates a Hilt_MyActivity superclass that, in onCreate, calls into the generated component to perform field injection. Each @Inject constructor becomes a generated Factory class with a get() method, and @Provides methods become factory classes too; scoped bindings are wrapped in a double-check DoubleCheck provider for thread-safe lazy singletons. Because the whole graph is resolved and validated during kapt/ksp, a missing or duplicate binding is a compile error rather than a runtime crash — the cost is that Hilt adds an annotation-processing pass to your build.

@Inject constructor(dep: Dep)
   ▼ generated
MyClass_Factory implements Provider<MyClass> {
    get() = MyClass(depProvider.get())
}
@HiltAndroidApp ──► SingletonComponent (DAG) ──► component.inject(activity)
scoped binding ──► DoubleCheck.provider(factory)   // lazy, thread-safe singleton

Introducing Modularization

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "I start by carving out infrastructure modules — :core:network, :core:db, :core:ui — that have no circular dependencies, then write new features as :feature:X modules so existing code isn't reworked. I gate the structure with Dependency Guard to keep the graph acyclic, and extract existing features one at a time starting with the most isolated. The mistake interviewers want me to call out is splitting too aggressively: a module that doesn't shrink the recompile scope is pure Gradle overhead, so I always measure with a build scan before and after."

See also 15.1 Interview Angles — "How would you introduce modularization gradually?"

Step-by-step:

  1. Create :core:network, :core:db, :core:ui — pure infrastructure, no circular deps.
  2. Run a build scan (./gradlew build --scan) before and after each extraction to measure

improvement.

  1. Extract :feature:X for new features — no rework of existing code.
  2. Add Dependency Guard (com.dropbox.dependency-guard) — enforce no circular dependencies.
  3. Extract existing features one at a time, starting with the most isolated.
  4. Define :api:X interfaces for cross-feature contracts.

Common mistake: Extracting too many modules too fast. Each extracted module that doesn't reduce compile scope is just overhead. Measure before and after.

Under the hood

Gradle models the build as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of tasks; modularization helps because Gradle can schedule independent modules' compile tasks across worker processes in parallel and skip any module whose inputs are unchanged (UP-TO-DATE checks via input/output fingerprints, plus the build cache keyed on a hash of inputs). The compile-avoidance win comes from the ABI: with implementation dependencies, a change to a module's internal code that doesn't alter its public API (its compile-classpath fingerprint) won't invalidate downstream modules' compilation — only api dependencies leak types transitively and force wider recompiles. That's why a module split only pays off if it actually reduces the ABI surface that consumers see; otherwise you've added a project-configuration and dependency-resolution cost without buying any compile-avoidance.

:app ──► :feature:profile ──► :core:network (implementation)
                          └──► :core:db (implementation)
edit :core:network internals (ABI unchanged) ──► only :core:network recompiles
edit :core:network public API ──► consumers recompile
parallel: :feature:a and :feature:b compile concurrently (independent DAG nodes)

Reducing Build Time

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "I diagnose before I optimize — a --scan or --profile run tells me where the time goes: annotation processing, configuration, and how many tasks missed the cache. Then I go roughly in impact order: KAPT to KSP (often ~2x on Room/Hilt/Moshi), modularization for parallelism, build and configuration caching, and tightening api down to implementation. The nuance interviewers want is why KSP is faster — KAPT generates Java stubs and runs the full javac apt pipeline, whereas KSP reads Kotlin symbols directly, skipping that stub-generation round trip entirely."

Diagnosis first:

./gradlew assembleDebug --scan   # Gradle build scan
./gradlew assembleDebug --profile  # HTML profile report

The three metrics to look for are annotation processing time, configuration time, and the number of tasks that were not up-to-date — those last ones tell you exactly how much incremental caching is being wasted.

Strategies (roughly ordered by impact):

  1. Migrate KAPT → KSP: KSP is 2x faster for most annotation processors (Room, Moshi, Hilt).
  2. Modularization: Parallel builds; only changed modules recompile.
  3. Avoid transitive api dependencies: Use implementation unless the type is in the public API.
  4. Build caching: org.gradle.caching=true in gradle.properties. Use remote build cache

(Gradle Enterprise or custom) in CI.

  1. Configuration cache: org.gradle.configuration-cache=true (Gradle 8+).
  2. Incremental annotation processing: Ensure all annotation processors support incremental mode.
  3. Avoid @JvmStatic + @JvmOverloads overuse — generates extra methods.
  4. Reduce unused dependencies: Run Dependency Analysis Gradle Plugin to find unused deps.
  5. R8 full mode in debug: Speeds up debug build dex step (trade-off: slower first build, faster incremental).
  6. Avoid resource merging overhead: Keep resources in the correct module; do not put all resources in :app.

Measurement: Track ./gradlew assembleDebug time in CI over time. Set a regression budget (e.g., max 10% increase per PR).

Under the hood

KAPT works by running the Kotlin compiler in "stub generation" mode: it produces Java source stubs for your Kotlin classes (signatures only, bodies stripped), then hands those stubs to the standard javac annotation-processing API (javax.annotation.processing.Processor). That stub round trip is the expensive part. KSP instead exposes a Kotlin-native symbol API resolved from the compiler's frontend, so processors read KSClassDeclaration/KSFunctionDeclaration directly without ever generating Java stubs — eliminating an entire compile pass. The build cache is content-addressed: each task's inputs (source files, classpath, args) are hashed into a cache key, and a hit copies the prior outputs instead of executing the task; the configuration cache goes further by serializing the configured task graph to disk so Gradle can skip the configuration phase entirely on subsequent runs. implementation vs api plugs into Gradle's compile-avoidance: only api exposes a dependency on the consumer's compile classpath, so dropping to implementation shrinks the classpath fingerprint that triggers downstream recompilation.

KAPT:  .kt ──► Kotlin compiler (stub mode) ──► .java stubs ──► javac apt ──► generated code
KSP:   .kt ──► KSP symbol API (frontend) ─────────────────► generated code   (no stubs)
build cache key = hash(inputs) ──► hit? copy outputs : run task
config cache = serialized task graph ──► skip configuration phase on reuse

Removing Memory Leaks

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "A memory leak on Android almost always means something with a short lifecycle — an Activity, a View, a Fragment's context — is being held by something with a longer lifecycle, so GC can't reclaim it. The usual culprits are static fields, un-unregistered listeners, and inner classes or lambdas that implicitly capture the outer this. My process is: let LeakCanary catch it in debug, fix the retention path, then write a leak-assert test so CI prevents the regression. The nuance interviewers probe is that a leak isn't a crash — it's slow heap growth that eventually causes an OutOfMemoryError somewhere unrelated, which is why you triage by retained-object graph, not by stack trace."

Detection:

  • LeakCanary: mandatory in debug builds. Every new leak generates a LeakCanary notification.
  • Sentry: track OutOfMemoryError events.
  • Android Studio Profiler: heap dumps to find retained objects.

Common sources and fixes:

Source Fix
Activity/Fragment in a static fieldNever store Context in static fields. Use WeakReference if unavoidable.
Registered listener not unregisteredRegister in onStart, unregister in onStop.
Handler with anonymous RunnableUse Handler(Looper.getMainLooper()) + remove callbacks in onDestroy.
Anonymous class/lambda capturing outer classUse a named class or WeakReference.
ViewModel holding View/Context referenceViewModels must not hold View or Activity references. Use Application context if needed.
Bitmap not recycled (pre-API 26)Use Glide/Coil which manage bitmap lifecycle.
Subscription not disposedUse CoroutineScope.cancel() or CompositeDisposable.clear().
registerReceiver without unregisterReceiverRegister in onResume/onStart, unregister in matching lifecycle method.

Process:

  1. Fix leak identified by LeakCanary.
  2. Write a test that detects the leak (using LeakCanary's LeakAssert).
  3. Run the test in CI to prevent regression.

Under the hood

LeakCanary works by installing ObjectWatcher hooks (via androidx.lifecycle and Application.ActivityLifecycleCallbacks) that wrap destroyed Activities/Fragments in a KeyedWeakReference registered against a ReferenceQueue. After the watched object is destroyed it triggers a GC and checks whether the weak reference was enqueued; if the reference is still live after GC, the object leaked. It then dumps the heap (.hprof) and runs Shark, which parses the hprof and computes the shortest strong reference path from a GC root to the leaked object — that path is the leak trace. The "inner class captures outer this" leak is real at the bytecode level: the Kotlin/Java compiler synthesizes a hidden field (e.g. this$0) on the anonymous/inner class holding the enclosing instance, so a Runnable posted to a Handler keeps the Activity reachable through the Message.callback → synthetic field chain until the message is dispatched or removed.

GC Root (e.g. static field / thread / Message in MessageQueue)
   └─> SomeManager.listener
        └─> AnonymousRunnable.this$0   (synthetic captured reference)
             └─> MainActivity          ← destroyed but still reachable = LEAK

Improving Test Coverage

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "I treat coverage as a risk-prioritization tool, not a target in itself. I measure the baseline with JaCoCo, then attack the bottom — but weighted by churn and complexity, because a high-churn, high-complexity class with low coverage is where bugs actually ship. I add a failing test with every bug fix, write tests before refactoring, and ratchet a CI coverage gate upward so it can't backslide. The gotcha interviewers love is that coverage measures lines executed, not assertions made — you can hit 90% coverage with tests that assert nothing, so I emphasize testing behavior at boundaries over chasing the percentage."

Approach:

  1. Measure current state: Run ./gradlew testWithCoverage. Generate JaCoCo report. Find

the bottom 20% (files with < 20% coverage).

  1. Prioritize by risk: Focus on high-churn, high-complexity classes with low coverage first.

Use git log --numstat to identify high-churn files.

  1. Add tests when fixing bugs: Every bug fix must include a failing test that proves the bug.
  2. Add tests when refactoring: Refactoring without tests is dangerous. Write tests first,

then refactor.

  1. Coverage gates: Add a JaCoCo coverage gate in CI (jacocoTestCoverageVerification).

Set minimum coverage (e.g., 70%) per module. Ratchet it up over time.

  1. Testing pyramid:
    • 70% unit tests (fast, cheap)
    • 20% integration tests (medium)
    • 10% UI/E2E tests (slow, fragile)
  2. Mock at boundaries: MockK for external dependencies. Fake implementations for internal

boundaries.

Common coverage antipatterns:

  • Testing implementation details (test behavior, not internals).
  • Testing only the happy path (add error and edge cases).
  • Brittle tests that test too much at once.

Under the hood

JaCoCo measures coverage through on-the-fly bytecode instrumentation: a Java agent (or Gradle transform) modifies class bytecode as it's loaded, injecting probes — boolean array writes — at the boundaries of basic blocks (the straight-line code segments between jump/branch instructions). Each probe records that a block executed. At the end of the run JaCoCo maps these probe hits back to source lines and branches using the LineNumberTable and the control-flow graph it built from the bytecode, producing line, branch, and instruction coverage. This is exactly why coverage measures execution, not verification — a probe fires when a line runs regardless of whether any assertion observed the result. Branch coverage counts how many of the conditional jump targets (the if_icmpne/ifnull-style opcodes) were taken in both directions, which is why a method with an untested else shows partial branch coverage even at 100% line coverage.

bytecode basic blocks → JaCoCo inserts probes (boolean[] writes)
  block A [probe 0] ──true──> block B [probe 1]
                    └─false─> block C [probe 2]   ← if probe 2 never set, the else branch is uncovered

Stabilizing Crashy Features

🎤 Say it out loud (~30–45s): "My first move on a crashy feature is to stop the bleeding and then fix the root cause. I triage Sentry by root-cause grouping and sort by users-affected, not raw event count, because one crash hitting ten thousand users beats one user crashing ten thousand times. If a feature is over a 1% crash rate I kill it with a flag immediately, then reproduce, fix conservatively with null-safety and fallbacks, and add a targeted test plus a Sentry alert on that grouping. The nuance interviewers want is reproducibility-first — if I can't reproduce it I can't prove the fix worked, so I add breadcrumb logging before the crash site to capture the missing context."

Framework for investigating and fixing crashes:

  1. Triage: Group Sentry events by root cause, not by crash type. Sort by volume × user impact.
  2. Reproduce: Every crash must be reproducible before fixing. If you can't reproduce, you

can't verify the fix.

  1. Add logging: Add ZLog.logErrorWithTeamTag() breadcrumbs before the crash site to capture

context.

  1. Fix conservatively: Add null checks, default values, and fallback states rather than

aggressive refactors. The goal is stability, not elegance.

  1. Feature flag: If a feature is causing 1%+ crash rate, flag it off immediately.
  2. Test the fix: Unit test the specific crash scenario. Integration test the flow.
  3. Monitor after fix: Set a Sentry alert for the specific crash grouping. Verify crash rate

drops in the next 24-48 hours after rollout.

Common crash types:

Type Fix
NPE on API response fieldAdd null-safety; use nullable types; default values for missing fields.
ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsExceptionBounds check before access; guard adapter positions.
IllegalStateException in FragmentCheck isAdded() before using requireContext().
ClassCastException in RecyclerViewVerify viewType in onCreateViewHolder/onBindViewHolder.
SQLiteExceptionValidate SQL migrations; test DB upgrade paths in unit tests.
ANRMove I/O off main thread; use StrictMode in debug to catch violations early.

Under the hood

A crash on Android is an uncaught exception propagating to the thread's UncaughtExceptionHandler. ART installs a default handler that calls into RuntimeInit, which logs the trace to logcat and asks ActivityManager to kill the process; crash reporters like Sentry/Crashlytics work by installing their own Thread.setDefaultUncaughtExceptionHandler that captures the throwable (and breadcrumbs buffered in a ring) before chaining to the original handler.
